1.1: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc'd by fate,
1.3: Expell'd and exil'd, left the Trojan shore.
1.4: Long labors, both by sea and land, he bore,
1.5: And in the doubtful war, before he won
1.6: The Latian realm, and built the destin'd town;
1.7: His banish'd gods restor'd to rites divine,
1.8: And settled sure succession in his line,
1.9: From whence the race of Alban fathers come,
1.10: And the long glories of majestic Rome.
1.11: O Muse! the causes and the crimes relate;
1.12: What goddess was provok'd, and whence her hate;
1.13: For what offense the Queen of Heav'n began
1.14: To persecute so brave, so just a man;
1.15: Involv'd his anxious life in endless cares,
1.16: Expos'd to wants, and hurried into wars!
1.17: Can heav'nly minds such high resentment show,
1.18: Or exercise their spite in human woe?
1.19: Against the Tiber's mouth, but far away,
1.20: An ancient town was seated on the sea;
1.21: A Tyrian colony; the people made
1.22: Stout for the war, and studious of their trade:
1.23: Carthage the name; belov'd by Juno more
1.24: Than her own Argos, or the Samian shore.
1.25: Here stood her chariot; here, if Heav'n were kind,
1.26: The seat of awful empire she design'd.
1.27: Yet she had heard an ancient rumor fly,
1.28: (Long cited by the people of the sky,)
1.29: That times to come should see the Trojan race
1.30: Her Carthage ruin, and her tow'rs deface;
1.31: Nor thus confin'd, the yoke of sov'reign sway
1.32: Should on the necks of all the nations lay.
1.33: She ponder'd this, and fear'd it was in fate;
1.34: Nor could forget the war she wag'd of late
1.35: For conqu'ring Greece against the Trojan state.
1.36: Besides, long causes working in her mind,
1.37: And secret seeds of envy, lay behind;
1.38: Deep graven in her heart the doom remain'd
1.39: Of partial Paris, and her form disdain'd;
1.40: The grace bestow'd on ravish'd Ganymed,
1.41: Electra's glories, and her injur'd bed.
1.42: Each was a cause alone; and all combin'd
1.43: To kindle vengeance in her haughty mind.
1.44: For this, far distant from the Latian coast
1.45: She drove the remnants of the Trojan host;
1.46: And sev'n long years th' unhappy wand'ring train
1.47: Were toss'd by storms, and scatter'd thro' the main.
1.48: Such time, such toil, requir'd the Roman name,
1.49: Such length of labor for so vast a frame.
1.50: Now scarce the Trojan fleet, with sails and oars,
1.51: Had left behind the fair Sicilian shores,
1.52: Ent'ring with cheerful shouts the wat'ry reign,
1.53: And plowing frothy furrows in the main;
1.54: When, lab'ring still with endless discontent,
1.55: The Queen of Heav'n did thus her fury vent:
1.56: "Then am I vanquish'd? must I yield?" said she,
1.57: "And must the Trojans reign in Italy?
1.58: So Fate will have it, and Jove adds his force;
1.59: Nor can my pow'r divert their happy course.
1.60: Could angry Pallas, with revengeful spleen,
1.61: The Grecian navy burn, and drown the men?
1.62: She, for the fault of one offending foe,
1.63: The bolts of Jove himself presum'd to throw:
1.64: With whirlwinds from beneath she toss'd the ship,
1.65: And bare expos'd the bosom of the deep;
1.66: Then, as an eagle gripes the trembling game,
1.67: The wretch, yet hissing with her father's flame,
1.68: She strongly seiz'd, and with a burning wound
1.69: Transfix'd, and naked, on a rock she bound.
1.70: But I, who walk in awful state above,
1.71: The majesty of heav'n, the sister wife of Jove,
1.72: For length of years my fruitless force employ
1.73: Against the thin remains of ruin'd Troy!
1.74: What nations now to Juno's pow'r will pray,
1.75: Or off'rings on my slighted altars lay?"
1.76: Thus rag'd the goddess; and, with fury fraught.
1.77: The restless regions of the storms she sought,
1.78: Where, in a spacious cave of living stone,
1.79: The tyrant Aeolus, from his airy throne,
1.80: With pow'r imperial curbs the struggling winds,
1.81: And sounding tempests in dark prisons binds.
1.82: This way and that th' impatient captives tend,
1.83: And, pressing for release, the mountains rend.
1.84: High in his hall th' undaunted monarch stands,
1.85: And shakes his scepter, and their rage commands;
1.86: Which did he not, their unresisted sway
1.87: Would sweep the world before them in their way;
1.88: Earth, air, and seas thro' empty space would roll,
1.89: And heav'n would fly before the driving soul.
1.90: In fear of this, the Father of the Gods
1.91: Confin'd their fury to those dark abodes,
1.92: And lock'd 'em safe within, oppress'd with mountain
1.93: Impos'd a king, with arbitrary sway,
1.94: To loose their fetters, or their force allay.
1.95: To whom the suppliant queen her pray'rs address'd,
1.96: And thus the tenor of her suit express'd:
1.97: "O Aeolus! for to thee the King of Heav'n
1.98: The pow'r of tempests and of winds has giv'n;
1.99: Thy force alone their fury can restrain,
1.100: And smooth the waves, or swell the troubled main-
1.101: A race of wand'ring slaves, abhorr'd by me,
1.102: With prosp'rous passage cut the Tuscan sea;
1.103: To fruitful Italy their course they steer,
1.104: And for their vanquish'd gods design new temples
1.105: Raise all thy winds; with night involve the skies;
1.106: Sink or disperse my fatal enemies.
1.107: Twice sev'n, the charming daughters of the main,
1.108: Around my person wait, and bear my train:
1.109: Succeed my wish, and second my design;
1.110: The fairest, Deiopeia, shall be thine,
1.111: And make thee father of a happy line."
1.112: To this the god: "'T is yours, O queen, to will
1.113: The work which duty binds me to fulfil.
1.114: These airy kingdoms, and this wide command,
1.115: Are all the presents of your bounteous hand:
1.116: Yours is my sov'reign's grace; and, as your guest,
1.117: I sit with gods at their celestial feast;
1.118: Raise tempests at your pleasure, or subdue;
1.119: Dispose of empire, which I hold from you."
1.120: He said, and hurl'd against the mountain side
1.121: His quiv'ring spear, and all the god applied.
1.122: The raging winds rush thro' the hollow wound,
1.123: And dance aloft in air, and skim along the ground;
1.124: Then, settling on the sea, the surges sweep,
1.125: Raise liquid mountains, and disclose the deep.
1.126: South, East, and West with mix'd confusion roar,
1.127: And roll the foaming billows to the shore.
1.128: The cables crack; the sailors' fearful cries
1.129: Ascend; and sable night involves the skies;
1.130: And heav'n itself is ravish'd from their eyes.
1.131: Loud peals of thunder from the poles ensue;
1.132: Then flashing fires the transient light renew;
1.133: The face of things a frightful image bears,
1.134: And present death in various forms appears.
1.135: Struck with unusual fright, the Trojan chief,
1.136: With lifted hands and eyes, invokes relief;
1.137: And, "Thrice and four times happy those," he cried,
1.138: "That under Ilian walls before their parents died!
1.139: Tydides, bravest of the Grecian train!
1.140: Why could not I by that strong arm be slain,
1.141: And lie by noble Hector on the plain,
1.142: Or great Sarpedon, in those bloody fields
1.143: Where Simois rolls the bodies and the shields
1.144: Of heroes, whose dismember'd hands yet bear
1.145: The dart aloft, and clench the pointed spear!"
1.146: Thus while the pious prince his fate bewails,
1.147: Fierce Boreas drove against his flying sails,
1.148: And rent the sheets; the raging billows rise,
1.149: And mount the tossing vessels to the skies:
1.150: Nor can the shiv'ring oars sustain the blow;
1.151: The galley gives her side, and turns her prow;
1.152: While those astern, descending down the steep,
1.153: Thro' gaping waves behold the boiling deep.
1.154: Three ships were hurried by the southern blast,
1.155: And on the secret shelves with fury cast.
1.156: Those hidden rocks th' Ausonian sailors knew:
1.157: They call'd them Altars, when they rose in view,
1.158: And show'd their spacious backs above the flood.
1.159: Three more fierce Eurus, in his angry mood,
1.160: Dash'd on the shallows of the moving sand,
1.161: And in mid ocean left them moor'd aland.
1.162: Orontes' bark, that bore the Lycian crew,
1.163: (A horrid sight!) ev'n in the hero's view,
1.164: From stem to stern by waves was overborne:
1.165: The trembling pilot, from his rudder torn,
1.166: Was headlong hurl'd; thrice round the ship was toss'd,
1.167: Then bulg'd at once, and in the deep was lost;
1.168: And here and there above the waves were seen
1.169: Arms, pictures, precious goods, and floating men.
1.170: The stoutest vessel to the storm gave way,
1.171: And suck'd thro' loosen'd planks the rushing sea.
1.172: Ilioneus was her chief: Alethes old,
1.173: Achates faithful, Abas young and bold,
1.174: Endur'd not less; their ships, with gaping seams,
1.175: Admit the deluge of the briny streams.
1.176: Meantime imperial Neptune heard the sound
1.177: Of raging billows breaking on the ground.
1.178: Displeas'd, and fearing for his wat'ry reign,
1.179: He rear'd his awful head above the main,
1.180: Serene in majesty; then roll'd his eyes
1.181: Around the space of earth, and seas, and skies.
1.182: He saw the Trojan fleet dispers'd, distress'd,
1.183: By stormy winds and wintry heav'n oppress'd.
1.184: Full well the god his sister's envy knew,
1.185: And what her aims and what her arts pursue.
1.186: He summon'd Eurus and the western blast,
1.187: And first an angry glance on both he cast;
1.188: Then thus rebuk'd: "Audacious winds! from whence
1.189: This bold attempt, this rebel insolence?
1.190: Is it for you to ravage seas and land,
1.192: To raise such mountains on the troubled main?
1.193: Whom I- but first 't is fit the billows to restrain;
1.194: And then you shall be taught obedience to my reign.
1.195: Hence! to your lord my royal mandate bear-
1.196: The realms of ocean and the fields of air
1.197: Are mine, not his. By fatal lot to me
1.198: The liquid empire fell, and trident of the sea.
1.199: His pow'r to hollow caverns is confin'd:
1.200: There let him reign, the jailer of the wind,
1.201: With hoarse commands his breathing subjects call,
1.202: And boast and bluster in his empty hall."
1.203: He spoke; and, while he spoke, he smooth'd the sea,
1.204: Dispell'd the darkness, and restor'd the day.
1.205: Cymothoe, Triton, and the sea-green train
1.206: Of beauteous nymphs, the daughters of the main,
1.207: Clear from the rocks the vessels with their hands:
1.208: The god himself with ready trident stands,
1.209: And opes the deep, and spreads the moving sands;
1.210: Then heaves them off the shoals. Where'er he guides
1.211: His finny coursers and in triumph rides,
1.212: The waves unruffle and the sea subsides.
1.213: As, when in tumults rise th' ignoble crowd,
1.214: Mad are their motions, and their tongues are loud;
1.215: And stones and brands in rattling volleys fly,
1.216: And all the rustic arms that fury can supply:
1.217: If then some grave and pious man appear,
1.218: They hush their noise, and lend a list'ning ear;
1.219: He soothes with sober words their angry mood,
1.220: And quenches their innate desire of blood:
1.221: So, when the Father of the Flood appears,
1.222: And o'er the seas his sov'reign trident rears,
1.223: Their fury falls: he skims the liquid plains,
1.224: High on his chariot, and, with loosen'd reins,
1.225: Majestic moves along, and awful peace maintains.
1.226: The weary Trojans ply their shatter'd oars
1.227: To nearest land, and make the Libyan shores.
1.228: Within a long recess there lies a bay:
1.229: An island shades it from the rolling sea,
1.230: And forms a port secure for ships to ride;
1.231: Broke by the jutting land, on either side,
1.232: In double streams the briny waters glide.
1.233: Betwixt two rows of rocks a sylvan scene
1.234: Appears above, and groves for ever green:
1.235: A grot is form'd beneath, with mossy seats,
1.236: To rest the Nereids, and exclude the heats.
1.237: Down thro' the crannies of the living walls
1.238: The crystal streams descend in murm'ring falls:
1.239: No haulsers need to bind the vessels here,
1.240: Nor bearded anchors; for no storms they fear.
1.241: Sev'n ships within this happy harbor meet,
1.242: The thin remainders of the scatter'd fleet.
1.243: The Trojans, worn with toils, and spent with woes,
1.244: Leap on the welcome land, and seek their wish'd
1.245: First, good Achates, with repeated strokes
1.246: Of clashing flints, their hidden fire provokes:
1.247: Short flame succeeds; a bed of wither'd leaves
1.248: The dying sparkles in their fall receives:
1.249: Caught into life, in fiery fumes they rise,
1.250: And, fed with stronger food, invade the skies.
1.251: The Trojans, dropping wet, or stand around
1.252: The cheerful blaze, or lie along the ground:
1.253: Some dry their corn, infected with the brine,
1.254: Then grind with marbles, and prepare to dine.
1.255: Aeneas climbs the mountain's airy brow,
1.256: And takes a prospect of the seas below,
1.257: If Capys thence, or Antheus he could spy,
1.258: Or see the streamers of Caicus fly.
1.259: No vessels were in view; but, on the plain,
1.260: Three beamy stags command a lordly train
1.261: Of branching heads: the more ignoble throng
1.262: Attend their stately steps, and slowly graze along.
1.263: He stood; and, while secure they fed below,
1.264: He took the quiver and the trusty bow
1.265: Achates us'd to bear: the leaders first
1.266: He laid along, and then the vulgar pierc'd;
1.267: Nor ceas'd his arrows, till the shady plain
1.268: Sev'n mighty bodies with their blood distain.
1.269: For the sev'n ships he made an equal share,
1.270: And to the port return'd, triumphant from the war.
1.271: The jars of gen'rous wine (Acestes' gift,
1.272: When his Trinacrian shores the navy left)
1.273: He set abroach, and for the feast prepar'd,
1.274: In equal portions with the ven'son shar'd.
1.275: Thus while he dealt it round, the pious chief
1.276: With cheerful words allay'd the common grief:
1.277: "Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose
1.278: To future good our past and present woes.
1.279: With me, the rocks of Scylla you have tried;
1.280: Th' inhuman Cyclops and his den defied.
1.281: What greater ills hereafter can you bear?
1.282: Resume your courage and dismiss your care,
1.283: An hour will come, with pleasure to relate
1.284: Your sorrows past, as benefits of Fate.
1.285: Thro' various hazards and events, we move
1.286: To Latium and the realms foredoom'd by Jove.
1.287: Call'd to the seat (the promise of the skies)
1.288: Where Trojan kingdoms once again may rise,
1.289: Endure the hardships of your present state;
1.290: Live, and reserve yourselves for better fate."
1.291: These words he spoke, but spoke not from his heart;
1.292: His outward smiles conceal'd his inward smart.
1.293: The jolly crew, unmindful of the past,
1.294: The quarry share, their plenteous dinner haste.
1.295: Some strip the skin; some portion out the spoil;
1.296: The limbs, yet trembling, in the caldrons boil;
1.297: Some on the fire the reeking entrails broil.
1.298: Stretch'd on the grassy turf, at ease they dine,
1.299: Restore their strength with meat, and cheer their souls with
1.300: Their hunger thus appeas'd, their care attends
1.301: The doubtful fortune of their absent friends:
1.302: Alternate hopes and fears their minds possess,
1.303: Whether to deem 'em dead, or in distress.
1.304: Above the rest, Aeneas mourns the fate
1.305: Of brave Orontes, and th' uncertain state
1.306: Of Gyas, Lycus, and of Amycus.
1.307: The day, but not their sorrows, ended thus.
1.308: When, from aloft, almighty Jove surveys
1.309: Earth, air, and shores, and navigable seas,
1.310: At length on Libyan realms he fix'd his eyes-
1.311: Whom, pond'ring thus on human miseries,
1.312: When Venus saw, she with a lowly look,
1.313: Not free from tears, her heav'nly sire bespoke:
1.314: "O King of Gods and Men! whose awful hand
1.315: Disperses thunder on the seas and land,
1.317: How could my pious son thy pow'r incense?
1.318: Or what, alas! is vanish'd Troy's offense?
1.319: Our hope of Italy not only lost,
1.320: On various seas by various tempests toss'd,
1.321: But shut from ev'ry shore, and barr'd from ev'ry
1.322: You promis'd once, a progeny divine
1.323: Of Romans, rising from the Trojan line,
1.324: In after times should hold the world in awe,
1.325: And to the land and ocean give the law.
1.326: How is your doom revers'd, which eas'd my care
1.327: When Troy was ruin'd in that cruel war?
1.328: Then fates to fates I could oppose; but now,
1.329: When Fortune still pursues her former blow,
1.330: What can I hope? What worse can still succeed?
1.331: What end of labors has your will decreed?
1.332: Antenor, from the midst of Grecian hosts,
1.333: Could pass secure, and pierce th' Illyrian coasts,
1.334: Where, rolling down the steep, Timavus raves
1.335: And thro' nine channels disembogues his waves.
1.336: At length he founded Padua's happy seat,
1.337: And gave his Trojans a secure retreat;
1.338: There fix'd their arms, and there renew'd their
1.339: And there in quiet rules, and crown'd with fame.
1.340: But we, descended from your sacred line,
1.341: Entitled to your heav'n and rites divine,
1.342: Are banish'd earth; and, for the wrath of one,
1.343: Remov'd from Latium and the promis'd throne.
1.344: Are these our scepters? these our due rewards?
1.345: And is it thus that Jove his plighted faith regards?"
1.346: To whom the Father of th' immortal race,
1.347: Smiling with that serene indulgent face,
1.348: With which he drives the clouds and clears the skies,
1.349: First gave a holy kiss; then thus replies:
1.350: "Daughter, dismiss thy fears; to thy desire
1.351: The fates of thine are fix'd, and stand entire.
1.352: Thou shalt behold thy wish'd Lavinian walls;
1.353: And, ripe for heav'n, when fate Aeneas calls,
1.354: Then shalt thou bear him up, sublime, to me:
1.355: No councils have revers'd my firm decree.
1.356: And, lest new fears disturb thy happy state,
1.357: Know, I have search'd the mystic rolls of Fate:
1.358: Thy son (nor is th' appointed season far)
1.359: In Italy shall wage successful war,
1.360: Shall tame fierce nations in the bloody field,
1.361: And sov'reign laws impose, and cities build,
1.362: Till, after ev'ry foe subdued, the sun
1.363: Thrice thro' the signs his annual race shall run:
1.364: This is his time prefix'd. Ascanius then,
1.365: Now call'd Iulus, shall begin his reign.
1.366: He thirty rolling years the crown shall wear,
1.367: Then from Lavinium shall the seat transfer,
1.368: And, with hard labor, Alba Longa build.
1.369: The throne with his succession shall be fill'd
1.370: Three hundred circuits more: then shall be seen
1.371: Ilia the fair, a priestess and a queen,
1.372: Who, full of Mars, in time, with kindly throes,
1.373: Shall at a birth two goodly boys disclose.
1.374: The royal babes a tawny wolf shall drain:
1.375: Then Romulus his grandsire's throne shall gain,
1.376: Of martial tow'rs the founder shall become,
1.377: The people Romans call, the city Rome.
1.378: To them no bounds of empire I assign,
1.379: Nor term of years to their immortal line.
1.380: Ev'n haughty Juno, who, with endless broils,
1.381: Earth, seas, and heav'n, and Jove himself turmoils;
1.382: At length aton'd, her friendly pow'r shall join,
1.383: To cherish and advance the Trojan line.
1.384: The subject world shall Rome's dominion own,
1.385: And, prostrate, shall adore the nation of the gown.
1.386: An age is ripening in revolving fate
1.387: When Troy shall overturn the Grecian state,
1.388: And sweet revenge her conqu'ring sons shall call,
1.389: To crush the people that conspir'd her fall.
1.390: Then Caesar from the Julian stock shall rise,
1.391: Whose empire ocean, and whose fame the skies
1.392: Alone shall bound; whom, fraught with eastern spoils,
1.393: Our heav'n, the just reward of human toils,
1.394: Securely shall repay with rites divine;
1.395: And incense shall ascend before his sacred shrine.
1.396: Then dire debate and impious war shall cease,
1.397: And the stern age be soften'd into peace:
1.398: Then banish'd Faith shall once again return,
1.399: And Vestal fires in hallow'd temples burn;
1.400: And Remus with Quirinus shall sustain
1.401: The righteous laws, and fraud and force restrain.
1.402: Janus himself before his fane shall wait,
1.403: And keep the dreadful issues of his gate,
1.404: With bolts and iron bars: within remains
1.405: Imprison'd Fury, bound in brazen chains;
1.406: High on a trophy rais'd, of useless arms,
1.407: He sits, and threats the world with vain alarms."
1.408: He said, and sent Cyllenius with command
1.409: To free the ports, and ope the Punic land
1.410: To Trojan guests; lest, ignorant of fate,
1.411: The queen might force them from her town and state.
1.412: Down from the steep of heav'n Cyllenius flies,
1.413: And cleaves with all his wings the yielding skies.
1.414: Soon on the Libyan shore descends the god,
1.415: Performs his message, and displays his rod:
1.416: The surly murmurs of the people cease;
1.417: And, as the fates requir'd, they give the peace:
1.418: The queen herself suspends the rigid laws,
1.419: The Trojans pities, and protects their cause.
1.420: Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
1.421: Care seiz'd his soul, and sleep forsook his eyes.
1.422: But, when the sun restor'd the cheerful day,
1.423: He rose, the coast and country to survey,
1.424: Anxious and eager to discover more.
1.425: It look'd a wild uncultivated shore;
1.426: But, whether humankind, or beasts alone
1.427: Possess'd the new-found region, was unknown.
1.428: Beneath a ledge of rocks his fleet he hides:
1.429: Tall trees surround the mountain's shady sides;
1.430: The bending brow above a safe retreat provides.
1.431: Arm'd with two pointed darts, he leaves his friends,
1.432: And true Achates on his steps attends.
1.433: Lo! in the deep recesses of the wood,
1.434: Before his eyes his goddess mother stood:
1.435: A huntress in her habit and her mien;
1.436: Her dress a maid, her air confess'd a queen.
1.437: Bare were her knees, and knots her garments bind;
1.438: Loose was her hair, and wanton'd in the wind;
1.439: Her hand sustain'd a bow; her quiver hung behind.
1.440: She seem'd a virgin of the Spartan blood:
1.442: Her Thracian courser and outstripp'd the rapid flood.
1.443: "Ho, strangers! have you lately seen," she said,
1.444: "One of my sisters, like myself array'd,
1.445: Who cross'd the lawn, or in the forest stray'd?
1.446: A painted quiver at her back she bore;
1.447: Varied with spots, a lynx's hide she wore;
1.448: And at full cry pursued the tusky boar."
1.449: Thus Venus: thus her son replied again:
1.450: "None of your sisters have we heard or seen,
1.451: O virgin! or what other name you bear
1.452: Above that style- O more than mortal fair!
1.453: Your voice and mien celestial birth betray!
1.454: If, as you seem, the sister of the day,
1.455: Or one at least of chaste Diana's train,
1.456: Let not an humble suppliant sue in vain;
1.457: But tell a stranger, long in tempests toss'd,
1.458: What earth we tread, and who commands the coast?
1.459: Then on your name shall wretched mortals call,
1.460: And offer'd victims at your altars fall."
1.461: "I dare not," she replied, "assume the name
1.462: Of goddess, or celestial honors claim:
1.463: For Tyrian virgins bows and quivers bear,
1.464: And purple buskins o'er their ankles wear.
1.465: Know, gentle youth, in Libyan lands you are-
1.466: A people rude in peace, and rough in war.
1.467: The rising city, which from far you see,
1.468: Is Carthage, and a Tyrian colony.
1.469: Phoenician Dido rules the growing state,
1.470: Who fled from Tyre, to shun her brother's hate.
1.471: Great were her wrongs, her story full of fate;
1.472: Which I will sum in short. Sichaeus, known
1.473: For wealth, and brother to the Punic throne,
1.474: Possess'd fair Dido's bed; and either heart
1.475: At once was wounded with an equal dart.
1.476: Her father gave her, yet a spotless maid;
1.477: Pygmalion then the Tyrian scepter sway'd:
1.478: One who condemn'd divine and human laws.
1.479: Then strife ensued, and cursed gold the cause.
1.480: The monarch, blinded with desire of wealth,
1.481: With steel invades his brother's life by stealth;
1.482: Before the sacred altar made him bleed,
1.483: And long from her conceal'd the cruel deed.
1.484: Some tale, some new pretense, he daily coin'd,
1.485: To soothe his sister, and delude her mind.
1.486: At length, in dead of night, the ghost appears
1.487: Of her unhappy lord: the specter stares,
1.488: And, with erected eyes, his bloody bosom bares.
1.489: The cruel altars and his fate he tells,
1.490: And the dire secret of his house reveals,
1.491: Then warns the widow, with her household gods,
1.492: To seek a refuge in remote abodes.
1.493: Last, to support her in so long a way,
1.494: He shows her where his hidden treasure lay.
1.495: Admonish'd thus, and seiz'd with mortal fright,
1.496: The queen provides companions of her flight:
1.497: They meet, and all combine to leave the state,
1.498: Who hate the tyrant, or who fear his hate.
1.499: They seize a fleet, which ready rigg'd they find;
1.500: Nor is Pygmalion's treasure left behind.
1.501: The vessels, heavy laden, put to sea
1.502: With prosp'rous winds; a woman leads the way.
1.503: I know not, if by stress of weather driv'n,
1.504: Or was their fatal course dispos'd by Heav'n;
1.505: At last they landed, where from far your eyes
1.506: May view the turrets of new Carthage rise;
1.507: There bought a space of ground, which (Byrsa call'd,
1.508: From the bull's hide) they first inclos'd, and wall'd.
1.509: But whence are you? what country claims your birth?
1.510: What seek you, strangers, on our Libyan earth?"
1.511: To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
1.512: And deeply sighing, thus her son replies:
1.513: "Could you with patience hear, or I relate,
1.514: O nymph, the tedious annals of our fate!
1.515: Thro' such a train of woes if I should run,
1.516: The day would sooner than the tale be done!
1.517: From ancient Troy, by force expell'd, we came-
1.518: If you by chance have heard the Trojan name.
1.519: On various seas by various tempests toss'd,
1.520: At length we landed on your Libyan coast.
1.521: The good Aeneas am I call'd- a name,
1.522: While Fortune favor'd, not unknown to fame.
1.523: My household gods, companions of my woes,
1.524: With pious care I rescued from our foes.
1.525: To fruitful Italy my course was bent;
1.526: And from the King of Heav'n is my descent.
1.527: With twice ten sail I cross'd the Phrygian sea;
1.528: Fate and my mother goddess led my way.
1.529: Scarce sev'n, the thin remainders of my fleet,
1.530: From storms preserv'd, within your harbor meet.
1.531: Myself distress'd, an exile, and unknown,
1.532: Debarr'd from Europe, and from Asia thrown,
1.533: In Libyan desarts wander thus alone."
1.534: His tender parent could no longer bear;
1.535: But, interposing, sought to soothe his care.
1.536: "Whoe'er you are- not unbelov'd by Heav'n,
1.537: Since on our friendly shore your ships are driv'n-
1.538: Have courage: to the gods permit the rest,
1.539: And to the queen expose your just request.
1.540: Now take this earnest of success, for more:
1.541: Your scatter'd fleet is join'd upon the shore;
1.542: The winds are chang'd, your friends from danger
1.543: Or I renounce my skill in augury.
1.544: Twelve swans behold in beauteous order move,
1.545: And stoop with closing pinions from above;
1.546: Whom late the bird of Jove had driv'n along,
1.547: And thro' the clouds pursued the scatt'ring throng:
1.548: Now, all united in a goodly team,
1.549: They skim the ground, and seek the quiet stream.
1.550: As they, with joy returning, clap their wings,
1.551: And ride the circuit of the skies in rings;
1.552: Not otherwise your ships, and ev'ry friend,
1.553: Already hold the port, or with swift sails descend.
1.554: No more advice is needful; but pursue
1.555: The path before you, and the town in view."
1.556: Thus having said, she turn'd, and made appear
1.557: Her neck refulgent, and dishevel'd hair,
1.558: Which, flowing from her shoulders, reach'd the ground.
1.559: And widely spread ambrosial scents around:
1.560: In length of train descends her sweeping gown;
1.561: And, by her graceful walk, the Queen of Love is
1.562: The prince pursued the parting deity
1.563: With words like these: "Ah! whither do you fly?
1.564: Unkind and cruel! to deceive your son
1.565: In borrow'd shapes, and his embrace to shun;
1.566: Never to bless my sight, but thus unknown;
1.567: And still to speak in accents not your own."
1.568: Against the goddess these complaints he made,
1.569: But took the path, and her commands obey'd.
1.570: They march, obscure; for Venus kindly shrouds
1.571: With mists their persons, and involves in clouds,
1.572: That, thus unseen, their passage none might stay,
1.573: Or force to tell the causes of their way.
1.574: This part perform'd, the goddess flies sublime
1.575: To visit Paphos and her native clime;
1.576: Where garlands, ever green and ever fair,
1.577: With vows are offer'd, and with solemn pray'r:
1.578: A hundred altars in her temple smoke;
1.579: A thousand bleeding hearts her pow'r invoke.
1.580: They climb the next ascent, and, looking down,
1.581: Now at a nearer distance view the town.
1.582: The prince with wonder sees the stately tow'rs,
1.583: Which late were huts and shepherds' homely bow'rs,
1.584: The gates and streets; and hears, from ev'ry part,
1.585: The noise and busy concourse of the mart.
1.586: The toiling Tyrians on each other call
1.587: To ply their labor: some extend the wall;
1.588: Some build the citadel; the brawny throng
1.589: Or dig, or push unwieldly stones along.
1.590: Some for their dwellings choose a spot of ground,
1.591: Which, first design'd, with ditches they surround.
1.592: Some laws ordain; and some attend the choice
1.593: Of holy senates, and elect by voice.
1.594: Here some design a mole, while others there
1.595: Lay deep foundations for a theater;
1.596: From marble quarries mighty columns hew,
1.597: For ornaments of scenes, and future view.
1.598: Such is their toil, and such their busy pains,
1.599: As exercise the bees in flow'ry plains,
1.600: When winter past, and summer scarce begun,
1.601: Invites them forth to labor in the sun;
1.602: Some lead their youth abroad, while some condense
1.603: Their liquid store, and some in cells dispense;
1.604: Some at the gate stand ready to receive
1.605: The golden burthen, and their friends relieve;
1.606: All with united force, combine to drive
1.607: The lazy drones from the laborious hive:
1.608: With envy stung, they view each other's deeds;
1.609: The fragrant work with diligence proceeds.
1.610: "Thrice happy you, whose walls already rise!"
1.611: Aeneas said, and view'd, with lifted eyes,
1.612: Their lofty tow'rs; then, entiring at the gate,
1.614: He mix'd, unmark'd, among the busy throng,
1.615: Borne by the tide, and pass'd unseen along.
1.616: Full in the center of the town there stood,
1.617: Thick set with trees, a venerable wood.
1.618: The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground,
1.619: And digging here, a prosp'rous omen found:
1.620: From under earth a courser's head they drew,
1.621: Their growth and future fortune to foreshew.
1.622: This fated sign their foundress Juno gave,
1.623: Of a soil fruitful, and a people brave.
1.624: Sidonian Dido here with solemn state
1.625: Did Juno's temple build, and consecrate,
1.626: Enrich'd with gifts, and with a golden shrine;
1.627: But more the goddess made the place divine.
1.628: On brazen steps the marble threshold rose,
1.629: And brazen plates the cedar beams inclose:
1.630: The rafters are with brazen cov'rings crown'd;
1.631: The lofty doors on brazen hinges sound.
1.632: What first Aeneas this place beheld,
1.633: Reviv'd his courage, and his fear expell'd.
1.634: For while, expecting there the queen, he rais'd
1.635: His wond'ring eyes, and round the temple gaz'd,
1.636: Admir'd the fortune of the rising town,
1.637: The striving artists, and their arts' renown;
1.638: He saw, in order painted on the wall,
1.640: The wars that fame around the world had blown,
1.641: All to the life, and ev'ry leader known.
1.642: There Agamemnon, Priam here, he spies,
1.643: And fierce Achilles, who both kings defies.
1.644: He stopp'd, and weeping said: "O friend! ev'n here
1.645: The monuments of Trojan woes appear!
1.646: Our known disasters fill ev'n foreign lands:
1.647: See there, where old unhappy Priam stands!
1.648: Ev'n the mute walls relate the warrior's fame,
1.649: And Trojan griefs the Tyrians' pity claim."
1.650: He said (his tears a ready passage find),
1.651: Devouring what he saw so well design'd,
1.652: And with an empty picture fed his mind:
1.653: For there he saw the fainting Grecians yield,
1.654: And here the trembling Trojans quit the field,
1.655: Pursued by fierce Achilles thro' the plain,
1.656: On his high chariot driving o'er the slain.
1.657: The tents of Rhesus next his grief renew,
1.658: By their white sails betray'd to nightly view;
1.659: And wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword
1.660: The sentries slew, nor spar'd their slumb'ring lord,
1.661: Then took the fiery steeds, ere yet the food
1.662: Of Troy they taste, or drink the Xanthian flood.
1.663: Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied
1.665: Then, where the boy disarm'd, with loosen'd reins,
1.666: Was by his horses hurried o'er the plains,
1.667: Hung by the neck and hair, and dragg'd around:
1.668: The hostile spear, yet sticking in his wound,
1.669: With tracks of blood inscrib'd the dusty ground.
1.670: Meantime the Trojan dames, oppress'd with woe,
1.671: To Pallas' fane in long procession go,
1.672: In hopes to reconcile their heav'nly foe.

1.675: But the stern goddess stands unmov'd with pray'r.
1.676: Thrice round the Trojan walls Achilles drew
1.677: The corpse of Hector, whom in fight he slew.
1.678: Here Priam sues; and there, for sums of gold,
1.679: The lifeless body of his son is sold.
1.680: So sad an object, and so well express'd,
1.681: Drew sighs and groans from the griev'd hero's breast,
1.682: To see the figure of his lifeless friend,
1.683: And his old sire his helpless hand extend.
1.684: Himself he saw amidst the Grecian train,
1.685: Mix'd in the bloody battle on the plain;
1.686: And swarthy Memnon in his arms he knew,
1.687: His pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew.
1.689: Leads to the wars an Amazonian race:
1.690: In their right hands a pointed dart they wield;
1.691: The left, for ward, sustains the lunar shield.
1.692: Athwart her breast a golden belt she throws,
1.693: Amidst the press alone provokes a thousand foes,
1.694: And dares her maiden arms to manly force oppose.
1.695: Thus while the Trojan prince employs his eyes,
1.696: Fix'd on the walls with wonder and surprise,
1.697: The beauteous Dido, with a num'rous train
1.698: And pomp of guards, ascends the sacred fane.
1.699: Such on Eurotas' banks, or Cynthus' height,
1.700: Diana seems; and so she charms the sight,
1.701: When in the dance the graceful goddess leads
1.702: The choir of nymphs, and overtops their heads:
1.703: Known by her quiver, and her lofty mien,
1.704: She walks majestic, and she looks their queen;
1.705: Latona sees her shine above the rest,
1.706: And feeds with secret joy her silent breast.
1.707: Such Dido was; with such becoming state,
1.708: Amidst the crowd, she walks serenely great.
1.709: Their labor to her future sway she speeds,
1.710: And passing with a gracious glance proceeds;
1.711: Then mounts the throne, high plac'd before the shrine:
1.712: In crowds around, the swarming people join.
1.713: She takes petitions, and dispenses laws,
1.714: Hears and determines ev'ry private cause;
1.715: Their tasks in equal portions she divides,
1.716: And, where unequal, there by lots decides.
1.717: Another way by chance Aeneas bends
1.718: His eyes, and unexpected sees his friends,
1.720: And at their backs a mighty Trojan throng,
1.721: Whom late the tempest on the billows toss'd,
1.722: And widely scatter'd on another coast.
1.723: The prince, unseen, surpris'd with wonder stands,
1.724: And longs, with joyful haste, to join their hands;
1.725: But, doubtful of the wish'd event, he stays,
1.726: And from the hollow cloud his friends surveys,
1.727: Impatient till they told their present state,
1.728: And where they left their ships, and what their

1.732: And gain admission to the gracious queen.
1.733: Ent'ring, with cries they fill'd the holy fane;

1.735: "O queen! indulg'd by favor of the gods
1.736: To found an empire in these new abodes,
1.737: To build a town, with statutes to restrain
1.738: The wild inhabitants beneath thy reign,
1.739: We wretched Trojans, toss'd on ev'ry shore,
1.740: From sea to sea, thy clemency implore.
1.741: Forbid the fires our shipping to deface!
1.742: Receive th' unhappy fugitives to grace,
1.743: And spare the remnant of a pious race!
1.744: We come not with design of wasteful prey,
1.745: To drive the country, force the swains away:
1.746: Nor such our strength, nor such is our desire;
1.747: The vanquish'd dare not to such thoughts aspire.
1.748: A land there is, Hesperia nam'd of old;
1.749: The soil is fruitful, and the men are bold-
1.750: Th' Oenotrians held it once- by common fame
1.751: Now call'd Italia, from the leader's name.
1.752: To that sweet region was our voyage bent,
1.753: When winds and ev'ry warring element
1.754: Disturb'd our course, and, far from sight of land,
1.755: Cast our torn vessels on the moving sand:
1.756: The sea came on; the South, with mighty roar,
1.757: Dispers'd and dash'd the rest upon the rocky shore.
1.758: Those few you see escap'd the Storm, and fear,
1.759: Unless you interpose, a shipwreck here.
1.760: What men, what monsters, what inhuman race,
1.761: What laws, what barb'rous customs of the place,
1.762: Shut up a desart shore to drowning men,
1.763: And drive us to the cruel seas again?
1.764: If our hard fortune no compassion draws,
1.765: Nor hospitable rights, nor human laws,
1.766: The gods are just, and will revenge our cause.
1.767: Aeneas was our prince: a juster lord,
1.768: Or nobler warrior, never drew a sword;
1.769: Observant of the right, religious of his word.
1.770: If yet he lives, and draws this vital air,
1.771: Nor we, his friends, of safety shall despair;
1.772: Nor you, great queen, these offices repent,
1.773: Which he will equal, and perhaps augment.
1.774: We want not cities, nor Sicilian coasts,
1.775: Where King Acestes Trojan lineage boasts.
1.776: Permit our ships a shelter on your shores,
1.777: Refitted from your woods with planks and oars,
1.778: That, if our prince be safe, we may renew
1.779: Our destin'd course, and Italy pursue.
1.780: But if, O best of men, the Fates ordain
1.781: That thou art swallow'd in the Libyan main,
1.782: And if our young Iulus be no more,
1.783: Dismiss our navy from your friendly shore,
1.784: That we to good Acestes may return,
1.785: And with our friends our common losses mourn."
1.786: Thus spoke Ilioneus: the Trojan crew
1.787: With cries and clamors his request renew.
1.788: The modest queen a while, with downcast eyes,
1.789: Ponder'd the speech; then briefly thus replies:
1.790: "Trojans, dismiss your fears; my cruel fate,
1.791: And doubts attending an unsettled state,
1.792: Force me to guard my coast from foreign foes.
1.793: Who has not heard the story of your woes,
1.794: The name and fortune of your native place,
1.795: The fame and valor of the Phrygian race?
1.796: We Tyrians are not so devoid of sense,
1.797: Nor so remote from Phoebus' influence.
1.798: Whether to Latian shores your course is bent,

1.800: You seek the good Acestes' government,
1.801: Your men shall be receiv'd, your fleet repair'd,
1.802: And sail, with ships of convoy for your guard:
1.803: Or, would you stay, and join your friendly pow'rs
1.804: To raise and to defend the Tyrian tow'rs,
1.805: My wealth, my city, and myself are yours.
1.806: And would to Heav'n, the Storm, you felt, would
1.807: On Carthaginian coasts your wand'ring king.
1.808: My people shall, by my command, explore
1.809: The ports and creeks of ev'ry winding shore,
1.810: And towns, and wilds, and shady woods, in quest
1.811: Of so renown'd and so desir'd a guest."
1.812: Rais'd in his mind the Trojan hero stood,
1.813: And long'd to break from out his ambient cloud:
1.814: Achates found it, and thus urg'd his way:
1.815: "From whence, O goddess-born, this long delay?
1.816: What more can you desire, your welcome sure,
1.817: Your fleet in safety, and your friends secure?
1.818: One only wants; and him we saw in vain
1.819: Oppose the Storm, and swallow'd in the main.
1.820: Orontes in his fate our forfeit paid;
1.821: The rest agrees with what your mother said."
1.822: Scarce had he spoken, when the cloud gave way,
1.823: The mists flew upward and dissolv'd in day.
1.824: The Trojan chief appear'd in open sight,
1.825: August in visage, and serenely bright.
1.826: His mother goddess, with her hands divine,
1.827: Had form'd his curling locks, and made his temples
1.828: And giv'n his rolling eyes a sparkling grace,
1.829: And breath'd a youthful vigor on his face;
1.830: Like polish'd ivory, beauteous to behold,
1.831: Or Parian marble, when enchas'd in gold:
1.832: Thus radiant from the circling cloud he broke,
1.833: And thus with manly modesty he spoke:
1.834: "He whom you seek am I; by tempests toss'd,
1.835: And sav'd from shipwreck on your Libyan coast;
1.836: Presenting, gracious queen, before your throne,
1.837: A prince that owes his life to you alone.
1.838: Fair majesty, the refuge and redress
1.839: Of those whom fate pursues, and wants oppress,
1.840: You, who your pious offices employ
1.841: To save the relics of abandon'd Troy;
1.842: Receive the shipwreck'd on your friendly shore,
1.843: With hospitable rites relieve the poor;
1.844: Associate in your town a wand'ring train,
1.845: And strangers in your palace entertain:
1.846: What thanks can wretched fugitives return,
1.847: Who, scatter'd thro' the world, in exile mourn?
1.848: The gods, if gods to goodness are inclin'd;
1.849: If acts of mercy touch their heav'nly mind,
1.850: And, more than all the gods, your gen'rous heart.
1.851: Conscious of worth, requite its own desert!
1.852: In you this age is happy, and this earth,
1.853: And parents more than mortal gave you birth.
1.854: While rolling rivers into seas shall run,
1.855: And round the space of heav'n the radiant sun;
1.856: While trees the mountain tops with shades supply,
1.857: Your honor, name, and praise shall never die.
1.858: Whate'er abode my fortune has assign'd,
1.859: Your image shall be present in my mind."
1.860: Thus having said, he turn'd with pious haste,
1.861: And joyful his expecting friends embrac'd:
1.862: With his right hand Ilioneus was grac'd,
1.863: Serestus with his left; then to his breast
1.864: Cloanthus and the noble Gyas press'd;
1.865: And so by turns descended to the rest.
1.866: The Tyrian queen stood fix'd upon his face,
1.867: Pleas'd with his motions, ravish'd with his grace;
1.868: Admir'd his fortunes, more admir'd the man;
1.869: Then recollected stood, and thus began:
1.870: "What fate, O goddess-born; what angry pow'rs
1.871: Have cast you shipwrack'd on our barren shores?
1.872: Are you the great Aeneas, known to fame,
1.873: Who from celestial seed your lineage claim?
1.874: The same Aeneas whom fair Venus bore
1.875: To fam'd Anchises on th' Idaean shore?
1.876: It calls into my mind, tho' then a child,
1.877: When Teucer came, from Salamis exil'd,
1.878: And sought my father's aid, to be restor'd:
1.879: My father Belus then with fire and sword
1.880: Invaded Cyprus, made the region bare,
1.881: And, conqu'ring, finish'd the successful war.
1.882: From him the Trojan siege I understood,
1.883: The Grecian chiefs, and your illustrious blood.
1.884: Your foe himself the Dardan valor prais'd,
1.885: And his own ancestry from Trojans rais'd.
1.886: Enter, my noble guest, and you shall find,
1.887: If not a costly welcome, yet a kind:
1.888: For I myself, like you, have been distress'd,
1.889: Till Heav'n afforded me this place of rest;
1.890: Like you, an alien in a land unknown,
1.891: I learn to pity woes so like my own."
1.892: She said, and to the palace led her guest;
1.893: Then offer'd incense, and proclaim'd a feast.
1.894: Nor yet less careful for her absent friends,
1.895: Twice ten fat oxen to the ships she sends;
1.896: Besides a hundred boars, a hundred lambs,
1.897: With bleating cries, attend their milky dams;

1.900: Now purple hangings clothe the palace walls,
1.901: And sumptuous feasts are made in splendid halls:
1.902: On Tyrian carpets, richly wrought, they dine;
1.903: With loads of massy plate the sideboards shine,
1.904: And antique vases, all of gold emboss'd

1.906: Of curious work, where on the sides were seen

1.910: Iulus' absence could no longer bear,
1.911: Dispatch'd Achates to the ships in haste,
1.912: To give a glad relation of the past,

1.915: A robe of tissue, stiff with golden wire;

1.925: Instructed thus, the wise Achates goes,
1.926: And in his diligence his duty shows.
1.927: But Venus, anxious for her son's affairs,
1.928: New counsels tries, and new designs prepares:
1.929: That Cupid should assume the shape and face
1.930: Of sweet Ascanius, and the sprightly grace;
1.931: Should bring the presents, in her nephew's stead,
1.932: And in Eliza's veins the gentle poison shed:
1.933: For much she fear'd the Tyrians, double-tongued,
1.934: And knew the town to Juno's care belong'd.
1.935: These thoughts by night her golden slumbers broke,
1.936: And thus alarm'd, to winged Love she spoke:
1.937: "My son, my strength, whose mighty pow'r alone
1.938: Controls the Thund'rer on his awful throne,
1.939: To thee thy much-afflicted mother flies,
1.940: And on thy succor and thy faith relies.
1.941: Thou know'st, my son, how Jove's revengeful wife,
1.942: By force and fraud, attempts thy brother's life;
1.943: And often hast thou mourn'd with me his pains.
1.944: Him Dido now with blandishment detains;
1.945: But I suspect the town where Juno reigns.
1.946: For this 't is needful to prevent her art,
1.947: And fire with love the proud Phoenician's heart:
1.948: A love so violent, so strong, so sure,
1.949: As neither age can change, nor art can cure.
1.950: How this may be perform'd, now take my mind:
1.951: Ascanius by his father is design'd
1.952: To come, with presents laden, from the port,
1.953: To gratify the queen, and gain the court.
1.954: I mean to plunge the boy in pleasing sleep,
1.955: And, ravish'd, in Idalian bow'rs to keep,
1.956: Or high Cythera, that the sweet deceit
1.957: May pass unseen, and none prevent the cheat.
1.958: Take thou his form and shape. I beg the grace
1.959: But only for a night's revolving space:
1.960: Thyself a boy, assume a boy's dissembled face;
1.961: That when, amidst the fervor of the feast,
1.962: The Tyrian hugs and fonds thee on her breast,
1.963: And with sweet kisses in her arms constrains,
1.964: Thou may'st infuse thy venom in her veins."
1.965: The God of Love obeys, and sets aside
1.966: His bow and quiver, and his plumy pride;
1.967: He walks Iulus in his mother's sight,
1.968: And in the sweet resemblance takes delight.
1.969: The goddess then to young Ascanius flies,
1.970: And in a pleasing slumber seals his eyes:
1.971: Lull'd in her lap, amidst a train of Loves,
1.972: She gently bears him to her blissful groves,
1.973: Then with a wreath of myrtle crowns his head,
1.974: And softly lays him on a flow'ry bed.
1.975: Cupid meantime assum'd his form and face,
1.976: Foll'wing Achates with a shorter pace,
1.977: And brought the gifts. The queen already sate
1.978: Amidst the Trojan lords, in shining state,
1.979: High on a golden bed: her princely guest
1.980: Was next her side; in order sate the rest.
1.981: Then canisters with bread are heap'd on high;
1.982: Th' attendants water for their hands supply,
1.983: And, having wash'd, with silken towels dry.
1.984: Next fifty handmaids in long order bore
1.985: The censers, and with fumes the gods adore:
1.986: Then youths, and virgins twice as many, join
1.987: To place the dishes, and to serve the wine.
1.988: The Tyrian train, admitted to the feast,
1.989: Approach, and on the painted couches rest.
1.990: All on the Trojan gifts with wonder gaze,
1.991: But view the beauteous boy with more amaze,
1.992: His rosy-color'd cheeks, his radiant eyes,
1.993: His motions, voice, and shape, and all the god's
1.994: Nor pass unprais'd the vest and veil divine,
1.995: Which wand'ring foliage and rich flow'rs entwine.
1.996: But, far above the rest, the royal dame,
1.998: With eyes insatiate, and tumultuous joy,
1.999: Beholds the presents, and admires the boy.
1.1000: The guileful god about the hero long,
1.1001: With children's play, and false embraces, hung;
1.1002: Then sought the queen: she took him to her arms
1.1003: With greedy pleasure, and devour'd his charms.
1.1004: Unhappy Dido little thought what guest,
1.1005: How dire a god, she drew so near her breast;
1.1006: But he, not mindless of his mother's pray'r,
1.1007: Works in the pliant bosom of the fair,
1.1008: And molds her heart anew, and blots her former care.
1.1009: The dead is to the living love resign'd;
1.1010: And all Aeneas enters in her mind.
1.1011: Now, when the rage of hunger was appeas'd,
1.1012: The meat remov'd, and ev'ry guest was pleas'd,
1.1013: The golden bowls with sparkling wine are crown'd,
1.1014: And thro' the palace cheerful cries resound.
1.1015: From gilded roofs depending lamps display
1.1016: Nocturnal beams, that emulate the day.
1.1017: A golden bowl, that shone with gems divine,
1.1018: The queen commanded to be crown'd with wine:
1.1019: The bowl that Belus us'd, and all the Tyrian line.
1.1020: Then, silence thro' the hall proclaim'd, she spoke:
1.1022: With solemn rites, thy sacred name and pow'r;
1.1023: Bless to both nations this auspicious hour!
1.1024: So may the Trojan and the Tyrian line
1.1025: In lasting concord from this day combine.
1.1026: Thou, Bacchus, god of joys and friendly cheer,
1.1027: And gracious Juno, both be present here!
1.1028: And you, my lords of Tyre, your vows address
1.1029: To Heav'n with mine, to ratify the peace."
1.1030: The goblet then she took, with nectar crown'd
1.1031: (Sprinkling the first libations on the ground,)
1.1032: And rais'd it to her mouth with sober grace;
1.1033: Then, sipping, offer'd to the next in place.
1.1034: 'T was Bitias whom she call'd, a thirsty soul;
1.1035: He took challenge, and embrac'd the bowl,
1.1036: With pleasure swill'd the gold, nor ceas'd to draw,
1.1037: Till he the bottom of the brimmer saw.
1.1038: The goblet goes around: Iopas brought
1.1039: His golden lyre, and sung what ancient Atlas taught:
1.1040: The various labors of the wand'ring moon,
1.1041: And whence proceed th' eclipses of the sun;
1.1042: Th' original of men and beasts; and whence
1.1043: The rains arise, and fires their warmth dispense,
1.1044: And fix'd and erring stars dispose their influence;
1.1045: What shakes the solid earth; what cause delays
1.1046: The summer nights and shortens winter days.
1.1047: With peals of shouts the Tyrians praise the song:
1.1048: Those peals are echo'd by the Trojan throng.
1.1049: Th' unhappy queen with talk prolong'd the night,
1.1050: And drank large draughts of love with vast delight;
1.1051: Of Priam much enquir'd, of Hector more;
1.1052: Then ask'd what arms the swarthy Memnon wore,
1.1053: What troops he landed on the Trojan shore;
1.1054: The steeds of Diomede varied the discourse,
1.1055: And fierce Achilles, with his matchless force;
1.1056: At length, as fate and her ill stars requir'd,
1.1057: To hear the series of the war desir'd.
1.1058: "Relate at large, my godlike guest," she said,
1.1060: The fatal issue of so long a war,
1.1061: Your flight, your wand'rings, and your woes, declare;
1.1062: For, since on ev'ry sea, on ev'ry coast,
1.1063: Your men have been distress'd, your navy toss'd,
1.1064: Sev'n times the sun has either tropic view'd,
1.1065: The winter banish'd, and the spring renew'd."

2.1: All were attentive to the godlike man,
2.2: When from his lofty couch he thus began:
2.3: "Great queen, what you command me to relate
2.4: Renews the sad remembrance of our fate:
2.5: An empire from its old foundations rent,
2.6: And ev'ry woe the Trojans underwent;
2.7: A peopled city made a desart place;
2.8: All that I saw, and part of which I was:
2.9: Not ev'n the hardest of our foes could hear,
2.10: Nor stern Ulysses tell without a tear.
2.11: And now the latter watch of wasting night,
2.12: And setting stars, to kindly rest invite;
2.13: But, since you take such int'rest in our woe,
2.14: And Troy's disastrous end desire to know,
2.15: I will restrain my tears, and briefly tell
2.16: What in our last and fatal night befell.
2.18: The Greeks grew weary of the tedious war,
2.19: And by Minerva's aid a fabric rear'd,
2.20: Which like a steed of monstrous height appear'd:
2.21: The sides were plank'd with pine; they feign'd it
2.22: For their return, and this the vow they paid.
2.23: Thus they pretend, but in the hollow side
2.24: Selected numbers of their soldiers hide:
2.25: With inward arms the dire machine they load,
2.26: And iron bowels stuff the dark abode.
2.27: In sight of Troy lies Tenedos, an isle
2.28: (While Fortune did on Priam's empire smile)
2.29: Renown'd for wealth; but, since, a faithless bay,
2.30: Where ships expos'd to wind and weather lay.
2.31: There was their fleet conceal'd. We thought, for
2.32: Their sails were hoisted, and our fears release.
2.33: The Trojans, coop'd within their walls so long,
2.34: Unbar their gates, and issue in a throng,
2.35: Like swarming bees, and with delight survey
2.36: The camp deserted, where the Grecians lay:
2.37: The quarters of the sev'ral chiefs they show'd;
2.38: Here Phoenix, here Achilles, made abode;
2.39: Here join'd the battles; there the navy rode.
2.40: Part on the pile their wond'ring eyes employ:
2.41: The pile by Pallas rais'd to ruin Troy.
2.42: Thymoetes first ('t is doubtful whether hir'd,
2.43: Or so the Trojan destiny requir'd)
2.44: Mov'd that the ramparts might be broken down,
2.45: To lodge the monster fabric in the town.
2.46: But Capys, and the rest of sounder mind,
2.47: The fatal present to the flames designed,
2.48: Or to the wat'ry deep; at least to bore
2.49: The hollow sides, and hidden frauds explore.
2.50: The giddy vulgar, as their fancies guide,
2.51: With noise say nothing, and in parts divide.
2.52: Laocoon, follow'd by a num'rous crowd,
2.53: Ran from the fort, and cried, from far, aloud:
2.55: What more than madness has possess'd your brains?
2.56: Think you the Grecians from your coasts are gone?
2.57: And are Ulysses' arts no better known?
2.58: This hollow fabric either must inclose,
2.59: Within its blind recess, our secret foes;
2.60: Or 't is an engine rais'd above the town,
2.61: T' o'erlook the walls, and then to batter down.
2.62: Somewhat is sure design'd, by fraud or force:
2.63: Trust not their presents, nor admit the horse.'
2.64: Thus having said, against the steed he threw
2.65: His forceful spear, which, hissing as flew,
2.66: Pierc'd thro' the yielding planks of jointed wood,
2.67: And trembling in the hollow belly stood.
2.68: The sides, transpierc'd, return a rattling sound,
2.69: And groans of Greeks inclos'd come issuing thro' the
2.70: And, had not Heav'n the fall of Troy design'd,
2.71: Or had not men been fated to be blind,
2.72: Enough was said and done t'inspire a better mind.
2.73: Then had our lances pierc'd the treach'rous wood,
2.74: And Ilian tow'rs and Priam's empire stood.
2.75: Meantime, with shouts, the Trojan shepherds bring
2.76: A captive Greek, in bands, before the king;
2.77: Taken to take; who made himself their prey,
2.78: T' impose on their belief, and Troy betray;
2.79: Fix'd on his aim, and obstinately bent
2.80: To die undaunted, or to circumvent.
2.81: About the captive, tides of Trojans flow;
2.82: All press to see, and some insult the foe.
2.83: Now hear how well the Greeks their wiles disguis'd;
2.84: Behold a nation in a man compris'd.
2.85: Trembling the miscreant stood, unarm'd and bound;
2.86: He star'd, and roll'd his haggard eyes around,
2.87: Then said: 'Alas! what earth remains, what sea
2.88: Is open to receive unhappy me?
2.89: What fate a wretched fugitive attends,
2.90: Scorn'd by my foes, abandon'd by my friends?'
2.91: He said, and sigh'd, and cast a rueful eye:
2.92: Our pity kindles, and our passions die.
2.93: We cheer youth to make his own defense,
2.94: And freely tell us what he was, and whence:
2.95: What news he could impart, we long to know,
2.96: And what to credit from a captive foe.
2.97: "His fear at length dismiss'd, he said: 'Whate'er
2.98: My fate ordains, my words shall be sincere:
2.99: I neither can nor dare my birth disclaim;
2.100: Greece is my country, Sinon is my name.
2.101: Tho' plung'd by Fortune's pow'r in misery,
2.102: 'T is not in Fortune's pow'r to make me lie.
2.103: If any chance has hither brought the name
2.104: Of Palamedes, not unknown to fame,
2.105: Who suffer'd from the malice of the times,
2.106: Accus'd and sentenc'd for pretended crimes,
2.107: Because these fatal wars he would prevent;
2.108: Whose death the wretched Greeks too late lament-
2.109: Me, then a boy, my father, poor and bare
2.110: Of other means, committed to his care,
2.111: His kinsman and companion in the war.
2.112: While Fortune favor'd, while his arms support
2.113: The cause, and rul'd the counsels, of the court,
2.114: I made some figure there; nor was my name
2.115: Obscure, nor I without my share of fame.
2.116: But when Ulysses, with fallacious arts,
2.117: Had made impression in the people's hearts,
2.118: And forg'd a treason in my patron's name
2.119: (I speak of things too far divulg'd by fame),
2.120: My kinsman fell. Then I, without support,
2.121: In private mourn'd his loss, and left the court.
2.122: Mad as I was, I could not bear his fate
2.123: With silent grief, but loudly blam'd the state,
2.124: And curs'd the direful author of my woes.
2.125: 'T was told again; and hence my ruin rose.
2.126: I threaten'd, if indulgent Heav'n once more
2.127: Would land me safely on my native shore,
2.128: His death with double vengeance to restore.
2.129: This mov'd the murderer's hate; and soon ensued
2.130: Th' effects of malice from a man so proud.
2.131: Ambiguous rumors thro' the camp he spread,
2.132: And sought, by treason, my devoted head;
2.133: New crimes invented; left unturn'd no stone,
2.134: To make my guilt appear, and hide his own;
2.135: Till Calchas was by force and threat'ning wrought-
2.136: But why- why dwell I on that anxious thought?
2.137: If on my nation just revenge you seek,
2.138: And 't is t' appear a foe, t' appear a Greek;
2.139: Already you my name and country know;
2.140: Assuage your thirst of blood, and strike the blow:
2.141: My death will both the kingly brothers please,
2.142: And set insatiate Ithacus at ease.'
2.143: This fair unfinish'd tale, these broken starts,
2.144: Rais'd expectations in our longing hearts:
2.145: Unknowing as we were in Grecian arts.
2.146: His former trembling once again renew'd,
2.147: With acted fear, the villain thus pursued:
2.148: "'Long had the Grecians (tir'd with fruitless care,
2.149: And wearied with an unsuccessful war)
2.150: Resolv'd to raise the siege, and leave the town;
2.151: And, had the gods permitted, they had gone;
2.152: But oft the wintry seas and southern winds
2.153: Withstood their passage home, and chang'd their
2.154: Portents and prodigies their souls amaz'd;
2.155: But most, when this stupendous pile was rais'd:
2.156: Then flaming meteors, hung in air, were seen,
2.157: And thunders rattled thro' a sky serene.
2.158: Dismay'd, and fearful of some dire event,
2.159: Eurypylus t' enquire their fate was sent.
2.160: He from the gods this dreadful answer brought:
2.161: "O Grecians, when the Trojan shores you sought,
2.162: Your passage with a virgin's blood was bought:
2.163: So must your safe return be bought again,
2.164: And Grecian blood once more atone the main."
2.165: The spreading rumor round the people ran;
2.166: All fear'd, and each believ'd himself the man.
2.167: Ulysses took th' advantage of their fright;
2.168: Call'd Calchas, and produc'd in open sight:
2.169: Then bade him name the wretch, ordain'd by fate
2.170: The public victim, to redeem the state.
2.171: Already some presag'd the dire event,
2.172: And saw what sacrifice Ulysses meant.
2.173: For twice five days the good old seer withstood
2.174: Th' intended treason, and was dumb to blood,
2.175: Till, tir'd, with endless clamors and pursuit
2.176: Of Ithacus, he stood no longer mute;
2.177: But, as it was agreed, pronounc'd that I
2.178: Was destin'd by the wrathful gods to die.
2.179: All prais'd the sentence, pleas'd the storm should
2.180: On one alone, whose fury threaten'd all.
2.181: The dismal day was come; the priests prepare
2.182: Their leaven'd cakes, and fillets for my hair.
2.183: I follow'd nature's laws, and must avow
2.184: I broke my bonds and fled the fatal blow.
2.185: Hid in a weedy lake all night I lay,
2.186: Secure of safety when they sail'd away.
2.187: But now what further hopes for me remain,
2.188: To see my friends, or native soil, again;
2.189: My tender infants, or my careful sire,
2.190: Whom they returning will to death require;
2.191: Will perpetrate on them their first design,
2.192: And take the forfeit of their heads for mine?
2.193: Which, O! if pity mortal minds can move,
2.194: If there be faith below, or gods above,
2.195: If innocence and truth can claim desert,
2.196: Ye Trojans, from an injur'd wretch avert.'
2.197: "False tears true pity move; the king commands
2.198: To loose his fetters, and unbind his hands:
2.199: Then adds these friendly words: 'Dismiss thy fears;
2.200: Forget the Greeks; be mine as thou wert theirs.
2.201: But truly tell, was it for force or guile,
2.202: Or some religious end, you rais'd the pile?'
2.203: Thus said the king. He, full of fraudful arts,
2.204: This well-invented tale for truth imparts:
2.205: 'Ye lamps of heav'n!' he said, and lifted high
2.206: His hands now free, 'thou venerable sky!
2.208: Ye fatal fillets, that once bound this head!
2.209: Ye sacred altars, from whose flames I fled!
2.210: Be all of you adjur'd; and grant I may,
2.211: Without a crime, th' ungrateful Greeks betray,
2.212: Reveal the secrets of the guilty state,
2.213: And justly punish whom I justly hate!
2.214: But you, O king, preserve the faith you gave,
2.215: If I, to save myself, your empire save.
2.216: The Grecian hopes, and all th' attempts they made,
2.217: Were only founded on Minerva's aid.
2.218: But from the time when impious Diomede,
2.219: And false Ulysses, that inventive head,
2.220: Her fatal image from the temple drew,
2.221: The sleeping guardians of the castle slew,
2.222: Her virgin statue with their bloody hands
2.223: Polluted, and profan'd her holy bands;
2.224: From thence the tide of fortune left their shore,
2.225: And ebb'd much faster than it flow'd before:
2.226: Their courage languish'd, as their hopes decay'd;
2.227: And Pallas, now averse, refus'd her aid.
2.228: Nor did the goddess doubtfully declare
2.229: Her alter'd mind and alienated care.
2.230: When first her fatal image touch'd the ground,
2.231: She sternly cast her glaring eyes around,
2.232: That sparkled as they roll'd, and seem'd to threat:
2.233: Her heav'nly limbs distill'd a briny sweat.
2.234: Thrice from the ground she leap'd, was seen to wield
2.235: Her brandish'd lance, and shake her horrid shield.
2.236: Then Calchas bade our host for flight
2.237: And hope no conquest from the tedious war,
2.238: Till first they sail'd for Greece; with pray'rs
2.239: Her injur'd pow'r, and better omens brought.
2.240: And now their navy plows the wat'ry main,
2.241: Yet soon expect it on your shores again,
2.242: With Pallas pleas'd; as Calchas did ordain.
2.243: But first, to reconcile the blue-ey'd maid
2.244: For her stol'n statue and her tow'r betray'd,
2.245: Warn'd by the seer, to her offended name
2.246: We rais'd and dedicate this wondrous frame,
2.247: So lofty, lest thro' your forbidden gates
2.248: It pass, and intercept our better fates:
2.249: For, once admitted there, our hopes are lost;
2.250: And Troy may then a new Palladium boast;
2.251: For so religion and the gods ordain,
2.252: That, if you violate with hands profane
2.253: Minerva's gift, your town in flames shall burn,
2.254: (Which omen, O ye gods, on Graecia turn!)
2.255: But if it climb, with your assisting hands,
2.256: The Trojan walls, and in the city stands;
2.257: Then Troy shall Argos and Mycenae burn,
2.258: And the reverse of fate on us return.'
2.259: "With such deceits he gain'd their easy hearts,
2.260: Too prone to credit his perfidious arts.
2.261: What Diomede, nor Thetis' greater son,
2.262: A thousand ships, nor ten years' siege, had done-
2.263: False tears and fawning words the city won.
2.264: "A greater omen, and of worse portent,
2.265: Did our unwary minds with fear torment,
2.266: Concurring to produce the dire event.
2.267: Laocoon, Neptune's priest by lot that year,
2.268: With solemn pomp then sacrific'd a steer;
2.269: When, dreadful to behold, from sea we spied
2.270: Two serpents, rank'd abreast, the seas divide,
2.271: And smoothly sweep along the swelling tide.
2.272: Their flaming crests above the waves they show;
2.273: Their bellies seem to burn the seas below;
2.274: Their speckled tails advance to steer their course,
2.275: And on the sounding shore the flying billows force.
2.276: And now the strand, and now the plain they held;
2.277: Their ardent eyes with bloody streaks were fill'd;
2.278: Their nimble tongues they brandish'd as they came,
2.279: And lick'd their hissing jaws, that sputter'd flame.
2.280: We fled amaz'd; their destin'd way they take,
2.281: And to Laocoon and his children make;
2.282: And first around the tender boys they wind,
2.283: Then with their sharpen'd fangs their limbs and bodies
2.284: The wretched father, running to their aid
2.285: With pious haste, but vain, they next invade;
2.286: Twice round his waist their winding volumes roll'd;
2.287: And twice about his gasping throat they fold.
2.288: The priest thus doubly chok'd, their crests divide,
2.289: And tow'ring o'er his head in triumph ride.
2.290: With both his hands he labors at the knots;
2.291: His holy fillets the blue venom blots;
2.292: His roaring fills the flitting air around.
2.293: Thus, when an ox receives a glancing wound,
2.294: He breaks his bands, the fatal altar flies,
2.295: And with loud bellowings breaks the yielding skies.
2.296: Their tasks perform'd, the serpents quit their prey,
2.297: And to the tow'r of Pallas make their way:
2.298: Couch'd at her feet, they lie protected there
2.299: By her large buckler and protended spear.
2.300: Amazement seizes all; the gen'ral cry
2.301: Proclaims Laocoon justly doom'd to die,
2.302: Whose hand the will of Pallas had withstood,
2.303: And dared to violate the sacred wood.
2.304: All vote t' admit the steed, that vows be paid
2.305: And incense offer'd to th' offended maid.
2.306: A spacious breach is made; the town lies bare;
2.307: Some hoisting-levers, some the wheels prepare
2.308: And fasten to the horse's feet; the rest
2.309: With cables haul along th' unwieldly beast.
2.310: Each on his fellow for assistance calls;
2.311: At length the fatal fabric mounts the walls,
2.312: Big with destruction. Boys with chaplets crown'd,
2.313: And choirs of virgins, sing and dance around.
2.314: Thus rais'd aloft, and then descending down,
2.315: It enters o'er our heads, and threats the town.
2.316: O sacred city, built by hands divine!
2.317: O valiant heroes of the Trojan line!
2.318: Four times he struck: as oft the clashing sound
2.319: Of arms was heard, and inward groans rebound.
2.320: Yet, mad with zeal, and blinded with our fate,
2.321: We haul along the horse in solemn state;
2.322: Then place the dire portent within the tow'r.
2.323: Cassandra cried, and curs'd th' unhappy hour;
2.324: Foretold our fate; but, by the god's decree,
2.325: All heard, and none believ'd the prophecy.
2.326: With branches we the fanes adorn, and waste,
2.327: In jollity, the day ordain'd to be the last.
2.328: Meantime the rapid heav'ns roll'd down the light,
2.329: And on the shaded ocean rush'd the night;
2.330: Our men, secure, nor guards nor sentries held,
2.331: But easy sleep their weary limbs compell'd.
2.332: The Grecians had embark'd their naval pow'rs
2.333: From Tenedos, and sought our well-known shores,
2.334: Safe under covert of the silent night,
2.335: And guided by th' imperial galley's light;
2.336: When Sinon, favor'd by the partial gods,
2.337: Unlock'd the horse, and op'd his dark abodes;
2.338: Restor'd to vital air our hidden foes,
2.339: Who joyful from their long confinement rose.
2.340: Tysander bold, and Sthenelus their guide,
2.341: And dire Ulysses down the cable slide:
2.342: Then Thoas, Athamas, and Pyrrhus haste;
2.343: Nor was the Podalirian hero last,
2.344: Nor injur'd Menelaus, nor the fam'd
2.345: Epeus, who the fatal engine fram'd.
2.346: A nameless crowd succeed; their forces join
2.347: T' invade the town, oppress'd with sleep and wine.
2.348: Those few they find awake first meet their fate;
2.349: Then to their fellows they unbar the gate.
2.350: "'T was in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
2.351: Our bodies worn with toils, our minds with cares,
2.352: When Hector's ghost before my sight appears:
2.353: A bloody shroud he seem'd, and bath'd in tears;
2.354: Such as he was, when, by Pelides slain,
2.355: Thessalian coursers dragg'd him o'er the plain.
2.356: Swoln were his feet, as when the thongs were thrust
2.357: Thro' the bor'd holes; his body black with dust;
2.358: Unlike that Hector who return'd from toils
2.359: Of war, triumphant, in Aeacian spoils,
2.360: Or him who made the fainting Greeks retire,
2.361: And launch'd against their navy Phrygian fire.
