2.838: Haste, where your trembling spouse and sire attend:
2.839: Haste; and a mother's care your passage shall befriend.'
2.840: She said, and swiftly vanish'd from my sight,
2.841: Obscure in clouds and gloomy shades of night.
2.842: I look'd, I listen'd; dreadful sounds I hear;
2.843: And the dire forms of hostile gods appear.
2.844: Troy sunk in flames I saw (nor could prevent),
2.845: And Ilium from its old foundations rent;
2.846: Rent like a mountain ash, which dar'd the winds,
2.847: And stood the sturdy strokes of lab'ring hinds.
2.848: About the roots the cruel ax resounds;
2.849: The stumps are pierc'd with oft-repeated wounds:
2.850: The war is felt on high; the nodding crown
2.851: Now threats a fall, and throws the leafy honors
2.852: To their united force it yields, tho' late,
2.853: And mourns with mortal groans th' approaching fate:
2.854: The roots no more their upper load sustain;
2.855: But down she falls, and spreads a ruin thro' the
2.856: "Descending thence, I scape thro' foes and fire:
2.857: Before the goddess, foes and flames retire.
2.858: Arriv'd at home, he, for whose only sake,
2.859: Or most for his, such toils I undertake,
2.860: The good Anchises, whom, by timely flight,
2.861: I purpos'd to secure on Ida's height,
2.862: Refus'd the journey, resolute to die
2.863: And add his fun'rals to the fate of Troy,
2.864: Rather than exile and old age sustain.
2.865: 'Go you, whose blood runs warm in ev'ry vein.
2.866: Had Heav'n decreed that I should life enjoy,
2.867: Heav'n had decreed to save unhappy Troy.
2.868: 'T is, sure, enough, if not too much, for one,
2.869: Twice to have seen our Ilium overthrown.
2.870: Make haste to save the poor remaining crew,
2.871: And give this useless corpse a long adieu.
2.872: These weak old hands suffice to stop my breath;
2.873: At least the pitying foes will aid my death,
2.874: To take my spoils, and leave my body bare:
2.875: As for my sepulcher, let Heav'n take care.
2.876: 'T is long since I, for my celestial wife
2.877: Loath'd by the gods, have dragg'd a ling'ring life;
2.878: Since ev'ry hour and moment I expire,
2.879: Blasted from heav'n by Jove's avenging fire.'
2.880: This oft repeated, he stood fix'd to die:
2.881: Myself, my wife, my son, my family,
2.882: Intreat, pray, beg, and raise a doleful cry-
2.883: 'What, will he still persist, on death resolve,
2.884: And in his ruin all his house involve!'
2.885: He still persists his reasons to maintain;
2.886: Our pray'rs, our tears, our loud laments, are vain.
2.887: "Urg'd by despair, again I go to try
2.888: The fate of arms, resolv'd in fight to die:
2.889: 'What hope remains, but what my death must give?
2.890: Can I, without so dear a father, live?
2.891: You term it prudence, what I baseness call:
2.892: Could such a word from such a parent fall?
2.893: If Fortune please, and so the gods ordain,
2.894: That nothing should of ruin'd Troy remain,
2.895: And you conspire with Fortune to be slain,
2.896: The way to death is wide, th' approaches near:
2.897: For soon relentless Pyrrhus will appear,
2.898: Reeking with Priam's blood- the wretch who slew
2.899: The son (inhuman) in the father's view,
2.900: And then the sire himself to the dire altar drew.
2.901: O goddess mother, give me back to Fate;
2.902: Your gift was undesir'd, and came too late!
2.903: Did you, for this, unhappy me convey
2.904: Thro' foes and fires, to see my house a prey?
2.905: Shall I my father, wife, and son behold,
2.906: Welt'ring in blood, each other's arms infold?
2.907: Haste! gird my sword, tho' spent and overcome:
2.908: 'T is the last summons to receive our doom.
2.909: I hear thee, Fate; and I obey thy call!
2.910: Not unreveng'd the foe shall see my fall.
2.911: Restore me to the yet unfinish'd fight:
2.912: My death is wanting to conclude the night.'
2.913: Arm'd once again, my glitt'ring sword I wield,
2.914: While th' other hand sustains my weighty shield,
2.915: And forth I rush to seek th' abandon'd field.
2.916: I went; but sad Creusa stopp'd my way,
2.917: And cross the threshold in my passage lay,
2.918: Embrac'd my knees, and, when I would have gone,
2.919: Shew'd me my feeble sire and tender son:
2.920: 'If death be your design, at least,' said she,
2.921: 'Take us along to share your destiny.
2.922: If any farther hopes in arms remain,
2.923: This place, these pledges of your love, maintain.
2.924: To whom do you expose your father's life,
2.925: Your son's, and mine, your now forgotten wife!'
2.926: While thus she fills the house with clam'rous cries,
2.927: Our hearing is diverted by our eyes:
2.928: For, while I held my son, in the short space
2.929: Betwixt our kisses and our last embrace;
2.930: Strange to relate, from young Iulus' head
2.931: A lambent flame arose, which gently spread
2.932: Around his brows, and on his temples fed.
2.933: Amaz'd, with running water we prepare
2.934: To quench the sacred fire, and slake his hair;
2.935: But old Anchises, vers'd in omens, rear'd
2.936: His hands to heav'n, and this request preferr'd:
2.937: 'If any vows, almighty Jove, can bend
2.938: Thy will; if piety can pray'rs commend,
2.939: Confirm the glad presage which thou art pleas'd to
2.940: Scarce had he said, when, on our left, we hear
2.941: A peal of rattling thunder roll in air:
2.942: There shot a streaming lamp along the sky,
2.943: Which on the winged lightning seem'd to fly;
2.944: From o'er the roof the blaze began to move,
2.945: And, trailing, vanish'd in th' Idaean grove.
2.946: It swept a path in heav'n, and shone a guide,
2.947: Then in a steaming stench of sulphur died.
2.948: "The good old man with suppliant hands implor'd
2.949: The gods' protection, and their star ador'd.
2.950: 'Now, now,' said he, 'my son, no more delay!
2.951: I yield, I follow where Heav'n shews the way.
2.952: Keep, O my country gods, our dwelling place,
2.953: And guard this relic of the Trojan race,
2.954: This tender child! These omens are your own,
2.955: And you can yet restore the ruin'd town.
2.956: At least accomplish what your signs foreshow:
2.957: I stand resign'd, and am prepar'd to go.'
2.958: "He said. The crackling flames appear on high.
2.959: And driving sparkles dance along the sky.
2.960: With Vulcan's rage the rising winds conspire,
2.961: And near our palace roll the flood of fire.
2.962: 'Haste, my dear father, ('t is no time to wait,)
2.963: And load my shoulders with a willing freight.
2.964: Whate'er befalls, your life shall be my care;
2.965: One death, or one deliv'rance, we will share.
2.966: My hand shall lead our little son; and you,
2.967: My faithful consort, shall our steps pursue.
2.968: Next, you, my servants, heed my strict commands:
2.969: Without the walls a ruin'd temple stands,
2.970: To Ceres hallow'd once; a cypress nigh
2.971: Shoots up her venerable head on high,
2.972: By long religion kept; there bend your feet,
2.973: And in divided parties let us meet.
2.974: Our country gods, the relics, and the bands,
2.975: Hold you, my father, in your guiltless hands:
2.976: In me 't is impious holy things to bear,
2.977: Red as I am with slaughter, new from war,
2.978: Till in some living stream I cleanse the guilt
2.979: Of dire debate, and blood in battle spilt.'
2.980: Thus, ord'ring all that prudence could provide,
2.981: I clothe my shoulders with a lion's hide
2.982: And yellow spoils; then, on my bending back,
2.983: The welcome load of my dear father take;
2.984: While on my better hand Ascanius hung,
2.985: And with unequal paces tripp'd along.
2.986: Creusa kept behind; by choice we stray
2.987: Thro' ev'ry dark and ev'ry devious way.
2.988: I, who so bold and dauntless, just before,
2.989: The Grecian darts and shock of lances bore,
2.990: At ev'ry shadow now am seiz'd with fear,
2.991: Not for myself, but for the charge I bear;
2.992: Till, near the ruin'd gate arriv'd at last,
2.993: Secure, and deeming all the danger past,
2.994: A frightful noise of trampling feet we hear.
2.995: My father, looking thro' the shades, with fear,
2.996: Cried out: 'Haste, haste, my son, the foes are nigh;
2.997: Their swords and shining armor I descry.'
2.998: Some hostile god, for some unknown offense,
2.999: Had sure bereft my mind of better sense;
2.1000: For, while thro' winding ways I took my flight,
2.1001: And sought the shelter of the gloomy night,
2.1002: Alas! I lost Creusa: hard to tell
2.1003: If by her fatal destiny she fell,
2.1004: Or weary sate, or wander'd with affright;
2.1005: But she was lost for ever to my sight.
2.1006: I knew not, or reflected, till I meet
2.1007: My friends, at Ceres' now deserted seat.
2.1008: We met: not one was wanting; only she
2.1009: Deceiv'd her friends, her son, and wretched me.
2.1010: "What mad expressions did my tongue refuse!
2.1011: Whom did I not, of gods or men, accuse!
2.1012: This was the fatal blow, that pain'd me more
2.1013: Than all I felt from ruin'd Troy before.
2.1014: Stung with my loss, and raving with despair,
2.1016: Of counsel, comfort, and of hope bereft,
2.1017: My sire, my son, my country gods I left.
2.1018: In shining armor once again I sheathe
2.1019: My limbs, not feeling wounds, nor fearing death.
2.1020: Then headlong to the burning walls I run,
2.1021: And seek the danger I was forc'd to shun.
2.1022: I tread my former tracks; thro' night explore
2.1023: Each passage, ev'ry street I cross'd before.
2.1024: All things were full of horror and affright,
2.1025: And dreadful ev'n the silence of the night.
2.1026: Then to my father's house I make repair,
2.1027: With some small glimpse of hope to find her there.
2.1028: Instead of her, the cruel Greeks I met;
2.1029: The house was fill'd with foes, with flames beset.
2.1030: Driv'n on the wings of winds, whole sheets of fire,
2.1031: Thro' air transported, to the roofs aspire.
2.1032: From thence to Priam's palace I resort,
2.1033: And search the citadel and desart court.
2.1034: Then, unobserv'd, I pass by Juno's church:
2.1035: A guard of Grecians had possess'd the porch;
2.1036: There Phoenix and Ulysses watch prey,
2.1037: And thither all the wealth of Troy convey:
2.1038: The spoils which they from ransack'd houses brought,
2.1039: And golden bowls from burning altars caught,
2.1040: The tables of the gods, the purple vests,
2.1041: The people's treasure, and the pomp of priests.
2.1042: A rank of wretched youths, with pinion'd hands,
2.1043: And captive matrons, in long order stands.
2.1044: Then, with ungovern'd madness, I proclaim,
2.1045: Thro' all the silent street, Creusa's name:
2.1046: Creusa still I call; at length she hears,
2.1047: And sudden thro' the shades of night appears-
2.1048: Appears, no more Creusa, nor my wife,
2.1049: But a pale specter, larger than the life.
2.1050: Aghast, astonish'd, and struck dumb with fear,
2.1051: I stood; like bristles rose my stiffen'd hair.
2.1052: Then thus the ghost began to soothe my grief
2.1053: 'Nor tears, nor cries, can give the dead relief.
2.1054: Desist, my much-lov'd lord,'t indulge your pain;
2.1055: You bear no more than what the gods ordain.
2.1056: My fates permit me not from hence to fly;
2.1057: Nor he, the great controller of the sky.
2.1058: Long wand'ring ways for you the pow'rs decree;
2.1059: On land hard labors, and a length of sea.
2.1060: Then, after many painful years are past,
2.1061: On Latium's happy shore you shall be cast,
2.1062: Where gentle Tiber from his bed beholds
2.1063: The flow'ry meadows, and the feeding folds.
2.1064: There end your toils; and there your fates provide
2.1065: A quiet kingdom, and a royal bride:
2.1066: There fortune shall the Trojan line restore,
2.1067: And you for lost Creusa weep no more.
2.1068: Fear not that I shall watch, with servile shame,
2.1069: Th' imperious looks of some proud Grecian dame;
2.1070: Or, stooping to the victor's lust, disgrace
2.1071: My goddess mother, or my royal race.
2.1072: And now, farewell! The parent of the gods
2.1073: Restrains my fleeting soul in her abodes:
2.1074: I trust our common issue to your care.'
2.1075: She said, and gliding pass'd unseen in air.
2.1076: I strove to speak: but horror tied my tongue;
2.1077: And thrice about her neck my arms I flung,
2.1078: And, thrice deceiv'd, on vain embraces hung.
2.1079: Light as an empty dream at break of day,
2.1080: Or as a blast of wind, she rush'd away.
2.1081: "Thus having pass'd the night in fruitless pain,
2.1082: I to my longing friends return again,
2.1083: Amaz'd th' augmented number to behold,
2.1084: Of men and matrons mix'd, of young and old;
2.1085: A wretched exil'd crew together brought,
2.1086: With arms appointed, and with treasure fraught,
2.1087: Resolv'd, and willing, under my command,
2.1088: To run all hazards both of sea and land.
2.1089: The Morn began, from Ida, to display
2.1090: Her rosy cheeks; and Phosphor led the day:
2.1091: Before the gates the Grecians took their post,
2.1092: And all pretense of late relief was lost.
2.1093: I yield to Fate, unwillingly retire,
2.1094: And, loaded, up the hill convey my sire."

3.1: "When Heav'n had overturn'd the Trojan state
3.2: And Priam's throne, by too severe a fate;
3.3: When ruin'd Troy became the Grecians' prey,
3.4: And Ilium's lofty tow'rs in ashes lay;
3.5: Warn'd by celestial omens, we retreat,
3.6: To seek in foreign lands a happier seat.
3.7: Near old Antandros, and at Ida's foot,
3.8: The timber of the sacred groves we cut,
3.9: And build our fleet; uncertain yet to find
3.10: What place the gods for our repose assign'd.
3.11: Friends daily flock; and scarce the kindly spring
3.12: Began to clothe the ground, and birds to sing,
3.13: When old Anchises summon'd all to sea:
3.14: The crew my father and the Fates obey.
3.15: With sighs and tears I leave my native shore,
3.16: And empty fields, where Ilium stood before.
3.17: My sire, my son, our less and greater gods,
3.18: All sail at once, and cleave the briny floods.
3.19: "Against our coast appears a spacious land,
3.20: Which once the fierce Lycurgus did command,
3.21: (Thracia the name- the people bold in war;
3.22: Vast are their fields, and tillage is their care,)
3.23: A hospitable realm while Fate was kind,
3.24: With Troy in friendship and religion join'd.
3.25: I land; with luckless omens then adore
3.26: Their gods, and draw a line along the shore;
3.27: I lay the deep foundations of a wall,
3.28: And Aenos, nam'd from me, the city call.
3.29: To Dionaean Venus vows are paid,
3.30: And all the pow'rs that rising labors aid;
3.31: A bull on Jove's imperial altar laid.
3.32: Not far, a rising hillock stood in view;
3.33: Sharp myrtles on the sides, and cornels grew.
3.34: There, while I went to crop the sylvan scenes,
3.35: And shade our altar with their leafy greens,
3.36: I pull'd a plant- with horror I relate
3.37: A prodigy so strange and full of fate.
3.38: The rooted fibers rose, and from the wound
3.39: Black bloody drops distill'd upon the ground.
3.40: Mute and amaz'd, my hair with terror stood;
3.41: Fear shrunk my sinews, and congeal'd my blood.
3.42: Mann'd once again, another plant I try:
3.43: That other gush'd with the same sanguine dye.
3.44: Then, fearing guilt for some offense unknown,
3.45: With pray'rs and vows the Dryads I atone,
3.46: With all the sisters of the woods, and most
3.47: The God of Arms, who rules the Thracian coast,
3.48: That they, or he, these omens would avert,
3.49: Release our fears, and better signs impart.
3.50: Clear'd, as I thought, and fully fix'd at length
3.51: To learn the cause, I tugged with all my strength:
3.52: I bent my knees against the ground; once more
3.53: The violated myrtle ran with gore.
3.54: Scarce dare I tell the sequel: from the womb
3.55: Of wounded earth, and caverns of the tomb,
3.56: A groan, as of a troubled ghost, renew'd
3.57: My fright, and then these dreadful words ensued:
3.58: 'Why dost thou thus my buried body rend?
3.59: O spare the corpse of thy unhappy friend!
3.60: Spare to pollute thy pious hands with blood:
3.61: The tears distil not from the wounded wood;
3.62: But ev'ry drop this living tree contains
3.63: Is kindred blood, and ran in Trojan veins.
3.64: O fly from this unhospitable shore,
3.65: Warn'd by my fate; for I am Polydore!
3.66: Here loads of lances, in my blood embrued,
3.67: Again shoot upward, by my blood renew'd.'
3.68: "My falt'ring tongue and shiv'ring limbs declare
3.69: My horror, and in bristles rose my hair.
3.70: When Troy with Grecian arms was closely pent,
3.71: Old Priam, fearful of the war's event,
3.72: This hapless Polydore to Thracia sent:
3.73: Loaded with gold, he sent his darling, far
3.74: From noise and tumults, and destructive war,
3.75: Committed to the faithless tyrant's care;
3.76: Who, when he saw the pow'r of Troy decline,
3.77: Forsook the weaker, with the strong to join;
3.78: Broke ev'ry bond of nature and of truth,
3.79: And murder'd, for his wealth, the royal youth.
3.80: O sacred hunger of pernicious gold!
3.81: What bands of faith can impious lucre hold?
3.82: Now, when my soul had shaken off her fears,
3.83: I call my father and the Trojan peers;
3.84: Relate the prodigies of Heav'n, require
3.85: What he commands, and their advice desire.
3.86: All vote to leave that execrable shore,
3.87: Polluted with the blood of Polydore;
3.88: But, ere we sail, his fun'ral rites prepare,
3.89: Then, to his ghost, a tomb and altars rear.
3.90: In mournful pomp the matrons walk the round,
3.91: With baleful cypress and blue fillets crown'd,
3.92: With eyes dejected, and with hair unbound.
3.93: Then bowls of tepid milk and blood we pour,
3.94: And thrice invoke the soul of Polydore.
3.95: "Now, when the raging storms no longer reign,
3.96: But southern gales invite us to the main,
3.97: We launch our vessels, with a prosp'rous wind,
3.98: And leave the cities and the shores behind.
3.99: "An island in th' Aegaean main appears;
3.100: Neptune and wat'ry Doris claim it theirs.
3.101: It floated once, till Phoebus fix'd the sides
3.102: To rooted earth, and now it braves the tides.
3.103: Here, borne by friendly winds, we come ashore,
3.104: With needful ease our weary limbs restore,
3.105: And the Sun's temple and his town adore.
3.106: "Anius, the priest and king, with laurel crown'd,
3.107: His hoary locks with purple fillets bound,
3.108: Who saw my sire the Delian shore ascend,
3.109: Came forth with eager haste to meet his friend;
3.110: Invites him to his palace; and, in sign
3.111: Of ancient love, their plighted hands they join.
3.112: Then to the temple of the god I went,
3.113: And thus, before the shrine, my vows present:
3.114: 'Give, O Thymbraeus, give a resting place
3.115: To the sad relics of the Trojan race;
3.116: A seat secure, a region of their own,
3.117: A lasting empire, and a happier town.
3.118: Where shall we fix? where shall our labors end?
3.119: Whom shall we follow, and what fate attend?
3.120: Let not my pray'rs a doubtful answer find;
3.121: But in clear auguries unveil thy mind.'
3.122: Scarce had I said: he shook the holy ground,
3.123: The laurels, and the lofty hills around;
3.124: And from the tripos rush'd a bellowing sound.
3.125: Prostrate we fell; confess'd the present god,
3.126: Who gave this answer from his dark abode:
3.127: 'Undaunted youths, go, seek that mother earth
3.128: From which your ancestors derive their birth.
3.129: The soil that sent you forth, her ancient race
3.130: In her old bosom shall again embrace.
3.131: Thro' the wide world th' Aeneian house shall reign,
3.132: And children's children shall the crown sustain.'
3.133: Thus Phoebus did our future fates disclose:
3.134: A mighty tumult, mix'd with joy, arose.
3.135: "All are concern'd to know what place the god
3.136: Assign'd, and where determin'd our abode.
3.137: My father, long revolving in his mind
3.138: The race and lineage of the Trojan kind,
3.139: Thus answer'd their demands: 'Ye princes, hear
3.140: Your pleasing fortune, and dispel your fear.
3.141: The fruitful isle of Crete, well known to fame,
3.142: Sacred of old to Jove's imperial name,
3.143: In the mid ocean lies, with large command,
3.144: And on its plains a hundred cities stand.
3.145: Another Ida rises there, and we
3.146: From thence derive our Trojan ancestry.
3.147: From thence, as 't is divulg'd by certain fame,
3.148: To the Rhoetean shores old Teucrus came;
3.149: There fix'd, and there the seat of empire chose,
3.150: Ere Ilium and the Trojan tow'rs arose.
3.151: In humble vales they built their soft abodes,
3.152: Till Cybele, the mother of the gods,
3.153: With tinkling cymbals charm'd th' Idaean woods,
3.154: She secret rites and ceremonies taught,
3.155: And to the yoke the savage lions brought.
3.156: Let us the land which Heav'n appoints, explore;
3.157: Appease the winds, and seek the Gnossian shore.
3.158: If Jove assists the passage of our fleet,
3.159: The third propitious dawn discovers Crete.'
3.160: Thus having said, the sacrifices, laid
3.161: On smoking altars, to the gods he paid:
3.162: A bull, to Neptune an oblation due,
3.163: Another bull to bright Apollo slew;
3.164: A milk-white ewe, the western winds to please,
3.165: And one coal-black, to calm the stormy seas.
3.166: Ere this, a flying rumor had been spread
3.167: That fierce Idomeneus from Crete was fled,
3.168: Expell'd and exil'd; that the coast was free
3.170: "We leave the Delian ports, and put to sea;
3.171: By Naxos, fam'd for vintage, make our way;
3.172: Then green Donysa pass; and sail in sight
3.173: Of Paros' isle, with marble quarries white.
3.174: We pass the scatter'd isles of Cyclades,
3.175: That, scarce distinguish'd, seem to stud the seas.
3.176: The shouts of sailors double near the shores;
3.177: They stretch their canvas, and they ply their oars.
3.178: 'All hands aloft! for Crete! for Crete!' they cry,
3.179: And swiftly thro' the foamy billows fly.
3.180: Full on the promis'd land at length we bore,
3.181: With joy descending on the Cretan shore.
3.182: With eager haste a rising town I frame,
3.183: Which from the Trojan Pergamus I name:
3.184: The name itself was grateful; I exhort
3.185: To found their houses, and erect a fort.
3.186: Our ships are haul'd upon the yellow strand;
3.187: The youth begin to till the labor'd land;
3.188: And I myself new marriages promote,
3.189: Give laws, and dwellings I divide by lot;
3.190: When rising vapors choke the wholesome air,
3.191: And blasts of noisome winds corrupt the year;
3.193: Parch'd was the grass, and blighted was the corn:
3.194: Nor 'scape the beasts; for Sirius, from on high,
3.195: With pestilential heat infects the sky:
3.196: My men- some fall, the rest in fevers fry.
3.197: Again my father bids me seek the shore
3.198: Of sacred Delos, and the god implore,
3.199: To learn what end of woes we might expect,
3.200: And to what clime our weary course direct.
3.201: "'T was night, when ev'ry creature, void of cares,
3.202: The common gift of balmy slumber shares:
3.203: The statues of my gods (for such they seem'd),
3.204: Those gods whom I from flaming Troy redeem'd,
3.206: Full in the beams of Phoebe's ent'ring light.
3.207: Then thus they spoke, and eas'd my troubled mind:
3.208: 'What from the Delian god thou go'st to find,
3.209: He tells thee here, and sends us to relate.
3.210: Those pow'rs are we, companions of thy fate,
3.211: Who from the burning town by thee were brought,
3.212: Thy fortune follow'd, and thy safety wrought.
3.213: Thro' seas and lands as we thy steps attend,
3.214: So shall our care thy glorious race befriend.
3.215: An ample realm for thee thy fates ordain,
3.216: A town that o'er the conquer'd world shall reign.
3.217: Thou, mighty walls for mighty nations build;
3.218: Nor let thy weary mind to labors yield:
3.219: But change thy seat; for not the Delian god,
3.220: Nor we, have giv'n thee Crete for our abode.
3.221: A land there is, Hesperia call'd of old,
3.222: (The soil is fruitful, and the natives bold-
3.223: Th' Oenotrians held it once,) by later fame
3.224: Now call'd Italia, from the leader's name.
3.225: lasius there and Dardanus were born;
3.226: From thence we came, and thither must return.
3.227: Rise, and thy sire with these glad tidings greet.
3.228: Search Italy; for Jove denies thee Crete.'
3.229: "Astonish'd at their voices and their sight,
3.230: (Nor were they dreams, but visions of the night;
3.231: I saw, I knew their faces, and descried,
3.232: In perfect view, their hair with fillets tied;)
3.233: I started from my couch; a clammy sweat
3.234: On all my limbs and shiv'ring body sate.
3.235: To heav'n I lift my hands with pious haste,
3.236: And sacred incense in the flames I cast.
3.237: Thus to the gods their perfect honors done,
3.238: More cheerful, to my good old sire I run,
3.239: And tell the pleasing news. In little space
3.240: He found his error of the double race;
3.241: Not, as before he deem'd, deriv'd from Crete;
3.242: No more deluded by the doubtful seat:
3.243: Then said: 'O son, turmoil'd in Trojan fate!
3.244: Such things as these Cassandra did relate.
3.245: This day revives within my mind what she
3.246: Foretold of Troy renew'd in Italy,
3.247: And Latian lands; but who could then have thought
3.248: That Phrygian gods to Latium should be brought,
3.249: Or who believ'd what mad Cassandra taught?
3.250: Now let us go where Phoebus leads the way.'
3.251: "He said; and we with glad consent obey,
3.252: Forsake the seat, and, leaving few behind,
3.253: We spread our sails before the willing wind.
3.254: Now from the sight of land our galleys move,
3.255: With only seas around and skies above;
3.256: When o'er our heads descends a burst of rain,
3.257: And night with sable clouds involves the main;
3.258: The ruffling winds the foamy billows raise;
3.259: The scatter'd fleet is forc'd to sev'ral ways;
3.260: The face of heav'n is ravish'd from our eyes,
3.261: And in redoubled peals the roaring thunder flies.
3.262: Cast from our course, we wander in the dark.
3.263: No stars to guide, no point of land to mark.
3.265: Betwixt the night and day; such darkness reign'd
3.266: Three starless nights the doubtful navy strays,
3.267: Without distinction, and three sunless days;
3.268: The fourth renews the light, and, from our shrouds,
3.269: We view a rising land, like distant clouds;
3.270: The mountain-tops confirm the pleasing sight,
3.271: And curling smoke ascending from their height.
3.272: The canvas falls; their oars the sailors ply;
3.273: From the rude strokes the whirling waters fly.
3.274: At length I land upon the Strophades,
3.275: Safe from the danger of the stormy seas.
3.276: Those isles are compass'd by th' Ionian main,
3.277: The dire abode where the foul Harpies reign,
3.278: Forc'd by the winged warriors to repair
3.279: To their old homes, and leave their costly fare.
3.280: Monsters more fierce offended Heav'n ne'er sent
3.281: From hell's abyss, for human punishment:
3.282: With virgin faces, but with wombs obscene,
3.283: Foul paunches, and with ordure still unclean;
3.284: With claws for hands, and looks for ever lean.
3.285: "We landed at the port, and soon beheld
3.286: Fat herds of oxen graze the flow'ry field,
3.287: And wanton goats without a keeper stray'd.
3.288: With weapons we the welcome prey invade,
3.289: Then call the gods for partners of our feast,
3.290: And Jove himself, the chief invited guest.
3.291: We spread the tables on the greensward ground;
3.292: We feed with hunger, and the bowls go round;
3.293: When from the mountain-tops, with hideous cry,
3.294: And clatt'ring wings, the hungry Harpies fly;
3.295: They snatch the meat, defiling all they find,
3.296: And, parting, leave a loathsome stench behind.
3.297: Close by a hollow rock, again we sit,
3.298: New dress the dinner, and the beds refit,
3.299: Secure from sight, beneath a pleasing shade,
3.300: Where tufted trees a native arbor made.
3.301: Again the holy fires on altars burn;
3.302: And once again the rav'nous birds return,
3.303: Or from the dark recesses where they lie,
3.304: Or from another quarter of the sky;
3.305: With filthy claws their odious meal repeat,
3.306: And mix their loathsome ordures with their meat.
3.307: I bid my friends for vengeance then prepare,
3.308: And with the hellish nation wage the war.
3.309: They, as commanded, for the fight provide,
3.310: And in the grass their glitt'ring weapons hide;
3.311: Then, when along the crooked shore we hear
3.312: Their clatt'ring wings, and saw the foes appear,
3.313: Misenus sounds a charge: we take th' alarm,
3.314: And our strong hands with swords and bucklers arm.
3.315: In this new kind of combat all employ
3.316: Their utmost force, the monsters to destroy.
3.317: In vain- the fated skin is proof to wounds;
3.318: And from their plumes the shining sword rebounds.
3.319: At length rebuff'd, they leave their mangled prey,
3.320: And their stretch'd pinions to the skies display.
3.321: Yet one remain'd- the messenger of Fate:
3.322: High on a craggy cliff Celaeno sate,
3.323: And thus her dismal errand did relate:
3.324: 'What! not contented with our oxen slain,
3.325: Dare you with Heav'n an impious war maintain,
3.326: And drive the Harpies from their native reign?
3.327: Heed therefore what I say; and keep in mind
3.328: What Jove decrees, what Phoebus has design'd,
3.329: And I, the Furies' queen, from both relate-
3.330: You seek th' Italian shores, foredoom'd by fate:
3.331: Th' Italian shores are granted you to find,
3.332: And a safe passage to the port assign'd.
3.333: But know, that ere your promis'd walls you build,
3.334: My curses shall severely be fulfill'd.
3.335: Fierce famine is your lot for this misdeed,
3.336: Reduc'd to grind the plates on which you feed.'
3.337: She said, and to the neighb'ring forest flew.
3.338: Our courage fails us, and our fears renew.
3.339: Hopeless to win by war, to pray'rs we fall,
3.340: And on th' offended Harpies humbly call,
3.341: And whether gods or birds obscene they were,
3.342: Our vows for pardon and for peace prefer.
3.344: And lifting up to heav'n his hands and eyes,
3.345: Ador'd the greater gods: 'Avert,' said he,
3.347: And from th' impending curse a pious people free!'
3.348: "Thus having said, he bids us put to sea;
3.349: We loose from shore our haulsers, and obey,
3.350: And soon with swelling sails pursue the wat'ry way.
3.351: Amidst our course, Zacynthian woods appear;
3.352: And next by rocky Neritos we steer:
3.353: We fly from Ithaca's detested shore,
3.354: And curse the land which dire Ulysses bore.
3.355: At length Leucate's cloudy top appears,
3.356: And the Sun's temple, which the sailor fears.
3.357: Resolv'd to breathe a while from labor past,
3.358: Our crooked anchors from the prow we cast,
3.359: And joyful to the little city haste.
3.360: Here, safe beyond our hopes, our vows we pay
3.361: To Jove, the guide and patron of our way.
3.362: The customs of our country we pursue,
3.363: And Trojan games on Actian shores renew.
3.364: Our youth their naked limbs besmear with oil,
3.365: And exercise the wrastlers' noble toil;
3.366: Pleas'd to have sail'd so long before the wind,
3.367: And left so many Grecian towns behind.
3.368: The sun had now fulfill'd his annual course,
3.369: And Boreas on the seas display'd his force:
3.370: I fix'd upon the temple's lofty door
3.371: The brazen shield which vanquish'd Abas bore;
3.372: The verse beneath my name and action speaks:
3.373: 'These arms Aeneas took from conqu'ring Greeks.'
3.374: Then I command to weigh; the seamen ply
3.375: Their sweeping oars; the smoking billows fly.
3.376: The sight of high Phaeacia soon we lost,
3.377: And skimm'd along Epirus' rocky coast.
3.378: "Then to Chaonia's port our course we bend,
3.379: And, landed, to Buthrotus' heights ascend.
3.380: Here wondrous things were loudly blaz'd fame:
3.381: How Helenus reviv'd the Trojan name,
3.382: And reign'd in Greece; that Priam's captive son
3.383: Succeeded Pyrrhus in his bed and throne;
3.384: And fair Andromache, restor'd by fate,
3.385: Once more was happy in a Trojan mate.
3.386: I leave my galleys riding in the port,
3.387: And long to see the new Dardanian court.
3.388: By chance, the mournful queen, before the gate,
3.389: Then solemniz'd her former husband's fate.
3.390: Green altars, rais'd of turf, with gifts she crown'd,
3.391: And sacred priests in order stand around,
3.392: And thrice the name of hapless Hector sound.
3.393: The grove itself resembles Ida's wood;
3.394: And Simois seem'd the well-dissembled flood.
3.395: But when at nearer distance she beheld
3.396: My shining armor and my Trojan shield,
3.397: Astonish'd at the sight, the vital heat
3.398: Forsakes her limbs; her veins no longer beat:
3.399: She faints, she falls, and scarce recov'ring strength,
3.400: Thus, with a falt'ring tongue, she speaks at length:
3.401: "'Are you alive, O goddess-born ?' she said,
3.402: 'Or if a ghost, then where is Hector's shade?'
3.403: At this, she cast a loud and frightful cry.
3.404: With broken words I made this brief reply:
3.405: 'All of me that remains appears in sight;
3.406: I live, if living be to loathe the light.
3.407: No phantom; but I drag a wretched life,
3.408: My fate resembling that of Hector's wife.
3.409: What have you suffer'd since you lost your lord?
3.410: By what strange blessing are you now restor'd?
3.411: Still are you Hector's? or is Hector fled,
3.412: And his remembrance lost in Pyrrhus' bed?'
3.413: With eyes dejected, in a lowly tone,
3.414: After a modest pause she thus begun:
3.415: "'O only happy maid of Priam's race,
3.416: Whom death deliver'd from the foes' embrace!
3.417: Commanded on Achilles' tomb to die,
3.418: Not forc'd, like us, to hard captivity,
3.419: Or in a haughty master's arms to lie.
3.420: In Grecian ships unhappy we were borne,
3.421: Endur'd the victor's lust, sustain'd the scorn:
3.422: Thus I submitted to the lawless pride
3.423: Of Pyrrhus, more a handmaid than a bride.
3.424: Cloy'd with possession, he forsook my bed,
3.425: And Helen's lovely daughter sought to wed;
3.426: Then me to Trojan Helenus resign'd,
3.427: And his two slaves in equal marriage join'd;
3.428: Till young Orestes, pierc'd with deep despair,
3.429: And longing to redeem the promis'd fair,
3.430: Before Apollo's altar slew the ravisher.
3.431: By Pyrrhus' death the kingdom we regain'd:
3.432: At least one half with Helenus remain'd.
3.433: Our part, from Chaon, he Chaonia calls,
3.434: And names from Pergamus his rising walls.
3.435: But you, what fates have landed on our coast?
3.436: What gods have sent you, or what storms have toss'd?
3.437: Does young Ascanius life and health enjoy,
3.438: Sav'd from the ruins of unhappy Troy?
3.439: O tell me how his mother's loss he bears,
3.440: What hopes are promis'd from his blooming years,
3.441: How much of Hector in his face appears?'
3.442: She spoke; and mix'd her speech with mournful cries,
3.443: And fruitless tears came trickling from her eyes.
3.444: "At length her lord descends upon the plain,
3.445: In pomp, attended with a num'rous train;
3.446: Receives his friends, and to the city leads,
3.447: And tears of joy amidst his welcome sheds.
3.448: Proceeding on, another Troy I see,
3.449: Or, in less compass, Troy's epitome.
3.450: A riv'let by the name of Xanthus ran,
3.451: And I embrace the Scaean gate again.
3.452: My friends in porticoes were entertain'd,
3.453: And feasts and pleasures thro' the city reign'd.
3.454: The tables fill'd the spacious hall around,
3.455: And golden bowls with sparkling wine were crown'd.
3.456: Two days we pass'd in mirth, till friendly gales,
3.457: Blown from the supplied our swelling sails.
3.458: Then to the royal seer I thus began:
3.459: 'O thou, who know'st, beyond the reach of man,
3.460: The laws of heav'n, and what the stars decree;
3.462: From his own tripod, and his holy tree;
3.463: Skill'd in the wing'd inhabitants of air,
3.464: What auspices their notes and flights declare:
3.465: O say- for all religious rites portend
3.466: A happy voyage, and a prosp'rous end;
3.467: And ev'ry power and omen of the sky
3.468: Direct my course for destin'd Italy;
3.469: But only dire Celaeno, from the gods,
3.471: O say what dangers I am first to shun,
3.472: What toils vanquish, and what course to run.'
3.474: The greater gods; their pardon then implores;
3.475: Unbinds the fillet from his holy head;
3.476: To Phoebus, next, my trembling steps he led,
3.477: Full of religious doubts and awful dread.
3.478: Then, with his god possess'd, before the shrine,
3.479: These words proceeded from his mouth divine:
3.481: With greater auspices of good than ill,
3.482: Foreshows thy voyage, and thy course directs;
3.483: Thy fates conspire, and Jove himself protects,)
3.484: Of many things some few I shall explain,
3.485: Teach thee to shun the dangers of the main,
3.486: And how at length the promis'd shore to gain.
3.487: The rest the fates from Helenus conceal,
3.488: And Juno's angry pow'r forbids to tell.
3.489: First, then, that happy shore, that seems so nigh,
3.490: Will far from your deluded wishes fly;
3.491: Long tracts of seas divide your hopes from Italy:
3.492: For you must cruise along Sicilian shores,
3.493: And stem the currents with your struggling oars;
3.494: Then round th' Italian coast your navy steer;
3.495: And, after this, to Circe's island veer;
3.496: And, last, before your new foundations rise,
3.497: Must pass the Stygian lake, and view the nether
3.498: Now mark the signs of future ease and rest,
3.499: And bear them safely treasur'd in thy breast.
3.500: When, in the shady shelter of a wood,
3.501: And near the margin of a gentle flood,
3.502: Thou shalt behold a sow upon the ground,
3.503: With thirty sucking young encompass'd round;
3.504: The dam and offspring white as falling snow-
3.505: These on thy city shall their name bestow,
3.506: And there shall end thy labors and thy woe.
3.507: Nor let the threaten'd famine fright thy mind,
3.508: For Phoebus will assist, and Fate the way will find.
3.509: Let not thy course to that ill coast be bent,
3.510: Which fronts from far th' Epirian continent:
3.511: Those parts are all by Grecian foes possess'd;
3.512: The salvage Locrians here the shores infest;
3.513: There fierce Idomeneus his city builds,
3.514: And guards with arms the Salentinian fields;
3.515: And on the mountain's brow Petilia stands,
3.516: Which Philoctetes with his troops commands.
3.517: Ev'n when thy fleet is landed on the shore,
3.518: And priests with holy vows the gods adore,
3.519: Then with a purple veil involve your eyes,
3.520: Lest hostile faces blast the sacrifice.
3.521: These rites and customs to the rest commend,
3.522: That to your pious race they may descend.
3.523: "'When, parted hence, the wind, that ready
3.524: For Sicily, shall bear you to the straits
3.525: Where proud Pelorus opes a wider way,
3.526: Tack to the larboard, and stand off to sea:
3.527: Veer starboard sea and land. Th' Italian shore
3.528: And fair Sicilia's coast were one, before
3.529: An earthquake caus'd the flaw: the roaring tides
3.530: The passage broke that land from land divides;
3.531: And where the lands retir'd, the rushing ocean rides.
3.532: Distinguish'd by the straits, on either hand,
3.533: Now rising cities in long order stand,
3.534: And fruitful fields: so much can time invade
3.535: The mold'ring work that beauteous Nature made.
3.536: Far on the right, her dogs foul Scylla hides:
3.537: Charybdis roaring on the left presides,
3.538: And in her greedy whirlpool sucks the tides;
3.539: Then spouts them from below: with fury driv'n,
3.540: The waves mount up and wash the face of heav'n.
3.541: But Scylla from her den, with open jaws,
3.542: The sinking vessel in her eddy draws,
3.543: Then dashes on the rocks. A human face,
3.544: And virgin bosom, hides her tail's disgrace:
3.545: Her parts obscene below the waves descend,
3.546: With dogs inclos'd, and in a dolphin end.
3.547: 'T is safer, then, to bear aloof to sea,
3.548: And coast Pachynus, tho' with more delay,
3.549: Than once to view misshapen Scylla near,
3.550: And the loud yell of wat'ry wolves to hear.
3.551: "'Besides, if faith to Helenus be due,
3.552: And if prophetic Phoebus tell me true,
3.553: Do not this precept of your friend forget,
3.554: Which therefore more than once I must repeat:
3.555: Above the rest, great Juno's name adore;
3.556: Pay vows to Juno; Juno's aid implore.
3.557: Let gifts be to the mighty queen design'd,
3.558: And mollify with pray'rs her haughty mind.
3.559: Thus, at the length, your passage shall be free,
3.560: And you shall safe descend on Italy.
3.561: Arriv'd at Cumae, when you view the flood
3.562: Of black Avernus, and the sounding wood,
3.563: The mad prophetic Sibyl you shall find,
3.564: Dark in a cave, and on a rock reclin'd.
3.565: She sings the fates, and, in her frantic fits,
3.566: The notes and names, inscrib'd, to leafs commits.
3.567: What she commits to leafs, in order laid,
3.568: Before the cavern's entrance are display'd:
3.569: Unmov'd they lie; but, if a blast of wind
3.570: Without, or vapors issue from behind,
3.571: The leafs are borne aloft in liquid air,
3.572: And she resumes no more her museful care,
3.573: Nor gathers from the rocks her scatter'd verse,
3.574: Nor sets in order what the winds disperse.
3.575: Thus, many not succeeding, most upbraid
3.576: The madness of the visionary maid,
3.577: And with loud curses leave the mystic shade.
3.578: "'Think it not loss of time a while to stay,
3.579: Tho' thy companions chide thy long delay;
3.580: Tho' summon'd to the seas, tho' pleasing gales
3.581: Invite thy course, and stretch thy swelling sails:
3.582: But beg the sacred priestess to relate
3.583: With willing words, and not to write thy fate.
3.584: The fierce Italian people she will show,
3.585: And all thy wars, and all thy future woe,
3.586: And what thou may'st avoid, and what must undergo.
3.587: She shall direct thy course, instruct thy mind,
3.588: And teach thee how the happy shores to find.
3.589: This is what Heav'n allows me to relate:
3.590: Now part in peace; pursue thy better fate,
3.591: And raise, by strength of arms, the Trojan state.'
3.592: "This when the priest with friendly voice declar'd,
3.593: He gave me license, and rich gifts prepar'd:
3.594: Bounteous of treasure, he supplied my want
3.595: With heavy gold, and polish'd elephant;
3.596: Then Dodonaean caldrons put on board,
3.597: And ev'ry ship with sums of silver stor'd.
3.598: A trusty coat of mail to me he sent,
3.599: Thrice chain'd with gold, for use and ornament;
3.600: The helm of Pyrrhus added to the rest,
3.601: That flourish'd with a plume and waving crest.
3.602: Nor was my sire forgotten, nor my friends;
3.603: And large recruits he to my navy sends:
3.604: Men, horses, captains, arms, and warlike stores;
3.605: Supplies new pilots, and new sweeping oars.
3.606: Meantime, my sire commands to hoist our sails,
3.607: Lest we should lose the first auspicious gales.
3.608: "The prophet bless'd the parting crew, and last,
3.609: With words like these, his ancient friend embrac'd:
3.610: 'Old happy man, the care of gods above,
3.611: Whom heav'nly Venus honor'd with her love,
3.612: And twice preserv'd thy life, when Troy was lost,
3.613: Behold from far the wish'd Ausonian coast:
3.614: There land; but take a larger compass round,
3.615: For that before is all forbidden ground.
3.616: The shore that Phoebus has design'd for you,
3.617: At farther distance lies, conceal'd from view.
3.618: Go happy hence, and seek your new abodes,
3.619: Blest in a son, and favor'd by the gods:
3.620: For I with useless words prolong your stay,
3.621: When southern gales have summon'd you away.'
3.622: "Nor less the queen our parting thence deplor'd,
3.623: Nor was less bounteous than her Trojan lord.
3.624: A noble present to my son she brought,
3.625: A robe with flow'rs on golden tissue wrought,
3.626: A phrygian vest; and loads with gifts beside
3.627: Of precious texture, and of Asian pride.
3.629: Which in my youth with happier hands I wove:
3.630: Regard these trifles for the giver's sake;
3.631: 'T is the last present Hector's wife can make.
3.632: Thou call'st my lost Astyanax to mind;
3.633: In thee his features and his form I find:
3.634: His eyes so sparkled with a lively flame;
3.635: Such were his motions; such was all his frame;
3.636: And ah! had Heav'n so pleas'd, his years had been the
3.637: "With tears I took my last adieu, and said:
3.639: Leaves you no farther wish. My diff'rent state,
3.641: To you a quiet seat the gods allow:
3.642: You have no shores to search, no seas to plow,
3.643: Nor fields of flying Italy to chase:
3.645: You see another Simois, and enjoy
3.646: The labor of your hands, another Troy,
3.647: With better auspice than her ancient tow'rs,
3.648: And less obnoxious to the Grecian pow'rs.
3.649: If e'er the gods, whom I with vows adore,
3.650: Conduct my steps to Tiber's happy shore;
3.651: If ever I ascend the Latian throne,
3.652: And build a city I may call my own;
3.653: As both of us our birth from Troy derive,
3.654: So let our kindred lines in concord live,
3.655: And both in acts of equal friendship strive.
3.656: Our fortunes, good or bad, shall be the same:
3.657: The double Troy shall differ but in name;
3.658: That what we now begin may never end,
3.659: But long to late posterity descend.'
3.660: "Near the Ceraunian rocks our course we bore;
3.661: The shortest passage to th' Italian shore.
3.662: Now had the sun withdrawn his radiant light,
3.663: And hills were hid in dusky shades of night:
3.664: We land, and, on the bosom Of the ground,
3.665: A safe retreat and a bare lodging found.
3.666: Close by the shore we lay; the sailors keep
3.667: Their watches, and the rest securely sleep.
3.668: The night, proceeding on with silent pace,
3.669: Stood in her noon, and view'd with equal face
3.670: Her steepy rise and her declining race.
3.671: Then wakeful Palinurus rose, to spy
3.672: The face of heav'n, and the nocturnal sky;
3.673: And listen'd ev'ry breath of air to try;
3.674: Observes the stars, and notes their sliding course,
3.675: The Pleiads, Hyads, and their wat'ry force;
3.676: And both the Bears is careful to behold,
3.677: And bright Orion, arm'd with burnish'd gold.
3.678: Then, when he saw no threat'ning tempest nigh,
3.679: But a sure promise of a settled sky,
3.680: He gave the sign to weigh; we break our sleep,
3.681: Forsake the pleasing shore, and plow the deep.
3.682: "And now the rising morn with rosy light
3.683: Adorns the skies, and puts the stars to flight;
3.684: When we from far, like bluish mists, descry
3.685: The hills, and then the plains, of Italy.
3.686: Achates first pronounc'd the joyful sound;
3.688: My sire Anchises crown'd a cup with wine,
3.689: And, off'ring, thus implor'd the pow'rs divine:
3.690: 'Ye gods, presiding over lands and seas,
3.691: And you who raging winds and waves appease,
3.692: Breathe on our swelling sails a prosp'rous wind,
3.693: And smooth our passage to the port assign'd!'
3.694: The gentle gales their flagging force renew,
3.695: And now the happy harbor is in view.
3.696: Minerva's temple then salutes our sight,
3.697: Plac'd, as a landmark, on the mountain's height.
3.698: We furl our sails, and turn the prows to shore;
3.699: The curling waters round the galleys roar.
3.700: The land lies open to the raging east,
3.701: Then, bending like a bow, with rocks compress'd,
3.702: Shuts out the storms; the winds and waves complain,
3.703: And vent their malice on the cliffs in vain.
3.704: The port lies hid within; on either side
3.705: Two tow'ring rocks the narrow mouth divide.
3.706: The temple, which aloft we view'd before,
3.707: To distance flies, and seems to shun the shore.
3.708: Scarce landed, the first omens I beheld
3.709: Were four white steeds that cropp'd the flow'ry
3.710: 'War, war is threaten'd from this foreign ground,'
3.711: My father cried, 'where warlike steeds are found.
3.712: Yet, since reclaim'd to chariots they submit,
3.713: And bend to stubborn yokes, and champ the bit,
3.714: Peace may succeed to war.' Our way we bend
3.715: To Pallas, and the sacred hill ascend;
3.716: There prostrate to the fierce virago pray,
3.717: Whose temple was the landmark of our way.
3.718: Each with a Phrygian mantle veil'd his head,
3.719: And all commands of Helenus obey'd,
3.720: And pious rites to Grecian Juno paid.

3.722: To sea, forsaking that suspected land.
3.723: "From hence Tarentum's bay appears in view,
3.724: For Hercules renown'd, if fame be true.
3.727: For shipwrecks fear'd. Mount Aetna thence we spy,
3.728: Known by the smoky flames which cloud the sky.
3.729: Far off we hear the waves with surly sound
3.730: Invade the rocks, the rocks their groans rebound.
3.731: The billows break upon the sounding strand,
3.732: And roll the rising tide, impure with sand.
3.733: Then thus Anchises, in experience old:
3.734: ''T is that Charybdis which the seer foretold,
3.735: And those the promis'd rocks! Bear off to sea!'
3.736: With haste the frighted mariners obey.
3.737: First Palinurus to the larboard veer'd;
3.738: Then all the fleet by his example steer'd.
3.739: To heav'n aloft on ridgy waves we ride,
3.740: Then down to hell descend, when they divide;
3.741: And thrice our galleys knock'd the stony ground,
3.742: And thrice the hollow rocks return'd the sound,
3.743: And thrice we saw the stars, that stood with dews
3.744: The flagging winds forsook us, with the sun;
3.745: And, wearied, on Cyclopian shores we run.
3.746: The port capacious, and secure from wind,
3.747: Is to the foot of thund'ring Aetna join'd.
3.748: By turns a pitchy cloud she rolls on high;
3.749: By turns hot embers from her entrails fly,
3.750: And flakes of mounting flames, that lick the sky.
3.751: Oft from her bowels massy rocks are thrown,
3.752: And, shiver'd by the force, come piecemeal down.
3.753: Oft liquid lakes of burning sulphur flow,
3.754: Fed from the fiery springs that boil below.
3.755: Enceladus, they say, transfix'd by Jove,
3.756: With blasted limbs came tumbling from above;
3.757: And, where he fell, th' avenging father drew
3.758: This flaming hill, and on his body threw.
3.759: As often as he turns his weary sides,
3.760: He shakes the solid isle, and smoke the heavens
3.761: In shady woods we pass the tedious night,

3.763: Of which no cause is offer'd to the sight;
3.764: For not one star was kindled in the sky,
3.765: Nor could the moon her borrow'd light supply;
3.766: For misty clouds involv'd the firmament,

3.768: "Scarce had the rising sun the day reveal'd,
3.769: Scarce had his heat the pearly dews dispell'd,
3.770: When from the woods there bolts, before our sight,
3.771: Somewhat betwixt a mortal and a sprite,
3.772: So thin, so ghastly meager, and so wan,
3.773: So bare of flesh, he scarce resembled man.
3.774: This thing, all tatter'd, seem'd from far t' implore
3.775: Our pious aid, and pointed to the shore.
3.776: We look behind, then view his shaggy beard;
3.777: His clothes were tagg'd with thorns, and filth his limbs
3.779: The rest, in mien, in habit, and in face,
3.780: Appear'd a Greek, and such indeed he was.
3.781: He cast on us, from far, a frightful view,
3.782: Whom soon for Trojans and for foes he knew;
3.783: Stood still, and paus'd; then all at once began
3.784: To stretch his limbs, and trembled as he ran.
3.785: Soon as approach'd, upon his knees he falls,
3.786: And thus with tears and sighs for pity calls:
3.787: 'Now, by the pow'rs above, and what we share
3.788: From Nature's common gift, this vital air,
3.789: O Trojans, take me hence! I beg no more;
3.790: But bear me far from this unhappy shore.
3.791: 'T is true, I am a Greek, and farther own,
3.792: Among your foes besieg'd th' imperial town.
3.793: For such demerits if my death be due,
3.794: No more for this abandon'd life I sue;
3.795: This only favor let my tears obtain,
3.796: To throw me headlong in the rapid main:
3.797: Since nothing more than death my crime demands,
3.798: I die content, to die by human hands.'
3.799: He said, and on his knees my knees embrac'd:
3.800: I bade him boldly tell his fortune past,
3.801: His present state, his lineage, and his name,
3.802: Th' occasion of his fears, and whence he came.
3.803: The good Anchises rais'd him with his hand;
3.804: Who, thus encourag'd, answer'd our demand:
3.805: 'From Ithaca, my native soil, I came
3.806: To Troy; and Achaemenides my name.
3.807: Me my poor father with Ulysses sent;
3.808: (O had I stay'd, with poverty content!)
3.809: But, fearful for themselves, my countrymen
3.810: Left me forsaken in the Cyclops' den.
3.811: The cave, tho' large, was dark; the dismal floor
3.812: Was pav'd with mangled limbs and putrid gore.
3.813: Our monstrous host, of more than human size,
3.814: Erects his head, and stares within the skies;
3.815: Bellowing his voice, and horrid is his hue.
3.816: Ye gods, remove this plague from mortal view!
3.817: The joints of slaughter'd wretches are his food;
3.818: And for his wine he quaffs the streaming blood.
3.819: These eyes beheld, when with his spacious hand
3.820: He seiz'd two captives of our Grecian band;
3.821: Stretch'd on his back, he dash'd against the stones
3.822: Their broken bodies, and their crackling bones:
3.823: With spouting blood the purple pavement swims,
3.824: While the dire glutton grinds the trembling limbs.
3.826: Nor thoughtless of his own unhappy state;

3.828: While fast asleep the giant lay supine,

3.830: His indigested foam, and morsels raw;
3.831: We pray; we cast the lots, and then surround

3.833: Each, as he could approach him, lends a hand

3.843: Such, and so vast as Polypheme appears,

3.858: While all around my longing eyes I cast,

3.860: On those I fix'd my hopes, to these I run;
3.861: 'T is all I ask, this cruel race to shun;
3.862: What other death you please, yourselves bestow.'

4.1: But anxious cares already seiz'd the queen:
4.2: She fed within her veins a flame unseen;
4.3: The hero's valor, acts, and birth inspire
4.4: Her soul with love, and fan the secret fire.
4.5: His words, his looks, imprinted in her heart,
4.6: Improve the passion, and increase the smart.
4.7: Now, when the purple morn had chas'd away
4.8: The dewy shadows, and restor'd the day,
4.9: Her sister first with early care she sought,
4.10: And thus in mournful accents eas'd her thought:
4.11: "My dearest Anna, what new dreams affright
4.12: My lab'ring soul! what visions of the night
4.13: Disturb my quiet, and distract my breast
4.14: With strange ideas of our Trojan guest!
4.15: His worth, his actions, and majestic air,
4.16: A man descended from the gods declare.
4.17: Fear ever argues a degenerate kind;
4.18: His birth is well asserted by his mind.
4.19: Then, what he suffer'd, when by Fate betray'd!
4.20: What brave attempts for falling Troy he made!
4.21: Such were his looks, so gracefully he spoke,
4.22: That, were I not resolv'd against the yoke
4.23: Of hapless marriage, never to be curst
4.24: With second love, so fatal was my first,
4.25: To this one error I might yield again;
4.26: For, since Sichaeus was untimely slain,
4.27: This only man is able to subvert
4.28: The fix'd foundations of my stubborn heart.
4.29: And, to confess my frailty, to my shame,
4.30: Somewhat I find within, if not the same,
4.31: Too like the sparkles of my former flame.
4.32: But first let yawning earth a passage rend,
4.33: And let me thro' the dark abyss descend;
4.34: First let avenging Jove, with flames from high,
4.35: Drive down this body to the nether sky,
4.36: Condemn'd with ghosts in endless night to lie,
4.37: Before I break the plighted faith I gave!
4.38: No! he who had my vows shall ever have;
4.39: For, whom I lov'd on earth, I worship in the grave."
4.40: She said: the tears ran gushing from her eyes,
4.41: And stopp'd her speech. Her sister thus replies:
4.42: "O dearer than the vital air I breathe,
4.43: Will you to grief your blooming years bequeath,
4.44: Condemn'd to waste in woes your lonely life,
4.45: Without the joys of mother or of wife?
4.46: Think you these tears, this pompous train of woe,
4.47: Are known or valued by the ghosts below?
4.48: I grant that, while your sorrows yet were green,
4.49: It well became a woman, and a queen,
4.50: The vows of Tyrian princes to neglect,
4.51: To scorn Hyarbas, and his love reject,
4.52: With all the Libyan lords of mighty name;
4.53: But will you fight against a pleasing flame!
4.54: This little spot of land, which Heav'n bestows,
4.55: On ev'ry side is hemm'd with warlike foes;
4.56: Gaetulian cities here are spread around,
4.57: And fierce Numidians there your frontiers bound;
4.58: Here lies a barren waste of thirsty land,
4.59: And there the Syrtes raise the moving sand;
4.60: Barcaean troops besiege the narrow shore,
4.61: And from the sea Pygmalion threatens more.
4.62: Propitious Heav'n, and gracious Juno, lead
4.63: This wand'ring navy to your needful aid:
4.64: How will your empire spread, your city rise,
4.65: From such a union, and with such allies?
4.66: Implore the favor of the pow'rs above,
4.67: And leave the conduct of the rest to love.
4.69: And still invent occasions of their stay,
4.70: Till storms and winter winds shall cease to threat,
4.71: And planks and oars repair their shatter'd fleet."
4.72: These words, which from a friend and sister came,
4.73: With ease resolv'd the scruples of her fame,
4.74: And added fury to the kindled flame.
4.75: Inspir'd with hope, the project they pursue;
4.77: A chosen ewe of two years old they pay
4.78: To Ceres, Bacchus, and the God of Day;
4.79: Preferring Juno's pow'r, for Juno ties
4.80: The nuptial knot and makes the marriage joys.
4.81: The beauteous queen before her altar stands,
4.82: And holds the golden goblet in her hands.
4.83: A milk-white heifer she with flow'rs adorns,
4.84: And pours the ruddy wine betwixt her horns;
4.85: And, while the priests with pray'r the gods invoke,
4.86: She feeds their altars with Sabaean smoke,
4.87: With hourly care the sacrifice renews,
4.88: And anxiously the panting entrails views.
4.89: What priestly rites, alas! what pious art,
4.90: What vows avail to cure a bleeding heart!
4.91: A gentle fire she feeds within her veins,
4.92: Where the soft god secure in silence reigns.
4.93: Sick with desire, and seeking him she loves,
4.94: From street to street the raving Dido roves.
4.95: So when the watchful shepherd, from the blind,
4.96: Wounds with a random shaft the careless hind,
4.97: Distracted with her pain she flies the woods,
4.98: Bounds o'er the lawn, and seeks the silent floods,
4.99: With fruitless care; for still the fatal dart
4.100: Sticks in her side, and rankles in her heart.
4.101: And now she leads the Trojan chief along
4.102: The lofty walls, amidst the busy throng;
4.103: Displays her Tyrian wealth, and rising town,
4.104: Which love, without his labor, makes his own.
4.105: This pomp she shows, to tempt her wand'ring guest;
4.106: Her falt'ring tongue forbids to speak the rest.
4.107: When day declines, and feasts renew the night,
4.108: Still on his face she feeds her famish'd sight;
4.109: She longs again to hear the prince relate
4.110: His own adventures and the Trojan fate.
4.111: He tells it o'er and o'er; but still in vain,
4.112: For still she begs to hear it once again.
4.113: The hearer on the speaker's mouth depends,
4.114: And thus the tragic story never ends.
4.115: Then, when they part, when Phoebe's paler light
4.116: Withdraws, and falling stars to sleep invite,
4.117: She last remains, when ev'ry guest is gone,
4.118: Sits on the bed he press'd, and sighs alone;
4.119: Absent, her absent hero sees and hears;
4.120: Or in her bosom young Ascanius bears,
4.121: And seeks the father's image in the child,
4.122: If love by likeness might be so beguil'd.
4.123: Meantime the rising tow'rs are at a stand;
4.124: No labors exercise the youthful band,
4.125: Nor use of arts, nor toils of arms they know;
4.126: The mole is left unfinish'd to the foe;
4.127: The mounds, the works, the walls, neglected lie,
4.128: Short of their promis'd heighth, that seem'd to threat the
4.129: But when imperial Juno, from above,
4.130: Saw Dido fetter'd in the chains of love,
4.131: Hot with the venom which her veins inflam'd,
4.132: And by no sense of shame to be reclaim'd,
4.133: With soothing words to Venus she begun:
4.134: "High praises, endless honors, you have won,
4.135: And mighty trophies, with your worthy son!
4.136: Two gods a silly woman have undone!
4.137: Nor am I ignorant, you both suspect
4.138: This rising city, which my hands erect:
4.139: But shall celestial discord never cease?
4.140: 'T is better ended in a lasting peace.
4.141: You stand possess'd of all your soul desir'd:
4.142: Poor Dido with consuming love is fir'd.
4.143: Your Trojan with my Tyrian let us join;
4.144: So Dido shall be yours, Aeneas mine:
4.145: One common kingdom, one united line.
4.146: Eliza shall a Dardan lord obey,
4.147: And lofty Carthage for a dow'r convey."
4.148: Then Venus, who her hidden fraud descried,
4.149: Which would the scepter of the world misguide
4.150: To Libyan shores, thus artfully replied:
4.151: "Who, but a fool, would wars with Juno choose,
4.152: And such alliance and such gifts refuse,
4.153: If Fortune with our joint desires comply?
4.154: The doubt is all from Jove and destiny;
4.155: Lest he forbid, with absolute command,
4.156: To mix the people in one common land-
4.157: Or will the Trojan and the Tyrian line
4.158: In lasting leagues and sure succession join?
4.159: But you, the partner of his bed and throne,
4.160: May move his mind; my wishes are your own."
4.162: Time urges, now, to perfect this affair:
4.163: Attend my counsel, and the secret share.
4.164: When next the Sun his rising light displays,
4.165: And gilds the world below with purple rays,
4.166: The queen, Aeneas, and the Tyrian court
4.167: Shall to the shady woods, for sylvan game, resort.
4.168: There, while the huntsmen pitch their toils around,
4.169: And cheerful horns from side to side resound,
4.170: A pitchy cloud shall cover all the plain
4.171: With hail, and thunder, and tempestuous rain;
4.172: The fearful train shall take their speedy flight,
4.173: Dispers'd, and all involv'd in gloomy night;
4.174: One cave a grateful shelter shall afford
4.175: To the fair princess and the Trojan lord.
4.176: I will myself the bridal bed prepare,
4.177: If you, to bless the nuptials, will be there:
4.178: So shall their loves be crown'd with due delights,
4.179: And Hymen shall be present at the rites."
4.180: The Queen of Love consents, and closely smiles
4.181: At her vain project, and discover'd wiles.
