4.226: The clanking lash, and goring of the steel.
4.227: Impatiently he views the feeble prey,
4.228: Wishing some nobler beast to cross his way,
4.229: And rather would the tusky boar attend,
4.230: Or see the tawny lion downward bend.
4.231: Meantime, the gath'ring clouds obscure the skies:
4.232: From pole to pole the forky lightning flies;
4.233: The rattling thunders roll; and Juno pours
4.234: A wintry deluge down, and sounding show'rs.
4.235: The company, dispers'd, to converts ride,
4.236: And seek the homely cots, or mountain's hollow side.
4.237: The rapid rains, descending from the hills,
4.238: To rolling torrents raise the creeping rills.
4.239: The queen and prince, as love or fortune guides,
4.240: One common cavern in her bosom hides.
4.241: Then first the trembling earth the signal gave,
4.242: And flashing fires enlighten all the cave;
4.243: Hell from below, and Juno from above,
4.244: And howling nymphs, were conscious of their love.
4.245: From this ill-omen'd hour in time arose
4.246: Debate and death, and all succeeding woes.
4.247: The queen, whom sense of honor could not move,
4.248: No longer made a secret of her love,
4.249: But call'd it marriage, by that specious name
4.250: To veil the crime and sanctify the shame.
4.251: The loud report thro' Libyan cities goes.
4.252: Fame, the great ill, from small beginnings grows:
4.253: Swift from the first; and ev'ry moment brings
4.254: New vigor to her flights, new pinions to her wings.
4.255: Soon grows the pigmy to gigantic size;
4.256: Her feet on earth, her forehead in the skies.
4.257: Inrag'd against the gods, revengeful Earth
4.258: Produc'd her last of the Titanian birth.
4.259: Swift is her walk, more swift her winged haste:
4.260: A monstrous phantom, horrible and vast.
4.261: As many plumes as raise her lofty flight,
4.262: So many piercing eyes inlarge her sight;
4.263: Millions of opening mouths to Fame belong,
4.264: And ev'ry mouth is furnish'd with a tongue,
4.265: And round with list'ning ears the flying plague is
4.266: She fills the peaceful universe with cries;
4.267: No slumbers ever close her wakeful eyes;
4.268: By day, from lofty tow'rs her head she shews,
4.269: And spreads thro' trembling crowds disastrous news;
4.270: With court informers haunts, and royal spies;
4.271: Things done relates, not done she feigns, and mingles truth
4.272: Talk is her business, and her chief delight
4.273: To tell of prodigies and cause affright.
4.274: She fills the people's ears with Dido's name,
4.275: Who, lost to honor and the sense of shame,
4.276: Admits into her throne and nuptial bed
4.277: A wand'ring guest, who from his country fled:
4.278: Whole days with him she passes in delights,
4.279: And wastes in luxury long winter nights,
4.280: Forgetful of her fame and royal trust,
4.281: Dissolv'd in ease, abandon'd to her lust.
4.282: The goddess widely spreads the loud report,
4.283: And flies at length to King Hyarba's court.
4.284: When first possess'd with this unwelcome news
4.285: Whom did he not of men and gods accuse?
4.286: This prince, from ravish'd Garamantis born,
4.287: A hundred temples did with spoils adorn,
4.288: In Ammon's honor, his celestial sire;
4.289: A hundred altars fed with wakeful fire;
4.290: And, thro' his vast dominions, priests ordain'd,
4.291: Whose watchful care these holy rites maintain'd.
4.292: The gates and columns were with garlands crown'd,
4.293: And blood of victim beasts enrich'd the ground.
4.294: He, when he heard a fugitive could move
4.295: The Tyrian princess, who disdain'd his love,
4.296: His breast with fury burn'd, his eyes with fire,
4.297: Mad with despair, impatient with desire;
4.298: Then on the sacred altars pouring wine,
4.299: He thus with pray'rs implor'd his sire divine:
4.300: "Great Jove! propitious to the Moorish race,
4.301: Who feast on painted beds, with off'rings grace
4.302: Thy temples, and adore thy pow'r divine
4.303: With blood of victims, and with sparkling wine,
4.304: Seest thou not this? or do we fear in vain
4.305: Thy boasted thunder, and thy thoughtless reign?
4.306: Do thy broad hands the forky lightnings lance?
4.307: Thine are the bolts, or the blind work of chance?
4.308: A wand'ring woman builds, within our state,
4.309: A little town, bought at an easy rate;
4.310: She pays me homage, and my grants allow
4.311: A narrow space of Libyan lands to plow;
4.312: Yet, scorning me, by passion blindly led,
4.313: Admits a banish'd Trojan to her bed!
4.314: And now this other Paris, with his train
4.315: Of conquer'd cowards, must in Afric reign!
4.316: (Whom, what they are, their looks and garb confess,
4.317: Their locks with oil perfum'd, their Lydian dress.)
4.318: He takes the spoil, enjoys the princely dame;
4.319: And I, rejected I, adore an empty name."
4.320: His vows, in haughty terms, he thus preferr'd,
4.321: And held his altar's horns. The mighty Thund'rer
4.322: Then cast his eyes on Carthage, where he found
4.323: The lustful pair in lawless pleasure drown'd,
4.324: Lost in their loves, insensible of shame,
4.325: And both forgetful of their better fame.
4.326: He calls Cyllenius, and the god attends,
4.327: By whom his menacing command he sends:
4.328: "Go, mount the western winds, and cleave the sky;
4.329: Then, with a swift descent, to Carthage fly:
4.330: There find the Trojan chief, who wastes his days
4.331: In slothful not and inglorious ease,
4.332: Nor minds the future city, giv'n by fate.
4.333: To him this message from my mouth relate:
4.334: 'Not so fair Venus hop'd, when twice she won
4.335: Thy life with pray'rs, nor promis'd such a son.
4.336: Hers was a hero, destin'd to command
4.337: A martial race, and rule the Latian land,
4.338: Who should his ancient line from Teucer draw,
4.339: And on the conquer'd world impose the law.'
4.340: If glory cannot move a mind so mean,
4.341: Nor future praise from fading pleasure wean,
4.342: Yet why should he defraud his son of fame,
4.343: And grudge the Romans their immortal name!
4.344: What are his vain designs! what hopes he more
4.345: From his long ling'ring on a hostile shore,
4.346: Regardless to redeem his honor lost,
4.347: And for his race to gain th' Ausonian coast!
4.348: Bid him with speed the Tyrian court forsake;
4.349: With this command the slumb'ring warrior wake."
4.350: Hermes obeys; with golden pinions binds
4.351: His flying feet, and mounts the western winds:
4.352: And, whether o'er the seas or earth he flies,
4.353: With rapid force they bear him down the skies.
4.354: But first he grasps within his awful hand
4.355: The mark of sov'reign pow'r, his magic wand;
4.356: With this he draws the ghosts from hollow graves;
4.357: With this he drives them down the Stygian waves;
4.358: With this he seals in sleep the wakeful sight,
4.359: And eyes, tho' clos'd in death, restores to light.
4.360: Thus arm'd, the god begins his airy race,
4.361: And drives the racking clouds along the liquid space;
4.362: Now sees the tops of Atlas, as he flies,
4.363: Whose brawny back supports the starry skies;
4.364: Atlas, whose head, with piny forests crown'd,
4.365: Is beaten by the winds, with foggy vapors bound.
4.366: Snows hide his shoulders; from beneath his chin
4.367: The founts of rolling streams their race begin;
4.368: A beard of ice on his large breast depends.
4.369: Here, pois'd upon his wings, the god descends:
4.370: Then, rested thus, he from the tow'ring height
4.372: Lights on the seas, and skims along the flood.
4.373: As waterfowl, who seek their fishy food,
4.374: Less, and yet less, to distant prospect show;
4.375: By turns they dance aloft, and dive below:
4.376: Like these, the steerage of his wings he plies,
4.377: And near the surface of the water flies,
4.378: Till, having pass'd the seas, and cross'd the sands,
4.379: He clos'd his wings, and stoop'd on Libyan lands:
4.380: Where shepherds once were hous'd in homely sheds,
4.381: Now tow'rs within the clouds advance their heads.
4.382: Arriving there, he found the Trojan prince
4.383: New ramparts raising for the town's defense.
4.384: A purple scarf, with gold embroider'd o'er,
4.385: (Queen Dido's gift,) about his waist he wore;
4.386: A sword, with glitt'ring gems diversified,
4.387: For ornament, not use, hung idly by his side.
4.388: Then thus, with winged words, the god began,
4.390: Thou woman's property, what mak'st thou here,
4.391: These foreign walls and Tyrian tow'rs to rear,
4.392: Forgetful of thy own? All-pow'rful Jove,
4.393: Who sways the world below and heav'n above,
4.394: Has sent me down with this severe command:
4.395: What means thy ling'ring in the Libyan land?
4.396: If glory cannot move a mind so mean,
4.397: Nor future praise from flitting pleasure wean,
4.398: Regard the fortunes of thy rising heir:
4.399: The promis'd crown let young Ascanius wear,
4.400: To whom th' Ausonian scepter, and the state
4.401: Of Rome's imperial name is ow'd by fate."
4.402: So spoke the god; and, speaking, took his flight,
4.403: Involv'd in clouds, and vanish'd out of sight.
4.404: The pious prince was seiz'd with sudden fear;
4.405: Mute was his tongue, and upright stood his hair.
4.406: Revolving in his mind the stern command,
4.407: He longs to fly, and loathes the charming land.
4.408: What should he say? or how should he begin?
4.409: What course, alas! remains to steer between
4.410: Th' offended lover and the pow'rful queen?
4.411: This way and that he turns his anxious mind,
4.412: And all expedients tries, and none can find.
4.413: Fix'd on the deed, but doubtful of the means,
4.414: After long thought, to this advice he leans:
4.415: Three chiefs he calls, commands them to repair
4.416: The fleet, and ship their men with silent care;
4.417: Some plausible pretense he bids them find,
4.418: To color what in secret he design'd.
4.419: Himself, meantime, the softest hours would choose,
4.420: Before the love-sick lady heard the news;
4.421: And move her tender mind, by slow degrees,
4.422: To suffer what the sov'reign pow'r decrees:
4.423: Jove will inspire him, when, and what to say.
4.424: They hear with pleasure, and with haste obey.
4.425: But soon the queen perceives the thin disguise:
4.426: (What arts can blind a jealous woman's eyes!)
4.427: She was the first to find the secret fraud,
4.428: Before the fatal news was blaz'd abroad.
4.429: Love the first motions of the lover hears,
4.430: Quick to presage, and ev'n in safety fears.
4.431: Nor impious Fame was wanting to report
4.432: The ships repair'd, the Trojans' thick resort,
4.433: And purpose to forsake the Tyrian court.
4.434: Frantic with fear, impatient of the wound,
4.435: And impotent of mind, she roves the city round.
4.436: Less wild the Bacchanalian dames appear,
4.437: When, from afar, their nightly god they hear,
4.438: And howl about the hills, and shake the wreathy
4.439: At length she finds the dear perfidious man;
4.440: Prevents his form'd excuse, and thus began:
4.441: "Base and ungrateful! could you hope to fly,
4.442: And undiscover'd scape a lover's eye?
4.443: Nor could my kindness your compassion move.
4.444: Nor plighted vows, nor dearer bands of love?
4.445: Or is the death of a despairing queen
4.446: Not worth preventing, tho' too well foreseen?
4.447: Ev'n when the wintry winds command your stay,
4.448: You dare the tempests, and defy the sea.
4.449: False as you are, suppose you were not bound
4.450: To lands unknown, and foreign coasts to sound;
4.451: Were Troy restor'd, and Priam's happy reign,
4.452: Now durst you tempt, for Troy, the raging main?
4.453: See whom you fly! am I the foe you shun?
4.454: Now, by those holy vows, so late begun,
4.455: By this right hand, (since I have nothing more
4.456: To challenge, but the faith you gave before;)
4.457: I beg you by these tears too truly shed,
4.458: By the new pleasures of our nuptial bed;
4.459: If ever Dido, when you most were kind,
4.460: Were pleasing in your eyes, or touch'd your mind;
4.461: By these my pray'rs, if pray'rs may yet have place,
4.462: Pity the fortunes of a falling race.
4.463: For you I have provok'd a tyrant's hate,
4.464: Incens'd the Libyan and the Tyrian state;
4.465: For you alone I suffer in my fame,
4.466: Bereft of honor, and expos'd to shame.
4.467: Whom have I now to trust, ungrateful guest?
4.468: (That only name remains of all the rest!)
4.469: What have I left? or whither can I fly?
4.471: Or till Hyarba shall in triumph lead
4.472: A queen that proudly scorn'd his proffer'd bed?
4.473: Had you deferr'd, at least, your hasty flight,
4.474: And left behind some pledge of our delight,
4.475: Some babe to bless the mother's mournful sight,
4.476: Some young Aeneas, to supply your place,
4.477: Whose features might express his father's face;
4.478: I should not then complain to live bereft
4.479: Of all my husband, or be wholly left."
4.480: Here paus'd the queen. Unmov'd he holds his eyes,
4.481: By Jove's command; nor suffer'd love to rise,
4.482: Tho' heaving in his heart; and thus at length replies:
4.483: "Fair queen, you never can enough repeat
4.484: Your boundless favors, or I own my debt;
4.485: Nor can my mind forget Eliza's name,
4.486: While vital breath inspires this mortal frame.
4.487: This only let me speak in my defense:
4.488: I never hop'd a secret flight from hence,
4.489: Much less pretended to the lawful claim
4.490: Of sacred nuptials, or a husband's name.
4.491: For, if indulgent Heav'n would leave me free,
4.492: And not submit my life to fate's decree,
4.493: My choice would lead me to the Trojan shore,
4.494: Those relics to review, their dust adore,
4.495: And Priam's ruin'd palace to restore.
4.496: But now the Delphian oracle commands,
4.497: And fate invites me to the Latian lands.
4.498: That is the promis'd place to which I steer,
4.499: And all my vows are terminated there.
4.500: If you, a Tyrian, and a stranger born,
4.501: With walls and tow'rs a Libyan town adorn,
4.502: Why may not we- like you, a foreign race-
4.503: Like you, seek shelter in a foreign place?
4.504: As often as the night obscures the skies
4.505: With humid shades, or twinkling stars arise,
4.506: Anchises' angry ghost in dreams appears,
4.507: Chides my delay, and fills my soul with fears;
4.508: And young Ascanius justly may complain
4.509: Of his defrauded and destin'd reign.
4.510: Ev'n now the herald of the gods appear'd:
4.511: Waking I saw him, and his message heard.
4.512: From Jove he came commission'd, heav'nly bright
4.513: With radiant beams, and manifest to sight
4.514: (The sender and the sent I both attest)
4.515: These walls he enter'd, and those words express'd.
4.516: Fair queen, oppose not what the gods command;
4.517: Forc'd by my fate, I leave your happy land."
4.518: Thus while he spoke, already she began,
4.519: With sparkling eyes, to view the guilty man;
4.520: From head to foot survey'd his person o'er,
4.521: Nor longer these outrageous threats forebore:
4.522: "False as thou art, and, more than false, forsworn!
4.523: Not sprung from noble blood, nor goddess-born,
4.524: But hewn from harden'd entrails of a rock!
4.525: And rough Hyrcanian tigers gave thee suck!
4.526: Why should I fawn? what have I worse to fear?
4.527: Did he once look, or lent a list'ning ear,
4.528: Sigh'd when I sobb'd, or shed one kindly tear?-
4.529: All symptoms of a base ungrateful mind,
4.530: So foul, that, which is worse, 'tis hard to find.
4.531: Of man's injustice why should I complain?
4.532: The gods, and Jove himself, behold in vain
4.533: Triumphant treason; yet no thunder flies,
4.534: Nor Juno views my wrongs with equal eyes;
4.535: Faithless is earth, and faithless are the skies!
4.536: Justice is fled, and Truth is now no more!
4.537: I sav'd the shipwrack'd exile on my shore;
4.538: With needful food his hungry Trojans fed;
4.539: I took the traitor to my throne and bed:
4.540: Fool that I was- 't is little to repeat
4.541: The rest- I stor'd and rigg'd his ruin'd fleet.
4.542: I rave, I rave! A god's command he pleads,
4.543: And makes Heav'n accessary to his deeds.
4.544: Now Lycian lots, and now the Delian god,
4.545: Now Hermes is employ'd from Jove's abode,
4.546: To warn him hence; as if the peaceful state
4.547: Of heav'nly pow'rs were touch'd with human fate!
4.548: But go! thy flight no longer I detain-
4.549: Go seek thy promis'd kingdom thro' the main!
4.550: Yet, if the heav'ns will hear my pious vow,
4.551: The faithless waves, not half so false as thou,
4.552: Or secret sands, shall sepulchers afford
4.553: To thy proud vessels, and their perjur'd lord.
4.554: Then shalt thou call on injur'd Dido's name:
4.555: Dido shall come in a black sulph'ry flame,
4.556: When death has once dissolv'd her mortal frame;
4.557: Shall smile to see the traitor vainly weep:
4.558: Her angry ghost, arising from the deep,
4.559: Shall haunt thee waking, and disturb thy sleep.
4.560: At least my shade thy punishment shall know,
4.561: And Fame shall spread the pleasing news below."
4.562: Abruptly here she stops; then turns away
4.563: Her loathing eyes, and shuns the sight of day.
4.564: Amaz'd he stood, revolving in his mind
4.565: What speech to frame, and what excuse to find.
4.566: Her fearful maids their fainting mistress led,
4.567: And softly laid her on her ivory bed.
4.568: But good Aeneas, tho' he much desir'd
4.569: To give that pity which her grief requir'd;
4.570: Tho' much he mourn'd, and labor'd with his love,
4.571: Resolv'd at length, obeys the will of Jove;
4.572: Reviews his forces: they with early care
4.573: Unmoor their vessels, and for sea prepare.
4.574: The fleet is soon afloat, in all its pride,
4.575: And well-calk'd galleys in the harbor ride.
4.576: Then oaks for oars they fell'd; or, as they stood,
4.577: Of its green arms despoil'd the growing wood,
4.578: Studious of flight. The beach is cover'd o'er
4.579: With Trojan bands, that blacken all the shore:
4.580: On ev'ry side are seen, descending down,
4.581: Thick swarms of soldiers, loaden from the town.
4.582: Thus, in battalia, march embodied ants,
4.583: Fearful of winter, and of future wants,
4.584: T' invade the corn, and to their cells convey
4.585: The plunder'd forage of their yellow prey.
4.586: The sable troops, along the narrow tracks,
4.587: Scarce bear the weighty burthen on their backs:
4.588: Some set their shoulders to the pond'rous grain;
4.589: Some guard the spoil; some lash the lagging train;
4.590: All ply their sev'ral tasks, and equal toil sustain.
4.591: What pangs the tender breast of Dido tore,
4.592: When, from the tow'r, she saw the cover'd shore,
4.593: And heard the shouts of sailors from afar,
4.594: Mix'd with the murmurs of the wat'ry war!
4.595: All-pow'rful Love! what changes canst thou cause
4.596: In human hearts, subjected to thy laws!
4.597: Once more her haughty soul the tyrant bends:
4.598: To pray'rs and mean submissions she descends.
4.599: No female arts or aids she left untried,
4.600: Nor counsels unexplor'd, before she died.
4.601: "Look, Anna! look! the Trojans crowd to sea;
4.602: They spread their canvas, and their anchors weigh.
4.603: The shouting crew their ships with garlands bind,
4.604: Invoke the sea gods, and invite the wind.
4.605: Could I have thought this threat'ning blow so near,
4.606: My tender soul had been forewarn'd to bear.
4.607: But do not you my last request deny;
4.608: With yon perfidious man your int'rest try,
4.609: And bring me news, if I must live or die.
4.610: You are his fav'rite; you alone can find
4.611: The dark recesses of his inmost mind:
4.612: In all his trusted secrets you have part,
4.613: And know the soft approaches to his heart.
4.614: Haste then, and humbly seek my haughty foe;
4.615: Tell him, I did not with the Grecians go,
4.616: Nor did my fleet against his friends employ,
4.617: Nor swore the ruin of unhappy Troy,
4.618: Nor mov'd with hands profane his father's dust:
4.619: Why should he then reject a just!
4.620: Whom does he shun, and whither would he fly!
4.621: Can he this last, this only pray'r deny!
4.622: Let him at least his dang'rous flight delay,
4.623: Wait better winds, and hope a calmer sea.
4.624: The nuptials he disclaims I urge no more:
4.625: Let him pursue the promis'd Latian shore.
4.626: A short delay is all I ask him now;
4.627: A pause of grief, an interval from woe,
4.628: Till my soft soul be temper'd to sustain
4.629: Accustom'd sorrows, and inur'd to pain.
4.630: If you in pity grant this one request,
4.631: My death shall glut the hatred of his breast."
4.632: This mournful message pious Anna bears,
4.633: And seconds with her own her sister's tears:
4.634: But all her arts are still employ'd in vain;
4.635: Again she comes, and is refus'd again.
4.636: His harden'd heart nor pray'rs nor threat'nings
4.637: Fate, and the god, had stopp'd his ears to love.
4.638: As, when the winds their airy quarrel try,
4.639: Justling from ev'ry quarter of the sky,
4.640: This way and that the mountain oak they bend,
4.641: His boughs they shatter, and his branches rend;
4.642: With leaves and falling mast they spread the ground;
4.643: The hollow valleys echo to the sound:
4.644: Unmov'd, the royal plant their fury mocks,
4.645: Or, shaken, clings more closely to the rocks;
4.646: Far as he shoots his tow'ring head on high,
4.647: So deep in earth his fix'd foundations lie.
4.648: No less a storm the Trojan hero bears;
4.649: Thick messages and loud complaints he hears,
4.650: And bandied words, still beating on his ears.
4.651: Sighs, groans, and tears proclaim his inward pains;
4.652: But the firm purpose of his heart remains.
4.653: The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
4.654: Begins at length the light of heav'n to hate,
4.655: And loathes to live. Then dire portents she sees,
4.656: To hasten on the death her soul decrees:
4.657: Strange to relate! for when, before the shrine,
4.658: She pours in sacrifice the purple wine,
4.659: The purple wine is turn'd to putrid blood,
4.660: And the white offer'd milk converts to mud.
4.661: This dire presage, to her alone reveal'd,
4.662: From all, and ev'n her sister, she conceal'd.
4.663: A marble temple stood within the grove,
4.664: Sacred to death, and to her murther'd love;
4.665: That honor'd chapel she had hung around
4.666: With snowy fleeces, and with garlands crown'd:
4.667: Oft, when she visited this lonely dome,
4.668: Strange voices issued from her husband's tomb;
4.669: She thought she heard him summon her away,
4.670: Invite her to his grave, and chide her stay.
4.671: Hourly 't is heard, when with a boding note
4.672: The solitary screech owl strains her throat,
4.673: And, on a chimney's top, or turret's height,
4.674: With songs obscene disturbs the silence of the night.
4.675: Besides, old prophecies augment her fears;
4.676: And stern Aeneas in her dreams appears,
4.677: Disdainful as by day: she seems, alone,
4.678: To wander in her sleep, thro' ways unknown,
4.679: Guideless and dark; or, in a desart plain,
4.680: To seek her subjects, and to seek in vain:
4.681: Like Pentheus, when, distracted with his fear,
4.682: He saw two suns, and double Thebes, appear;
4.683: Or mad Orestes, when his mother's ghost
4.684: Full in his face infernal torches toss'd,
4.685: And shook her snaky locks: he shuns the sight,
4.686: Flies o'er the stage, surpris'd with mortal fright;
4.687: The Furies guard the door and intercept his flight.
4.688: Now, sinking underneath a load of grief,
4.689: From death alone she seeks her last relief;
4.690: The time and means resolv'd within her breast,
4.691: She to her mournful sister thus address'd
4.692: (Dissembling hope, her cloudy front she clears,
4.693: And a false vigor in her eyes appears):
4.695: My lover I shall gain, or lose my love.
4.696: Nigh rising Atlas, next the falling sun,
4.697: Long tracts of Ethiopian climates run:
4.698: There a Massylian priestess I have found,
4.699: Honor'd for age, for magic arts renown'd:
4.700: Th' Hesperian temple was her trusted care;

5.161: In the great Centaur took the leading place;
5.162: Cloanthus on the sea-green Scylla stood,

5.168: In peace below the gentle waters run;

5.191: Not fiery coursers, in a chariot race,

5.193: Not the fierce driver with more fury lends

5.201: Gyas outstripp'd the rest, and sprung before:

5.207: And now the speedy Dolphin gets ahead;
5.208: Now board to board the rival vessels row,

5.265: Betwixt the rival galley and the rock,

5.269: The trembling rowers from their banks arise,

5.273: The crew of Mnestheus, with elated minds,
5.274: Urge their success, and call the willing winds;
5.275: Then ply their oars, and cut their liquid way
5.276: In larger compass on the roomy sea.

5.304: When to the seas Cloanthus holds his hands,

5.313: The choir of nymphs, and Phorcus, from below,

5.315: And old Portunus, with his breadth of hand,

5.317: Swift as a shaft, or winged wind, she flies,

5.319: The herald summons all, and then proclaims
5.320: Cloanthus conqu'ror of the naval games.
5.321: The prince with laurel crowns the victor's head,
5.322: And three fat steers are to his vessel led,
5.323: The ship's reward; with gen'rous wine beside,
5.324: And sums of silver, which the crew divide.
5.325: The leaders are distinguish'd from the rest;
5.326: The victor honor'd with a nobler vest,
5.327: Where gold and purple strive in equal rows,
5.328: And needlework its happy cost bestows.
5.329: There Ganymede is wrought with living art,

5.331: Breathless he seems, yet eager to pursue;
5.332: When from aloft descends, in open view,
5.333: The bird of Jove, and, sousing on his prey,

5.335: In vain, with lifted hands and gazing eyes,

5.337: And dogs pursue his flight with imitated cries.
5.338: Mnestheus the second victor was declar'd;
5.339: And, summon'd there, the second prize he shard.
5.340: A coat of mail, brave Demoleus bore,
5.341: More brave Aeneas from his shoulders tore,
5.342: In single combat on the Trojan shore:
5.343: This was ordain'd for Mnestheus to possess;
5.344: In war for his defense, for ornament in peace.
5.345: Rich was the gift, and glorious to behold,

5.350: The third, succeeding to the last reward,

5.354: Thus all, rewarded by the hero's hands,
5.355: Their conqu'ring temples bound with purple bands;
5.356: And now Sergesthus, clearing from the rock,

5.358: Forlorn she look'd, without an aiding oar,
5.359: And, houted by the vulgar, made to shore.
5.360: As when a snake, surpris'd upon the road,

5.362: Of heavy wheels; or with a mortal wound
5.363: Her belly bruis'd, and trodden to the ground:
5.364: In vain, with loosen'd curls, she crawls along;

5.372: Pholoe, the Cretan slave, rewards his care,
5.373: Beauteous herself, with lovely twins as fair.
5.374: From thence his way the Trojan hero bent
5.375: Into the neighb'ring plain, with mountains pent,

5.377: Full in the midst of this fair valley stood

5.379: By just degrees, o'erlook'd the ground below.
5.380: High on a sylvan throne the leader sate;
5.381: A num'rous train attend in solemn state.
5.382: Here those that in the rapid course delight,
5.383: Desire of honor and the prize invite.
5.384: The rival runners without order stand;
5.385: The Trojans mix'd with the Sicilian band.
5.387: Euryalus a boy of blooming years,
5.388: With sprightly grace and equal beauty crown'd;
5.389: Nisus, for friendship to the youth renown'd.
5.390: Diores next, of Priam's royal race,
5.391: Then Salius joined with Patron, took their place;

5.394: Then two Sicilian youths- the names of these,

5.398: With sev'ral others of ignobler name,

5.402: "One common largess is for all design'd,
5.403: (The vanquish'd and the victor shall be join'd,)
5.404: Two darts of polish'd steel and Gnosian wood,

5.409: The quiver of an Amazonian dame,
5.410: With feather'd Thracian arrows well supplied:

5.412: Which with a sparkling diamond shall be tied.
5.413: The third this Grecian helmet shall content."
5.414: He said. To their appointed base they went;
5.415: With beating hearts th' expected sign receive,
5.416: And, starting all at once, the barrier leave.
5.417: Spread out, as on the winged winds, they flew,
5.418: And seiz'd the distant goal with greedy view.
5.419: Shot from the crowd, swift Nisus all o'erpass'd;
5.420: Nor storms, nor thunder, equal half his haste.
5.421: The next, but tho' the next, yet far disjoin'd,
5.423: Then Helymus, whom young Diores plied,
5.424: Step after step, and almost side by side,

5.429: Slipp'd first, and, slipping, fell upon the plain,
5.430: Soak'd with the blood of oxen newly slain.
5.431: The careless victor had not mark'd his way;
5.432: But, treading where the treach'rous puddle lay,
5.433: His heels flew up; and on the grassy floor
5.434: He fell, besmear'd with filth and holy gore.
5.435: Not mindless then, Euryalus, of thee,
5.436: Nor of the sacred bonds of amity,
5.437: He strove th' immediate rival's hope to cross,

5.439: So Salius lay extended on the plain;
5.440: Euryalus springs out, the prize to gain,

5.443: Next Helymus; and then Diores came,

5.499: His brawny back and ample breast he shows,
5.500: His lifted arms around his head he throws,
5.501: And deals in whistling air his empty blows.
5.502: His match is sought; but, thro' the trembling band,

5.561: This said, Entellus for the strife prepares;

5.564: A goodly tow'ring object on the sands.

5.572: One on his sinews and his giant size.

5.584: Heavy with age, Entellus stands his ground,
5.585: But with his warping body wards the wound.
5.586: His hand and watchful eye keep even pace;
5.587: While Dares traverses and shifts his place,
5.588: And, like a captain who beleaguers round
5.589: Some strong-built castle on a rising ground,
5.590: Views all th' approaches with observing eyes:
5.591: This and that other part in vain he tries,
5.592: And more on industry than force relies.
5.593: With hands on high, Entellus threats the foe;
5.594: But Dares watch'd the motion from below,
5.595: And slipp'd aside, and shunn'd the long descending
5.596: Entellus wastes his forces on the wind,
5.597: And, thus deluded of the stroke design'd,
5.598: Headlong and heavy fell; his ample breast
5.599: And weighty limbs his ancient mother press'd.
5.600: So falls a hollow pine, that long had stood
5.601: On Ida's height, or Erymanthus' wood,
5.602: Torn from the roots. The diff'ring nations rise,
5.603: And shouts and mingled murmurs rend the skies,
5.604: Acestus runs with eager haste, to raise
5.605: The fall'n companion of his youthful days.
5.606: Dauntless he rose, and to the fight return'd;
5.607: With shame his glowing cheeks, his eyes with fury
5.608: Disdain and conscious virtue fir'd his breast,
5.609: And with redoubled force his foe he press'd.
5.610: He lays on load with either hand, amain,
5.611: And headlong drives the Trojan o'er the plain;
5.612: Nor stops, nor stays; nor rest nor breath allows;
5.613: But storms of strokes descend about his brows,
5.614: A rattling tempest, and a hail of blows.
5.615: But now the prince, who saw the wild increase
5.616: Of wounds, commands the combatants to cease,
5.617: And bounds Entellus' wrath, and bids the peace.
5.618: First to the Trojan, spent with toil, he came,
5.619: And sooth'd his sorrow for the suffer'd shame.
5.620: "What fury seiz'd my friend? The gods," said he,
5.621: "To him propitious, and averse to thee,
5.622: Have giv'n his arm superior force to thine.
5.623: 'T is madness to contend with strength divine."
5.624: The gauntlet fight thus ended, from the shore
5.625: His faithful friends unhappy Dares bore:
5.626: His mouth and nostrils pour'd a purple flood,
5.627: And pounded teeth came rushing with his blood.
5.628: Faintly he stagger'd thro' the hissing throng,
5.629: And hung his head, and trail'd his legs along.
5.630: The sword and casque are carried by his train;
5.631: But with his foe the palm and ox remain.
5.632: The champion, then, before Aeneas came,

5.1101: Now steal an hour of sweet repose; and I
5.1102: Will take the rudder and thy room supply."
5.1103: To whom the yawning pilot, half asleep:
5.1104: "Me dost thou bid to trust the treach'rous deep,
5.1105: The harlot smiles of her dissembling face,
5.1106: And to her faith commit the Trojan race?
5.1107: Shall I believe the Siren South again,
5.1108: And, oft betray'd, not know the monster main?"
5.1109: He said: his fasten'd hands the rudder keep,
5.1110: And, fix'd on heav'n, his eyes repel invading sleep.
5.1111: The god was wroth, and at his temples threw
5.1112: A branch in Lethe dipp'd, and drunk with Stygian
5.1113: The pilot, vanquish'd by the pow'r divine,
5.1114: Soon clos'd his swimming eyes, and lay supine.
5.1115: Scarce were his limbs extended at their length,
5.1116: The god, insulting with superior strength,
5.1117: Fell heavy on him, plung'd him in the sea,
5.1118: And, with the stern, the rudder tore away.
5.1119: Headlong he fell, and, struggling in the main,
5.1120: Cried out for helping hands, but cried in vain.
5.1121: The victor daemon mounts obscure in air,
5.1122: While the ship sails without the pilot's care.
5.1123: On Neptune's faith the floating fleet relies;
5.1124: But what the man forsook, the god supplies,
5.1125: And o'er the dang'rous deep secure the navy flies;
5.1126: Glides by the Sirens' cliffs, a shelfy coast,
5.1127: Long infamous for ships and sailors lost,
5.1128: And white with bones. Th' impetuous ocean roars,
5.1129: And rocks rebellow from the sounding shores.
5.1130: The watchful hero felt the knocks, and found
5.1131: The tossing vessel sail'd on shoaly ground.
5.1132: Sure of his pilot's loss, he takes himself
5.1133: The helm, and steers aloof, and shuns the shelf.
5.1134: Inly he griev'd, and, groaning from the breast,
5.1135: Deplor'd his death; and thus his pain express'd:
5.1136: "For faith repos'd on seas, and on the flatt'ring
5.1137: Thy naked corpse is doom'd on shores unknown to

6.1: He said, and wept; then spread his sails before
6.2: The winds, and reach'd at length the Cumaean shore:
6.3: Their anchors dropp'd, his crew the vessels moor.
6.4: They turn their heads to sea, their sterns to land,
6.5: And greet with greedy joy th' Italian strand.
6.6: Some strike from clashing flints their fiery seed;
6.7: Some gather sticks, the kindled flames to feed,
6.8: Or search for hollow trees, and fell the woods,
6.9: Or trace thro' valleys the discover'd floods.
6.10: Thus, while their sev'ral charges they fulfil,
6.11: The pious prince ascends the sacred hill
6.12: Where Phoebus is ador'd; and seeks the shade
6.13: Which hides from sight his venerable maid.
6.14: Deep in a cave the Sibyl makes abode;
6.15: Thence full of fate returns, and of the god.
6.16: Thro' Trivia's grove they walk; and now behold,
6.17: And enter now, the temple roof'd with gold.
6.18: When Daedalus, to fly the Cretan shore,
6.19: His heavy limbs on jointed pinions bore,
6.20: (The first who sail'd in air,) 't is sung by Fame,
6.21: To the Cumaean coast at length he came,
6.22: And here alighting, built this costly frame.
6.23: Inscrib'd to Phoebus, here he hung on high
6.24: The steerage of his wings, that cut the sky:
6.25: Then o'er the lofty gate his art emboss'd
6.26: Androgeos' death, and off'rings to his ghost;
6.27: Sev'n youths from Athens yearly sent, to meet
6.28: The fate appointed by revengeful Crete.
6.29: And next to those the dreadful urn was plac'd,
6.30: In which the destin'd names by lots were cast:
6.31: The mournful parents stand around in tears,
6.32: And rising Crete against their shore appears.
6.33: There too, in living sculpture, might be seen
6.34: The mad affection of the Cretan queen;
6.35: Then how she cheats her bellowing lover's eye;
6.36: The rushing leap, the doubtful progeny,
6.37: The lower part a beast, a man above,
6.38: The monument of their polluted love.
6.39: Not far from thence he grav'd the wondrous maze,
6.40: A thousand doors, a thousand winding ways:
6.41: Here dwells the monster, hid from human view,
6.42: Not to be found, but by the faithful clew;
6.43: Till the kind artist, mov'd with pious grief,
6.44: Lent to the loving maid this last relief,
6.45: And all those erring paths describ'd so well
6.46: That Theseus conquer'd and the monster fell.
6.47: Here hapless Icarus had found his part,
6.48: Had not the father's grief restrain'd his art.
6.49: He twice assay'd to cast his son in gold;
6.50: Twice from his hands he dropp'd the forming mold.
6.51: All this with wond'ring eyes Aeneas view'd;
6.52: Each varying object his delight renew'd:
6.53: Eager to read the rest- Achates came,
6.54: And by his side the mad divining dame,
6.55: The priestess of the god, Deiphobe her name.
6.56: "Time suffers not," she said, "to feed your eyes
6.57: With empty pleasures; haste the sacrifice.
6.58: Sev'n bullocks, yet unyok'd, for Phoebus choose,
6.59: And for Diana sev'n unspotted ewes."
6.60: This said, the servants urge the sacred rites,
6.61: While to the temple she the prince invites.
6.62: A spacious cave, within its farmost part,
6.63: Was hew'd and fashion'd by laborious art
6.64: Thro' the hill's hollow sides: before the place,
6.65: A hundred doors a hundred entries grace;
6.66: As many voices issue, and the sound
6.67: Of Sybil's words as many times rebound.
6.68: Now to the mouth they come. Aloud she cries:
6.69: "This is the time; enquire your destinies.
6.70: He comes; behold the god!" Thus while she said,
6.71: (And shiv'ring at the sacred entry stay'd,)
6.72: Her color chang'd; her face was not the same,
6.73: And hollow groans from her deep spirit came.
6.74: Her hair stood up; convulsive rage possess'd
6.75: Her trembling limbs, and heav'd her lab'ring breast.
6.76: Greater than humankind she seem'd to look,
6.77: And with an accent more than mortal spoke.
6.78: Her staring eyes with sparkling fury roll;
6.79: When all the god came rushing on her soul.
6.80: Swiftly she turn'd, and, foaming as she spoke:
6.81: "Why this delay?" she cried- "the pow'rs invoke!
6.82: Thy pray'rs alone can open this abode;
6.83: Else vain are my demands, and dumb the god."
6.84: She said no more. The trembling Trojans hear,
6.85: O'erspread with a damp sweat and holy fear.
6.86: The prince himself, with awful dread possess'd,
6.87: His vows to great Apollo thus address'd:
6.89: Swift to relieve, unwilling to destroy,
6.90: Directed by whose hand the Dardan dart
6.91: Pierc'd the proud Grecian's only mortal part:
6.92: Thus far, by fate's decrees and thy commands,
6.93: Thro' ambient seas and thro' devouring sands,
6.94: Our exil'd crew has sought th' Ausonian ground;
6.95: And now, at length, the flying coast is found.
6.96: Thus far the fate of Troy, from place to place,
6.97: With fury has pursued her wand'ring race.
6.98: Here cease, ye pow'rs, and let your vengeance end:
6.99: Troy is no more, and can no more offend.
6.100: And thou, O sacred maid, inspir'd to see
6.101: Th' event of things in dark futurity;
6.102: Give me what Heav'n has promis'd to my fate,
6.103: To conquer and command the Latian state;
6.104: To fix my wand'ring gods, and find a place
6.105: For the long exiles of the Trojan race.
6.106: Then shall my grateful hands a temple rear
6.107: To the twin gods, with vows and solemn pray'r;
6.108: And annual rites, and festivals, and games,
6.109: Shall be perform'd to their auspicious names.
6.110: Nor shalt thou want thy honors in my land;
6.111: For there thy faithful oracles shall stand,
6.112: Preserv'd in shrines; and ev'ry sacred lay,
6.113: Which, by thy mouth, Apollo shall convey:
6.114: All shall be treasur'd by a chosen train
6.115: Of holy priests, and ever shall remain.
6.116: But O! commit not thy prophetic mind
6.117: To flitting leaves, the sport of ev'ry wind,
6.118: Lest they disperse in air our empty fate;
6.119: Write not, but, what the pow'rs ordain, relate."
6.120: Struggling in vain, impatient of her load,
6.121: And lab'ring underneath the pond'rous god,
6.122: The more she strove to shake him from her breast,
6.123: With more and far superior force he press'd;
6.124: Commands his entrance, and, without control,
6.125: Usurps her organs and inspires her soul.
6.126: Now, with a furious blast, the hundred doors
6.127: Ope of themselves; a rushing whirlwind roars
6.128: Within the cave, and Sibyl's voice restores:
6.129: "Escap'd the dangers of the wat'ry reign,
6.130: Yet more and greater ills by land remain.
6.131: The coast, so long desir'd (nor doubt th' event),
6.132: Thy troops shall reach, but, having reach'd, repent.
6.133: Wars, horrid wars, I view- a field of blood,
6.134: And Tiber rolling with a purple flood.
6.135: Simois nor Xanthus shall be wanting there:
6.136: A new Achilles shall in arms appear,
6.137: And he, too, goddess-born. Fierce Juno's hate,
6.138: Added to hostile force, shall urge thy fate.
6.139: To what strange nations shalt not thou resort,
6.140: Driv'n to solicit aid at ev'ry court!
6.141: The cause the same which Ilium once oppress'd;
6.142: A foreign mistress, and a foreign guest.
6.143: But thou, secure of soul, unbent with woes,
6.144: The more thy fortune frowns, the more oppose.
6.145: The dawnings of thy safety shall be shown
6.146: From whence thou least shalt hope, a Grecian town."
6.147: Thus, from the dark recess, the Sibyl spoke,
6.148: And the resisting air the thunder broke;
6.149: The cave rebellow'd, and the temple shook.
6.150: Th' ambiguous god, who rul'd her lab'ring breast,
6.151: In these mysterious words his mind express'd;
6.152: Some truths reveal'd, in terms involv'd the rest.
6.153: At length her fury fell, her foaming ceas'd,
6.154: And, ebbing in her soul, the god decreas'd.
6.155: Then thus the chief: "No terror to my view,
6.156: No frightful face of danger can be new.
6.157: Inur'd to suffer, and resolv'd to dare,
6.158: The Fates, without my pow'r, shall be without my
6.159: This let me crave, since near your grove the road
6.160: To hell lies open, and the dark abode
6.161: Which Acheron surrounds, th' innavigable flood;
6.162: Conduct me thro' the regions void of light,
6.163: And lead me longing to my father's sight.
6.164: For him, a thousand dangers I have sought,
6.165: And, rushing where the thickest Grecians fought,
6.166: Safe on my back the sacred burthen brought.
6.167: He, for my sake, the raging ocean tried,
6.168: And wrath of Heav'n, my still auspicious guide,
6.169: And bore beyond the strength decrepid age supplied.
6.170: Oft, since he breath'd his last, in dead of night
6.171: His reverend image stood before my sight;
6.172: Enjoin'd to seek, below, his holy shade;
6.173: Conducted there by your unerring aid.
6.174: But you, if pious minds by pray'rs are won,
6.175: Oblige the father, and protect the son.
6.176: Yours is the pow'r; nor Proserpine in vain
6.177: Has made you priestess of her nightly reign.
6.178: If Orpheus, arm'd with his enchanting lyre,
6.179: The ruthless king with pity could inspire,
6.180: And from the shades below redeem his wife;
6.181: If Pollux, off'ring his alternate life,
6.182: Could free his brother, and can daily go
6.183: By turns aloft, by turns descend below-
6.184: Why name I Theseus, or his greater friend,
6.185: Who trod the downward path, and upward could ascend?
6.186: Not less than theirs from Jove my lineage came;
6.187: My mother greater, my descent the same."
6.188: So pray'd the Trojan prince, and, while he pray'd,
6.189: His hand upon the holy altar laid.
6.190: Then thus replied the prophetess divine:
6.192: The gates of hell are open night and day;
6.193: Smooth the descent, and easy is the way:
6.194: But to return, and view the cheerful skies,
6.195: In this the task and mighty labor lies.
6.196: To few great Jupiter imparts this grace,
6.197: And those of shining worth and heav'nly race.
6.198: Betwixt those regions and our upper light,
6.200: Possess the middle space: th' infernal bounds
6.201: Cocytus, with his sable waves, surrounds.
6.202: But if so dire a love your soul invades,
6.203: As twice below to view the trembling shades;
6.204: If you so hard a toil will undertake,
6.205: As twice to pass th' innavigable lake;
6.206: Receive my counsel. In the neighb'ring grove
6.207: There stands a tree; the queen of Stygian Jove
6.208: Claims it her own; thick woods and gloomy night
6.209: Conceal the happy plant from human sight.
6.210: One bough it bears; but (wondrous to behold!)
6.211: The ductile rind and leaves of radiant gold:
6.212: This from the vulgar branches must be torn,
6.213: And to fair Proserpine the present borne,
6.214: Ere leave be giv'n to tempt the nether skies.
6.215: The first thus rent a second will arise,
6.216: And the same metal the same room supplies.
6.217: Look round the wood, with lifted eyes, to see
6.218: The lurking gold upon the fatal tree:
6.219: Then rend it off, as holy rites command;
6.220: The willing metal will obey thy hand,
6.221: Following with ease, if favor'd by thy fate,
6.222: Thou art foredoom'd to view the Stygian state:
6.223: If not, no labor can the tree constrain;
6.224: And strength of stubborn arms and steel are vain.
6.225: Besides, you know not, while you here attend,
6.226: Th' unworthy fate of your unhappy friend:
6.227: Breathless he lies; and his unburied ghost,
6.228: Depriv'd of fun'ral rites, pollutes your host.
6.229: Pay first his pious dues; and, for the dead,
6.230: Two sable sheep around his hearse be led;
6.231: Then, living turfs upon his body lay:
6.232: This done, securely take the destin'd way,
6.233: To find the regions destitute of day."
6.234: She said, and held her peace. Aeneas went
6.235: Sad from the cave, and full of discontent,
6.236: Unknowing whom the sacred Sibyl meant.
6.237: Achates, the companion of his breast,
6.238: Goes grieving by his side, with equal cares oppress'd.
6.239: Walking, they talk'd, and fruitlessly divin'd
6.240: What friend the priestess by those words design'd.
6.241: But soon they found an object to deplore:
6.243: Son of the God of Winds: none so renown'd
6.244: The warrior trumpet in the field to sound;
6.245: With breathing brass to kindle fierce alarms,
6.246: And rouse to dare their fate in honorable arms.
6.247: He serv'd great Hector, and was ever near,
6.248: Not with his trumpet only, but his spear.
6.249: But by Pelides' arms when Hector fell,
6.250: He chose Aeneas; and he chose as well.
6.251: Swoln with applause, and aiming still at more,
6.252: He now provokes the sea gods from the shore;
6.253: With envy Triton heard the martial sound,
6.254: And the bold champion, for his challenge, drown'd;
6.255: Then cast his mangled carcass on the strand:
6.256: The gazing crowd around the body stand.
6.257: All weep; but most Aeneas mourns his fate,
6.258: And hastens to perform the funeral state.
6.259: In altar-wise, a stately pile they rear;
6.260: The basis broad below, and top advanc'd in air.
6.261: An ancient wood, fit for the work design'd,
6.262: (The shady covert of the salvage kind,)
6.263: The Trojans found: the sounding ax is plied;
6.264: Firs, pines, and pitch trees, and the tow'ring pride
6.265: Of forest ashes, feel the fatal stroke,
6.266: And piercing wedges cleave the stubborn oak.
6.267: Huge trunks of trees, fell'd from the steepy crown
6.268: Of the bare mountains, roll with ruin down.
6.269: Arm'd like the rest the Trojan prince appears,
6.270: And by his pious labor urges theirs.
6.271: Thus while he wrought, revolving in his mind
6.272: The ways to compass what his wish design'd,
6.273: He cast his eyes upon the gloomy grove,
6.274: And then with vows implor'd the Queen of Love:
6.275: "O may thy pow'r, propitious still to me,
6.276: Conduct my steps to find the fatal tree,
6.277: In this deep forest; since the Sibyl's breath
6.278: Foretold, alas! too true, Misenus' death."
6.279: Scarce had he said, when, full before his sight,
6.280: Two doves, descending from their airy flight,
6.281: Secure upon the grassy plain alight.
6.282: He knew his mother's birds; and thus he pray'd:
6.283: "Be you my guides, with your auspicious aid,
6.284: And lead my footsteps, till the branch be found,
6.285: Whose glitt'ring shadow gilds the sacred ground.
6.286: And thou, great parent, with celestial care,
6.287: In this distress be present to my pray'r!"
6.288: Thus having said, he stopp'd with watchful sight,
6.289: Observing still the motions of their flight,
6.290: What course they took, what happy signs they shew.
6.291: They fed, and, flutt'ring, by degrees withdrew
6.292: Still farther from the place, but still in view:
6.293: Hopping and flying, thus they led him on
6.294: To the slow lake, whose baleful stench to shun
6.295: They wing'd their flight aloft; then, stooping low,
6.296: Perch'd on the double tree that bears the golden
6.297: Thro' the green leafs the glitt'ring shadows glow;
6.298: As, on the sacred oak, the wintry mistletoe,
6.299: Where the proud mother views her precious brood,
6.300: And happier branches, which she never sow'd.
6.301: Such was the glitt'ring; such the ruddy rind,
6.302: And dancing leaves, that wanton'd in the wind.
6.303: He seiz'd the shining bough with griping hold,
6.304: And rent away, with ease, the ling'ring gold;
6.305: Then to the Sibyl's palace bore the prize.
6.306: Meantime the Trojan troops, with weeping eyes,
6.307: To dead Misenus pay his obsequies.
6.308: First, from the ground a lofty pile they rear,
6.309: Of pitch trees, oaks, and pines, and unctuous fir:
6.310: The fabric's front with cypress twigs they strew,
6.311: And stick the sides with boughs of baleful yew.
6.312: The topmost part his glitt'ring arms adorn;
6.313: Warm waters, then, in brazen caldrons borne,
6.314: Are pour'd to wash his body, joint by joint,
6.315: And fragrant oils the stiffen'd limbs anoint.
6.316: With groans and cries Misenus they deplore:
6.317: Then on a bier, with purple cover'd o'er,
6.318: The breathless body, thus bewail'd, they lay,
6.319: And fire the pile, their faces turn'd away-
6.320: Such reverend rites their fathers us'd to pay.
6.321: Pure oil and incense on the fire they throw,
6.322: And fat of victims, which his friends bestow.
6.323: These gifts the greedy flames to dust devour;
6.324: Then on the living coals red wine they pour;
6.325: And, last, the relics by themselves dispose,
6.326: Which in a brazen urn the priests inclose.
6.327: Old Corynaeus compass'd thrice the crew,
6.328: And dipp'd an olive branch in holy dew;
6.329: Which thrice he sprinkled round, and thrice aloud
6.330: Invok'd the dead, and then dismissed the crowd.
6.331: But good Aeneas order'd on the shore
6.332: A stately tomb, whose top a trumpet bore,
6.333: A soldier's fauchion, and a seaman's oar.
6.334: Thus was his friend interr'd; and deathless fame
6.335: Still to the lofty cape consigns his name.
6.336: These rites perform'd, the prince, without delay,
6.337: Hastes to the nether world his destin'd way.
6.338: Deep was the cave; and, downward as it went
6.339: From the wide mouth, a rocky rough descent;
6.340: And here th' access a gloomy grove defends,
6.341: And there th' unnavigable lake extends,
6.342: O'er whose unhappy waters, void of light,
6.343: No bird presumes to steer his airy flight;
6.344: Such deadly stenches from the depths arise,
6.345: And steaming sulphur, that infects the skies.
6.346: From hence the Grecian bards their legends make,
6.347: And give the name Avernus to the lake.
6.348: Four sable bullocks, in the yoke untaught,
6.349: For sacrifice the pious hero brought.
6.350: The priestess pours the wine betwixt their horns;
6.351: Then cuts the curling hair; that first oblation
6.353: A pow'rful name in hell and upper air.
6.354: The sacred priests with ready knives bereave
6.355: The beasts of life, and in full bowls receive
6.356: The streaming blood: a lamb to Hell and Night
6.357: (The sable wool without a streak of white)
6.358: Aeneas offers; and, by fate's decree,
6.359: A barren heifer, Proserpine, to thee,
6.360: With holocausts he Pluto's altar fills;
6.361: Sev'n brawny bulls with his own hand he kills;
6.362: Then on the broiling entrails oil he pours;
6.363: Which, ointed thus, the raging flame devours.
6.365: Nor ended till the next returning sun.
6.366: Then earth began to bellow, trees to dance,
6.367: And howling dogs in glimm'ring light advance,
6.368: Ere Hecate came. "Far hence be souls profane!"
6.369: The Sibyl cried, "and from the grove abstain!
6.370: Now, Trojan, take the way thy fates afford;
6.371: Assume thy courage, and unsheathe thy sword."
6.372: She said, and pass'd along the gloomy space;
6.373: The prince pursued her steps with equal pace.
6.374: Ye realms, yet unreveal'd to human sight,
6.375: Ye gods who rule the regions of the night,
6.376: Ye gliding ghosts, permit me to relate
6.377: The mystic wonders of your silent state!
6.378: Obscure they went thro' dreary shades, that led
6.379: Along the waste dominions of the dead.
6.380: Thus wander travelers in woods by night,
6.381: By the moon's doubtful and malignant light,
6.382: When Jove in dusky clouds involves the skies,
6.383: And the faint crescent shoots by fits before their
6.384: Just in the gate and in the jaws of hell,
6.385: Revengeful Cares and sullen Sorrows dwell,
6.386: And pale Diseases, and repining Age,
6.387: Want, Fear, and Famine's unresisted rage;
6.388: Here Toils, and Death, and Death's half-brother,
6.389: Forms terrible to view, their sentry keep;
6.390: With anxious Pleasures of a guilty mind,
6.391: Deep Frauds before, and open Force behind;
6.392: The Furies' iron beds; and Strife, that shakes
6.393: Her hissing tresses and unfolds her snakes.
6.394: Full in the midst of this infernal road,
6.395: An elm displays her dusky arms abroad:
6.396: The God of Sleep there hides his heavy head,
6.397: And empty dreams on ev'ry leaf are spread.
6.398: Of various forms unnumber'd specters more,
6.399: Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door.
6.400: Before the passage, horrid Hydra stands,
6.401: And Briareus with all his hundred hands;
6.402: Gorgons, Geryon with his triple frame;
6.403: And vain Chimaera vomits empty flame.
6.404: The chief unsheath'd his shining steel, prepar'd,
6.405: Tho' seiz'd with sudden fear, to force the guard,
6.406: Off'ring his brandish'd weapon at their face;
6.407: Had not the Sibyl stopp'd his eager pace,
6.408: And told him what those empty phantoms were:
6.409: Forms without bodies, and impassive air.
6.410: Hence to deep Acheron they take their way,
6.411: Whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay,
6.412: Are whirl'd aloft, and in Cocytus lost.
6.413: There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast-
6.414: A sordid god: down from his hoary chin
6.415: A length of beard descends, uncomb'd, unclean;
6.416: His eyes, like hollow furnaces on fire;
6.417: A girdle, foul with grease, binds his obscene attire.
6.418: He spreads his canvas; with his pole he steers;
6.419: The freights of flitting ghosts in his thin bottom
6.420: He look'd in years; yet in his years were seen
6.421: A youthful vigor and autumnal green.
6.422: An airy crowd came rushing where he stood,
6.423: Which fill'd the margin of the fatal flood:
6.424: Husbands and wives, boys and unmarried maids,
6.425: And mighty heroes' more majestic shades,
6.426: And youths, intomb'd before their fathers' eyes,
6.427: With hollow groans, and shrieks, and feeble cries.
6.428: Thick as the leaves in autumn strow the woods,
6.429: Or fowls, by winter forc'd, forsake the floods,
6.430: And wing their hasty flight to happier lands;
6.431: Such, and so thick, the shiv'ring army stands,
6.432: And press for passage with extended hands.
6.433: Now these, now those, the surly boatman bore:
6.434: The rest he drove to distance from the shore.

7.68: Latinus, old and mild, had long possess'd
7.69: The Latin scepter, and his people blest:

7.71: His mother; fair Marica was her name.

7.73: His birth from Saturn, if records be true.

7.126: Fly, when distress'd, and thence relief demand.
7.127: The priest on skins of off'rings takes his ease,
7.128: And nightly visions in his slumber sees;
7.129: A swarm of thin aerial shapes appears,
7.130: And, flutt'ring round his temples, deafs his ears:
7.131: These he consults, the future fates to know,
7.132: From pow'rs above, and from the fiends below.
7.133: Here, for the gods' advice, Latinus flies,
7.134: Off'ring a hundred sheep for sacrifice:
7.135: Their woolly fleeces, as the rites requir'd,
7.136: He laid beneath him, and to rest retir'd.
7.137: No sooner were his eyes in slumber bound,
7.138: When, from above, a more than mortal sound
7.139: Invades his ears; and thus the vision spoke:
7.140: "Seek not, my seed, in Latian bands to yoke
7.141: Our fair Lavinia, nor the gods provoke.
7.142: A foreign son upon thy shore descends,
7.143: Whose martial fame from pole to pole extends.
7.144: His race, in arms and arts of peace renown'd,
7.145: Not Latium shall contain, nor Europe bound:
7.146: 'T is theirs whate'er the sun surveys around."
7.147: These answers, in the silent night receiv'd,
7.148: The king himself divulg'd, the land believ'd:
7.149: The fame thro' all the neighb'ring nations flew,
7.150: When now the Trojan navy was in view.
7.151: Beneath a shady tree, the hero spread
7.152: His table on the turf, with cakes of bread;
7.153: And, with his chiefs, on forest fruits he fed.
7.154: They sate; and, (not without the god's command,)
7.155: Their homely fare dispatch'd, the hungry band
7.156: Invade their trenchers next, and soon devour,
7.157: To mend the scanty meal, their cakes of flour.
7.158: Ascanius this observ'd, and smiling said:
7.159: "See, we devour the plates on which we fed."
7.160: The speech had omen, that the Trojan race
7.161: Should find repose, and this the time and place.
7.162: Aeneas took the word, and thus replies,
7.163: Confessing fate with wonder in his eyes:
7.164: "All hail, O earth! all hail, my household gods!
7.165: Behold the destin'd place of your abodes!
7.166: For thus Anchises prophesied of old,
7.167: And this our fatal place of rest foretold:
7.168: 'When, on a foreign shore, instead of meat,
7.169: By famine forc'd, your trenchers you shall eat,
7.170: Then ease your weary Trojans will attend,
7.171: And the long labors of your voyage end.
7.172: Remember on that happy coast to build,
7.173: And with a trench inclose the fruitful field.'
7.174: This was that famine, this the fatal place
7.175: Which ends the wand'ring of our exil'd race.
7.176: Then, on to-morrow's dawn, your care employ,
7.177: To search the land, and where the cities lie,
7.178: And what the men; but give this day to joy.
7.179: Now pour to Jove; and, after Jove is blest,
7.180: Call great Anchises to the genial feast:
7.181: Crown high the goblets with a cheerful draught;
7.182: Enjoy the present hour; adjourn the future thought."
7.183: Thus having said, the hero bound his brows
7.184: With leafy branches, then perform'd his vows;
7.185: Adoring first the genius of the place,
7.186: Then Earth, the mother of the heav'nly race,
7.187: The nymphs, and native godheads yet unknown,
7.188: And Night, and all the stars that gild her sable
7.189: And ancient Cybel, and Idaean Jove,
7.190: And last his sire below, and mother queen above.
7.191: Then heav'n's high monarch thunder'd thrice aloud,
7.192: And thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud.
7.193: Soon thro' the joyful camp a rumor flew,
7.194: The time was come their city to renew.
7.195: Then ev'ry brow with cheerful green is crown'd,
7.196: The feasts are doubled, and the bowls go round.
7.197: When next the rosy morn disclos'd the day,
7.198: The scouts to sev'ral parts divide their way,
7.199: To learn the natives' names, their towns explore,
7.200: The coasts and trendings of the crooked shore:
7.201: Here Tiber flows, and here Numicus stands;
7.202: Here warlike Latins hold the happy lands.
7.203: The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways
7.204: To found his empire, and his town to raise,
7.205: A hundred youths from all his train selects,
7.206: And to the Latian court their course directs,
7.207: (The spacious palace where their prince resides,)
7.208: And all their heads with wreaths of olive hides.
7.209: They go commission'd to require a peace,
7.210: And carry presents to procure access.
7.211: Thus while they speed their pace, the prince designs
7.212: His new-elected seat, and draws the lines.
7.213: The Trojans round the place a rampire cast,
7.214: And palisades about the trenches plac'd.
7.215: Meantime the train, proceeding on their way,
7.216: From far the town and lofty tow'rs survey;
7.217: At length approach the walls. Without the gate,
7.218: They see the boys and Latian youth debate
7.219: The martial prizes on the dusty plain:
7.220: Some drive the cars, and some the coursers rein;
7.221: Some bend the stubborn bow for victory,
7.222: And some with darts their active sinews try.
7.223: A posting messenger, dispatch'd from hence,
7.224: Of this fair troop advis'd their aged prince,
7.225: That foreign men of mighty stature came;
7.226: Uncouth their habit, and unknown their name.
7.227: The king ordains their entrance, and ascends
7.228: His regal seat, surrounded by his friends.
7.229: The palace built by Picus, vast and proud,
7.230: Supported by a hundred pillars stood,
7.231: And round incompass'd with a rising wood.
7.232: The pile o'erlook'd the town, and drew the sight;
7.233: Surpris'd at once with reverence and delight.
7.234: There kings receiv'd the marks of sov'reign pow'r;
7.235: In state the monarchs march'd; the lictors bore
7.236: Their awful axes and the rods before.
7.237: Here the tribunal stood, the house of pray'r,
7.238: And here the sacred senators repair;
7.239: All at large tables, in long order set,
7.240: A ram their off'ring, and a ram their meat.
7.241: Above the portal, carv'd in cedar wood,
7.242: Plac'd in their ranks, their godlike grandsires
7.243: Old Saturn, with his crooked scythe, on high;
7.244: And Italus, that led the colony;
7.245: And ancient Janus, with his double face,
7.246: And bunch of keys, the porter of the place.
7.247: There good Sabinus, planter of the vines,
7.248: On a short pruning hook his head reclines,
7.249: And studiously surveys his gen'rous wines;
7.250: Then warlike kings, who for their country fought,
7.251: And honorable wounds from battle brought.
7.252: Around the posts hung helmets, darts, and spears,
7.253: And captive chariots, axes, shields, and bars,
7.254: And broken beaks of ships, the trophies of their
7.255: Above the rest, as chief of all the band,
7.256: Was Picus plac'd, a buckler in his hand;
7.257: His other wav'd a long divining wand.
7.258: Girt in his Gabin gown the hero sate,
7.259: Yet could not with his art avoid his fate:
7.260: For Circe long had lov'd the youth in vain,
7.261: Till love, refus'd, converted to disdain:
7.262: Then, mixing pow'rful herbs, with magic art,
7.263: She chang'd his form, who could not change his heart;
7.264: Constrain'd him in a bird, and made him fly,
7.265: With party-color'd plumes, a chatt'ring pie.
7.266: In this high temple, on a chair of state,
7.267: The seat of audience, old Latinus sate;
7.268: Then gave admission to the Trojan train;
7.269: And thus with pleasing accents he began:
7.270: "Tell me, ye Trojans, for that name you own,
7.271: Nor is your course upon our coasts unknown-
7.272: Say what you seek, and whither were you bound:
7.273: Were you by stress of weather cast aground?
7.274: (Such dangers as on seas are often seen,
7.275: And oft befall to miserable men,)
7.276: Or come, your shipping in our ports to lay,
7.277: Spent and disabled in so long a way?
7.278: Say what you want: the Latians you shall find
7.279: Not forc'd to goodness, but by will inclin'd;
7.280: For, since the time of Saturn's holy reign,
7.282: I call to mind (but time the tale has worn)
7.283: Th' Arunci told, that Dardanus, tho' born
7.284: On Latian plains, yet sought the Phrygian shore,
7.286: From Tuscan Coritum he claim'd his birth;
7.287: But after, when exempt from mortal earth,
7.288: From thence ascended to his kindred skies,
7.289: A god, and, as a god, augments their sacrifice,"
7.290: He said. Ilioneus made this reply:
7.292: Nor wintry winds to Latium forc'd our way,
7.293: Nor did the stars our wand'ring course betray.
7.294: Willing we sought your shores; and, hither bound,
7.295: The port, so long desir'd, at length we found;
7.296: From our sweet homes and ancient realms expell'd;
7.297: Great as the greatest that the sun beheld.
7.298: The god began our line, who rules above;
7.299: And, as our race, our king descends from Jove:
7.300: And hither are we come, by his command,
7.301: To crave admission in your happy land.
7.302: How dire a tempest, from Mycenae pour'd,
7.303: Our plains, our temples, and our town devour'd;
7.304: What was the waste of war, what fierce alarms
7.305: Shook Asia's crown with European arms;
7.306: Ev'n such have heard, if any such there be,
7.307: Whose earth is bounded by the frozen sea;
7.308: And such as, born beneath the burning sky
7.309: And sultry sun, betwixt the tropics lie.
7.310: From that dire deluge, thro' the wat'ry waste,
7.311: Such length of years, such various perils past,
7.312: At last escap'd, to Latium we repair,
7.313: To beg what you without your want may spare:
7.314: The common water, and the common air;
7.315: Sheds which ourselves will build, and mean abodes,
7.316: Fit to receive and serve our banish'd gods.
7.317: Nor our admission shall your realm disgrace,
7.318: Nor length of time our gratitude efface.
7.319: Besides, what endless honor you shall gain,
7.320: To save and shelter Troy's unhappy train!
7.321: Now, by my sov'reign, and his fate, I swear,
7.322: Renown'd for faith in peace, for force in war;
7.323: Oft our alliance other lands desir'd,
7.324: And, what we seek of you, of us requir'd.
7.325: Despite not then, that in our hands we bear
7.326: These holy boughs, sue with words of pray'r.
7.327: Fate and the gods, by their supreme command,
7.328: Have doom'd our ships to seek the Latian land.
7.329: To these abodes our fleet Apollo sends;
7.330: Here Dardanus was born, and hither tends;
7.331: Where Tuscan Tiber rolls with rapid force,
7.332: And where Numicus opes his holy source.
7.333: Besides, our prince presents, with his request,
7.334: Some small remains of what his sire possess'd.
7.335: This golden charger, snatch'd from burning Troy,
7.337: This royal robe and this tiara wore
7.338: Old Priam, and this golden scepter bore
7.339: In full assemblies, and in solemn games;
7.340: These purple vests were weav'd by Dardan dames."
7.341: Thus while he spoke, Latinus roll'd around
7.342: His eyes, and fix'd a while upon the ground.
7.343: Intent he seem'd, and anxious in his breast;
7.344: Not by the scepter mov'd, or kingly vest,
7.345: But pond'ring future things of wondrous weight;
7.346: Succession, empire, and his daughter's fate.
7.347: On these he mus'd within his thoughtful mind,
7.348: And then revolv'd what Faunus had divin'd.
7.349: This was the foreign prince, by fate decreed
7.350: To share his scepter, and Lavinia's bed;
7.351: This was the race that sure portents foreshew
7.352: To sway the world, and land and sea subdue.
7.353: At length he rais'd his cheerful head, and spoke:
7.354: "The pow'rs," said he, "the pow'rs we both invoke,
7.355: To you, and yours, and mine, propitious be,
7.356: And firm our purpose with their augury!
7.357: Have what you ask; your presents I receive;
7.358: Land, where and when you please, with ample leave;
7.359: Partake and use my kingdom as your own;
7.360: All shall be yours, while I command the crown:
7.361: And, if my wish'd alliance please your king,
7.362: Tell him he should not send the peace, but bring.
7.363: Then let him not a friend's embraces fear;
7.364: The peace is made when I behold him here.
7.365: Besides this answer, tell my royal guest,
7.366: I add to his commands my own request:
7.367: One only daughter heirs my crown and state,
7.368: Whom not our oracles, nor Heav'n, nor fate,
7.369: Nor frequent prodigies, permit to join
7.370: With any native of th' Ausonian line.
7.371: A foreign son-in-law shall come from far
7.372: (Such is our doom), a chief renown'd in war,
7.373: Whose race shall bear aloft the Latian name,
7.374: And thro' the conquer'd world diffuse our fame.
7.375: Himself to be the man the fates require,
7.376: I firmly judge, and, what I judge, desire."
7.377: He said, and then on each bestow'd a steed.
7.378: Three hundred horses, in high stables fed,
7.379: Stood ready, shining all, and smoothly dress'd:
7.380: Of these he chose the fairest and the best,
7.381: To mount the Trojan troop. At his command
7.382: The steeds caparison'd with purple stand,
7.383: With golden trappings, glorious to behold,
7.384: And champ betwixt their teeth the foaming gold.
7.385: Then to his absent guest the king decreed
7.386: A pair of coursers born of heav'nly breed,
7.387: Who from their nostrils breath'd ethereal fire;
7.388: Whom Circe stole from her celestial sire,
7.389: By substituting mares produc'd on earth,
7.390: Whose wombs conceiv'd a more than mortal birth.
7.391: These draw the chariot which Latinus sends,
7.392: And the rich present to the prince commends.
7.393: Sublime on stately steeds the Trojans borne,
7.394: To their expecting lord with peace return.
7.395: But jealous Juno, from Pachynus' height,
7.396: As she from Argos took her airy flight,
7.397: Beheld with envious eyes this hateful sight.
7.398: She saw the Trojan and his joyful train
7.399: Descend upon the shore, desert the main,
7.400: Design a town, and, with unhop'd success,
7.401: Th' embassadors return with promis'd peace.
7.402: Then, pierc'd with pain, she shook her haughty head,
7.403: Sigh'd from her inward soul, and thus she said:
7.404: "O hated offspring of my Phrygian foes!
7.405: O fates of Troy, which Juno's fates oppose!
7.406: Could they not fall unpitied on the plain,
7.407: But slain revive, and, taken, scape again?
7.408: When execrable Troy in ashes lay,
7.409: Thro' fires and swords and seas they forc'd their
7.410: Then vanquish'd Juno must in vain contend,
7.411: Her rage disarm'd, her empire at an end.
7.412: Breathless and tir'd, is all my fury spent?
7.413: Or does my glutted spleen at length relent?
7.414: As if 't were little from their town to chase,
7.415: I thro' the seas pursued their exil'd race;
7.416: Ingag'd the heav'ns, oppos'd the stormy main;
7.417: But billows roar'd, and tempests rag'd in vain.
7.418: What have my Scyllas and my Syrtes done,
7.419: When these they overpass, and those they shun?
7.420: On Tiber's shores they land, secure of fate,
7.421: Triumphant o'er the storms and Juno's hate.
7.422: Mars could in mutual blood the Centaurs bathe,
7.423: And Jove himself gave way to Cynthia's wrath,
7.424: Who sent the tusky boar to Calydon;
7.425: (What great offense had either people done?)
7.426: But I, the consort of the Thunderer,
7.427: Have wag'd a long and unsuccessful war,
7.428: With various arts and arms in vain have toil'd,
7.429: And by a mortal man at length am foil'd.
7.430: If native pow'r prevail not, shall I doubt
7.431: To seek for needful succor from without?
7.432: If Jove and Heav'n my just desires deny,
7.433: Hell shall the pow'r of Heav'n and Jove supply.
7.434: Grant that the Fates have firm'd, by their decree,
7.435: The Trojan race to reign in Italy;
7.436: At least I can defer the nuptial day,
7.437: And with protracted wars the peace delay:
7.438: With blood the dear alliance shall be bought,
7.439: And both the people near destruction brought;
7.440: So shall the son-in-law and father join,
7.441: With ruin, war, and waste of either line.
7.442: O fatal maid, thy marriage is endow'd
7.444: Bellona leads thee to thy lover's hand;
7.445: Another queen brings forth another brand,
7.446: To burn with foreign fires another land!
7.447: A second Paris, diff'ring but in name,
7.448: Shall fire his country with a second flame."
7.449: Thus having said, she sinks beneath the ground,
7.450: With furious haste, and shoots the Stygian sound,
7.451: To rouse Alecto from th' infernal seat
7.452: Of her dire sisters, and their dark retreat.
7.453: This Fury, fit for her intent, she chose;
7.454: One who delights in wars and human woes.
7.455: Ev'n Pluto hates his own misshapen race;
7.456: Her sister Furies fly her hideous face;
7.457: So frightful are the forms the monster takes,
7.458: So fierce the hissings of her speckled snakes.
7.459: Her Juno finds, and thus inflames her spite:
7.461: Give me this once thy labor, to sustain
7.462: My right, and execute my just disdain.
7.463: Let not the Trojans, with a feign'd pretense
7.464: Of proffer'd peace, delude the Latian prince.
7.465: Expel from Italy that odious name,
7.466: And let not Juno suffer in her fame.
7.467: 'T is thine to ruin realms, o'erturn a state,
7.468: Betwixt the dearest friends to raise debate,
7.469: And kindle kindred blood to mutual hate.
7.470: Thy hand o'er towns the fun'ral torch displays,
7.471: And forms a thousand ills ten thousand ways.
7.472: Now shake, out thy fruitful breast, the seeds
7.473: Of envy, discord, and of cruel deeds:
7.474: Confound the peace establish'd, and prepare
7.475: Their souls to hatred, and their hands to war."
7.476: Smear'd as she was with black Gorgonian blood,
7.477: The Fury sprang above the Stygian flood;
7.478: And on her wicker wings, sublime thro' night,
7.479: She to the Latian palace took her flight:
7.480: There sought the queen's apartment, stood before
7.481: The peaceful threshold, and besieg'd the door.
7.482: Restless Amata lay, her swelling breast
7.483: Fir'd with disdain for Turnus dispossess'd,
7.484: And the new nuptials of the Trojan guest.
7.485: From her black bloody locks the Fury shakes
7.486: Her darling plague, the fav'rite of her snakes;
7.487: With her full force she threw the poisonous dart,
7.488: And fix'd it deep within Amata's heart,
7.489: That, thus envenom'd, she might kindle rage,
7.490: And sacrifice to strife her house husband's age.
7.491: Unseen, unfelt, the fiery serpent skims
7.492: Betwixt her linen and her naked limbs;
7.493: His baleful breath inspiring, as he glides,
7.494: Now like a chain around her neck he rides,
7.495: Now like a fillet to her head repairs,
7.496: And with his circling volumes folds her hairs.
7.497: At first the silent venom slid with ease,
7.498: And seiz'd her cooler senses by degrees;
7.499: Then, ere th' infected mass was fir'd too far,
7.500: In plaintive accents she began the war,
7.501: And thus bespoke her husband: "Shall," she said,
7.503: If nature plead not in a parent's heart,
7.504: Pity my tears, and pity her desert.
7.505: I know, my dearest lord, the time will come,
7.506: You in vain, reverse your cruel doom;
7.507: The faithless pirate soon will set to sea,
7.508: And bear the royal virgin far away!
7.509: A guest like him, a Trojan guest before,
7.510: In shew of friendship sought the Spartan shore,
7.511: And ravish'd Helen from her husband bore.
7.512: Think on a king's inviolable word;
7.513: And think on Turnus, her once plighted lord:
7.514: To this false foreigner you give your throne,
7.515: And wrong a friend, a kinsman, and a son.
7.516: Resume your ancient care; and, if the god
7.517: Your sire, and you, resolve on foreign blood,
7.518: Know all are foreign, in a larger sense,
7.519: Not born your subjects, or deriv'd from hence.
7.520: Then, if the line of Turnus you retrace,
7.521: He springs from Inachus of Argive race."
7.522: But when she saw her reasons idly spent,
7.523: And could not move him from his fix'd intent,
7.524: She flew to rage; for now the snake possess'd
7.525: Her vital parts, and poison'd all her breast;
7.526: She raves, she runs with a distracted pace,
7.527: And fills with horrid howls the public place.
7.528: And, as young striplings whip the top for sport,
7.529: On the smooth pavement of an empty court;
7.530: The wooden engine flies and whirls about,
7.531: Admir'd, with clamors, of the beardless rout;
7.532: They lash aloud; each other they provoke,
7.533: And lend their little souls at ev'ry stroke:
7.534: Thus fares the queen; and thus her fury blows
7.535: Amidst the crowd, and kindles as she goes.
7.536: Nor yet content, she strains her malice more,
7.537: And adds new ills to those contriv'd before:
7.538: She flies the town, and, mixing with a throng
7.539: Of madding matrons, bears the bride along,
7.540: Wand'ring thro' woods and wilds, and devious ways,
7.541: And with these arts the Trojan match delays.
7.542: She feign'd the rites of Bacchus; cried aloud,
7.543: And to the buxom god the virgin vow'd.
7.544: "Evoe! O Bacchus!" thus began the song;
7.545: And "Evoe!" answer'd all the female throng.
7.546: "O virgin! worthy thee alone!" she cried;
7.547: "O worthy thee alone!" the crew replied.
7.548: "For thee she feeds her hair, she leads thy dance,
7.549: And with thy winding ivy wreathes her lance."
7.550: Like fury seiz'd the rest; the progress known,
7.551: All seek the mountains, and forsake the town:
7.552: All, clad in skins of beasts, the jav'lin bear,
7.553: Give to the wanton winds their flowing hair,
7.554: And shrieks and shoutings rend the suff'ring air.
7.555: The queen herself, inspir'd with rage divine,
7.556: Shook high above her head a flaming pine;
7.557: Then roll'd her haggard eyes around the throng,
7.558: And sung, in Turnus' name, the nuptial song:
7.559: "Io, ye Latian dames! if any here
7.560: Hold your unhappy queen, Amata, dear;
7.561: If there be here," she said, who dare maintain
7.562: My right, nor think the name of mother vain;
7.563: Unbind your fillets, loose your flowing hair,
7.564: And orgies and nocturnal rites prepare."
7.565: Amata's breast the Fury thus invades,
7.566: And fires with rage, amid the sylvan shades;
7.567: Then, when she found her venom spread so far,
7.568: The royal house embroil'd in civil war,
7.569: Rais'd on her dusky wings, she cleaves the skies,
7.570: And seeks the palace where young Turnus lies.
7.571: His town, as fame reports, was built of old
7.572: By Danae, pregnant with almighty gold,
7.573: Who fled her father's rage, and, with a train
7.574: Of following Argives, thro' the stormy main,
7.575: Driv'n by the southern blasts, was fated here to
7.576: 'T was Ardua once; now Ardea's name it bears;
7.577: Once a fair city, now consum'd with years.
7.578: Here, in his lofty palace, Turnus lay,
7.579: Betwixt the confines of the night and day,
7.580: Secure in sleep. The Fury laid aside
7.581: Her looks and limbs, and with new methods tried
7.582: The foulness of th' infernal form to hide.
7.583: Propp'd on a staff, she takes a trembling mien:
7.584: Her face is furrow'd, and her front obscene;
7.585: Deep-dinted wrinkles on her cheek she draws;
7.586: Sunk are her eyes, and toothless are her jaws;
7.587: Her hoary hair with holy fillets bound,
7.588: Her temples with an olive wreath are crown'd.
7.589: Old Chalybe, who kept the sacred fane
7.590: Of Juno, now she seem'd, and thus began,
7.591: Appearing in a dream, to rouse the careless man:
7.592: "Shall Turnus then such endless toil sustain
7.593: In fighting fields, and conquer towns in vain?
7.594: Win, for a Trojan head to wear the prize,
7.595: Usurp thy crown, enjoy thy victories?
7.596: The bride and scepter which thy blood has bought,
7.597: The king transfers; and foreign heirs are sought.
7.598: Go now, deluded man, and seek again
7.599: New toils, new dangers, on the dusty plain.
7.600: Repel the Tuscan foes; their city seize;
7.601: Protect the Latians in luxurious ease.
7.602: This dream all-pow'rful Juno sends; I bear
7.603: Her mighty mandates, and her words you hear.
7.604: Haste; arm your Ardeans; issue to the plain;
