7.1072: High o'er the rest in arms the graceful Turnus rode:
7.1073: A triple of plumes his crest adorn'd,
7.1074: On which with belching flames Chimaera burn'd:
7.1075: The more the kindled combat rises high'r,
7.1076: The more with fury burns the blazing fire.
7.1077: Fair Io grac'd his shield; but Io now
7.1078: With horns exalted stands, and seems to low-
7.1079: A noble charge! Her keeper by her side,
7.1080: To watch her walks, his hundred eyes applied;
7.1081: And on the brims her sire, the wat'ry god,
7.1082: Roll'd from a silver urn his crystal flood.
7.1083: A cloud of foot succeeds, and fills the fields
7.1084: With swords, and pointed spears, and clatt'ring
7.1085: Of Argives, and of old Sicanian bands,
7.1086: And those who plow the rich Rutulian lands;
7.1087: Auruncan youth, and those Sacrana yields,
7.1088: And the proud Labicans, with painted shields,
7.1089: And those who near Numician streams reside,
7.1090: And those whom Tiber's holy forests hide,
7.1091: Or Circe's hills from the main land divide;
7.1092: Where Ufens glides along the lowly lands,
7.1093: Or the black water of Pomptina stands.
7.1094: Last, from the Volscians fair Camilla came,
7.1095: And led her warlike troops, a warrior dame;
7.1096: Unbred to spinning, in the loom unskill'd,
7.1097: She chose the nobler Pallas of the field.
7.1098: Mix'd with the first, the fierce virago fought,
7.1099: Sustain'd the toils of arms, the danger sought,
7.1100: Outstripp'd the winds in speed upon the plain,
7.1101: Flew o'er the fields, nor hurt the bearded grain:
7.1102: She swept the seas, and, as she skimm'd along,
7.1103: Her flying feet unbath'd on billows hung.
7.1104: Men, boys, and women, stupid with surprise,
7.1105: Where'er she passes, fix their wond'ring eyes:
7.1106: Longing they look, and, gaping at the sight,
7.1107: Devour her o'er and o'er with vast delight;
7.1108: Her purple habit sits with such a grace
7.1109: On her smooth shoulders, and so suits her face;
7.1110: Her head with ringlets of her hair is crown'd,
7.1111: And in a golden caul the curls are bound.
7.1112: She shakes her myrtle jav'lin; and, behind,
7.1113: Her Lycian quiver dances in the wind.

8.1: When Turnus had assembled all his pow'rs,
8.2: His standard planted on Laurentum's tow'rs;
8.3: When now the sprightly trumpet, from afar,
8.4: Had giv'n the signal of approaching war,
8.5: Had rous'd the neighing steeds to scour the fields,
8.6: While the fierce riders clatter'd on their shields;
8.7: Trembling with rage, the Latian youth prepare
8.8: To join th' allies, and headlong rush to war.
8.9: Fierce Ufens, and Messapus, led the crowd,
8.10: With bold Mezentius, who blasphem'd aloud.
8.11: These thro' the country took their wasteful course,
8.12: The fields to forage, and to gather force.
8.13: Then Venulus to Diomede they send,
8.14: To beg his aid Ausonia to defend,
8.15: Declare the common danger, and inform
8.16: The Grecian leader of the growing storm:
8.17: Aeneas, landed on the Latian coast,
8.18: With banish'd gods, and with a baffled host,
8.19: Yet now aspir'd to conquest of the state,
8.20: And claim'd a title from the gods and fate;
8.21: What num'rous nations in his quarrel came,
8.22: And how they spread his formidable name.
8.23: What he design'd, what mischief might arise,
8.24: If fortune favor'd his first enterprise,
8.25: Was left for him to weigh, whose equal fears,
8.26: And common interest, was involv'd in theirs.
8.27: While Turnus and th' allies thus urge the war,
8.28: The Trojan, floating in a flood of care,
8.29: Beholds the tempest which his foes prepare.
8.30: This way and that he turns his anxious mind;
8.31: Thinks, and rejects the counsels he design'd;
8.32: Explores himself in vain, in ev'ry part,
8.33: And gives no rest to his distracted heart.
8.34: So, when the sun by day, or moon by night,
8.35: Strike on the polish'd brass their trembling light,
8.36: The glitt'ring species here and there divide,
8.37: And cast their dubious beams from side to side;
8.38: Now on the walls, now on the pavement play,
8.39: And to the ceiling flash the glaring day.
8.40: 'T was night; and weary nature lull'd asleep
8.41: The birds of air, and fishes of the deep,
8.42: And beasts, and mortal men. The Trojan chief
8.43: Was laid on Tiber's banks, oppress'd with grief,
8.44: And found in silent slumber late relief.
8.45: Then, thro' the shadows of the poplar wood,
8.46: Arose the father of the Roman flood;
8.47: An azure robe was o'er his body spread,
8.48: A wreath of shady reeds adorn'd his head:
8.49: Thus, manifest to sight, the god appear'd,
8.50: And with these pleasing words his sorrow cheer'd:
8.52: O long expected in this promis'd place!
8.53: Who thro' the foes hast borne thy banish'd gods,
8.54: Restor'd them to their hearths, and old abodes;
8.55: This is thy happy home, the clime where fate
8.56: Ordains thee to restore the Trojan state.
8.57: Fear not! The war shall end in lasting peace,
8.58: And all the rage of haughty Juno cease.
8.59: And that this nightly vision may not seem
8.60: Th' effect of fancy, or an idle dream,
8.61: A sow beneath an oak shall lie along,
8.62: All white herself, and white her thirty young.
8.63: When thirty rolling years have run their race,
8.64: Thy son Ascanius, on this empty space,
8.65: Shall build a royal town, of lasting fame,
8.66: Which from this omen shall receive the name.
8.67: Time shall approve the truth. For what remains,
8.68: And how with sure success to crown thy pains,
8.69: With patience next attend. A banish'd band,
8.70: Driv'n with Evander from th' Arcadian land,
8.71: Have planted here, and plac'd on high their walls;
8.72: Their town the founder Pallanteum calls,
8.73: Deriv'd from Pallas, his great-grandsire's name:
8.74: But the fierce Latians old possession claim,
8.75: With war infesting the new colony.
8.76: These make thy friends, and on their aid rely.
8.77: To thy free passage I submit my streams.
8.78: Wake, son of Venus, from thy pleasing dreams;
8.79: And, when the setting stars are lost in day,
8.80: To Juno's pow'r thy just devotion pay;
8.81: With sacrifice the wrathful queen appease:
8.82: Her pride at length shall fall, her fury cease.
8.83: When thou return'st victorious from the war,
8.84: Perform thy vows to me with grateful care.
8.85: The god am I, whose yellow water flows
8.86: Around these fields, and fattens as it goes:
8.87: Tiber my name; among the rolling floods
8.88: Renown'd on earth, esteem'd among the gods.
8.89: This is my certain seat. In times to come,
8.90: My waves shall wash the walls of mighty Rome."
8.91: He said, and plung'd below. While yet he spoke,
8.92: His dream Aeneas and his sleep forsook.
8.93: He rose, and looking up, beheld the skies
8.94: With purple blushing, and the day arise.
8.95: Then water in his hollow palm he took
8.96: From Tiber's flood, and thus the pow'rs bespoke:
8.97: "Laurentian nymphs, by whom the streams are fed,
8.98: And Father Tiber, in thy sacred bed
8.99: Receive Aeneas, and from danger keep.
8.101: Conceals thy wat'ry stores; where'er they rise,
8.102: And, bubbling from below, salute the skies;
8.103: Thou, king of horned floods, whose plenteous urn
8.104: Suffices fatness to the fruitful corn,
8.105: For this thy kind compassion of our woes,
8.106: Shalt share my morning song and ev'ning vows.
8.107: But, O be present to thy people's aid,
8.108: And firm the gracious promise thou hast made!"
8.109: Thus having said, two galleys from his stores,
8.110: With care he chooses, mans, and fits with oars.
8.111: Now on the shore the fatal swine is found.
8.112: Wondrous to tell!- She lay along the ground:
8.113: Her well-fed offspring at her udders hung;
8.114: She white herself, and white her thirty young.
8.115: Aeneas takes the mother and her brood,
8.116: And all on Juno's altar are bestow'd.
8.117: The foll'wing night, and the succeeding day,
8.118: Propitious Tiber smooth'd his wat'ry way:
8.119: He roll'd his river back, and pois'd he stood,
8.120: A gentle swelling, and a peaceful flood.
8.121: The Trojans mount their ships; they put from shore,
8.122: Borne on the waves, and scarcely dip an oar.
8.123: Shouts from the land give omen to their course,
8.124: And the pitch'd vessels glide with easy force.
8.125: The woods and waters wonder at the gleam
8.126: Of shields, and painted ships that stem the stream.
8.127: One summer's night and one whole day they pass
8.128: Betwixt the greenwood shades, and cut the liquid
8.129: The fiery sun had finish'd half his race,
8.130: Look'd back, and doubted in the middle space,
8.131: When they from far beheld the rising tow'rs,
8.132: The tops of sheds, and shepherds' lowly bow'rs,
8.133: Thin as they stood, which, then of homely clay,
8.134: Now rise in marble, from the Roman sway.
8.135: These cots (Evander's kingdom, mean and poor)
8.136: The Trojan saw, and turn'd his ships to shore.
8.137: 'T was on a solemn day: th' Arcadian states,
8.138: The king and prince, without the city gates,
8.139: Then paid their off'rings in a sacred grove
8.140: To Hercules, the warrior son of Jove.
8.141: Thick clouds of rolling smoke involve the skies,
8.142: And fat of entrails on his altar fries.
8.143: But, when they saw the ships that stemm'd the flood,
8.144: And glitter'd thro' the covert of the wood,
8.145: They rose with fear, and left th' unfinish'd feast,
8.146: Till dauntless Pallas reassur'd the rest
8.147: To pay the rites. Himself without delay
8.148: A jav'lin seiz'd, and singly took his way;
8.149: Then gain'd a rising ground, and call'd from far:
8.150: "Resolve me, strangers, whence, and what you are;
8.151: Your bus'ness here; and bring you peace or war?"
8.152: High on the stern Aeneas his stand,
8.153: And held a branch of olive in his hand,
8.154: While thus he spoke: "The Phrygians' arms you see,
8.155: Expell'd from Troy, provok'd in Italy
8.156: By Latian foes, with war unjustly made;
8.157: At first affianc'd, and at last betray'd.
8.158: This message bear: 'The Trojans and their chief
8.159: Bring holy peace, and beg the king's relief.'
8.160: Struck with so great a name, and all on fire,
8.162: Your fame exacts. Upon our shores descend.
8.163: A welcome guest, and, what you wish, a friend."
8.164: He said, and, downward hasting to the strand,
8.165: Embrac'd the stranger prince, and join'd his hand.
8.166: Conducted to the grove, Aeneas broke
8.167: The silence first, and thus the king bespoke:
8.168: "Best of the Greeks, to whom, by fate's command,
8.169: I bear these peaceful branches in my hand,
8.170: Undaunted I approach you, tho' I know
8.171: Your birth is Grecian, and your land my foe;
8.172: From Atreus tho' your ancient lineage came,
8.173: And both the brother kings your kindred claim;
8.174: Yet, my self-conscious worth, your high renown,
8.175: Your virtue, thro' the neighb'ring nations blown,
8.176: Our fathers' mingled blood, Apollo's voice,
8.177: Have led me hither, less by need than choice.
8.178: Our founder Dardanus, as fame has sung,
8.179: And Greeks acknowledge, from Electra sprung:
8.180: Electra from the loins of Atlas came;
8.181: Atlas, whose head sustains the starry frame.
8.182: Your sire is Mercury, whom long before
8.183: On cold Cyllene's top fair Maia bore.
8.184: Maia the fair, on fame if we rely,
8.185: Was Atlas' daughter, who sustains the sky.
8.186: Thus from one common source our streams divide;
8.187: Ours is the Trojan, yours th' Areadian side.
8.188: Rais'd by these hopes, I sent no news before,
8.189: Nor ask'd your leave, nor did your faith implore;
8.190: But come, without a pledge, my own ambassador.
8.191: The same Rutulians, who with arms pursue
8.192: The Trojan race, are equal foes to you.
8.193: Our host expell'd, what farther force can stay
8.194: The victor troops from universal sway?
8.195: Then will they stretch their pow'r athwart the land,
8.196: And either sea from side to side command.
8.197: Receive our offer'd faith, and give us thine;
8.198: Ours is a gen'rous and experienc'd line:
8.199: We want not hearts nor bodies for the war;
8.200: In council cautious, and in fields we dare."
8.201: He said; and while spoke, with piercing eyes
8.202: Evander view'd the man with vast surprise,
8.203: Pleas'd with his action, ravish'd with his face:
8.204: Then answer'd briefly, with a royal grace:
8.205: "O valiant leader of the Trojan line,
8.206: In whom the features of thy father shine,
8.207: How I recall Anchises! how I see
8.208: His motions, mien, and all my friend, in thee!
8.209: Long tho' it be, 't is fresh within my mind,
8.210: When Priam to his sister's court design'd
8.211: A welcome visit, with a friendly stay,
8.212: And thro' th' Arcadian kingdom took his way.
8.213: Then, past a boy, the callow down began
8.214: To shade my chin, and call me first a man.
8.215: I saw the shining train with vast delight,
8.216: And Priam's goodly person pleas'd my sight:
8.217: But great Anchises, far above the rest,
8.218: With awful wonder fir'd my youthful breast.
8.219: I long'd to join in friendship's holy bands
8.220: Our mutual hearts, and plight our mutual hands.
8.221: I first accosted him: I sued, I sought,
8.222: And, with a loving force, to Pheneus brought.
8.223: He gave me, when at length constrain'd to go,
8.224: A Lycian quiver and a Gnossian bow,
8.225: A vest embroider'd, glorious to behold,
8.226: And two rich bridles, with their bits of gold,
8.227: Which my son's coursers in obedience hold.
8.228: The league you ask, I offer, as your right;
8.229: And, when to-morrow's sun reveals the light,
8.230: With swift supplies you shall be sent away.
8.231: Now celebrate with us this solemn day,
8.232: Whose holy rites admit no long delay.
8.233: Honor our annual feast; and take your seat,
8.234: With friendly welcome, at a homely treat."
8.235: Thus having said, the bowls (remov'd for fear)
8.236: The youths replac'd, and soon restor'd the cheer.
8.237: On sods of turf he set the soldiers round:
8.238: A maple throne, rais'd higher from the ground,
8.239: Receiv'd the Trojan chief; and, o'er the bed,
8.240: A lion's shaggy hide for ornament they spread.
8.241: The loaves were serv'd in canisters; the wine
8.242: In bowls; the priest renew'd the rites divine:
8.243: Broil'd entrails are their food, and beef's continued
8.244: But when the rage of hunger was repress'd,
8.245: Thus spoke Evander to his royal guest:
8.246: "These rites, these altars, and this feast, O king,
8.247: From no vain fears or superstition spring,
8.248: Or blind devotion, or from blinder chance,
8.249: Or heady zeal, or brutal ignorance;
8.250: But, sav'd from danger, with a grateful sense,
8.251: The labors of a god we recompense.
8.252: See, from afar, yon rock that mates the sky,
8.253: About whose feet such heaps of rubbish lie;
8.254: Such indigested ruin; bleak and bare,
8.255: How desart now it stands, expos'd in air!
8.256: 'T was once a robber's den, inclos'd around
8.257: With living stone, and deep beneath the ground.
8.258: The monster Cacus, more than half a beast,
8.259: This hold, impervious to the sun, possess'd.
8.260: The pavement ever foul with human gore;
8.261: Heads, and their mangled members, hung the door.
8.262: Vulcan this plague begot; and, like his sire,
8.263: Black clouds he belch'd, and flakes of livid fire.
8.264: Time, long expected, eas'd us of our load,
8.265: And brought the needful presence of a god.
8.266: Th' avenging force of Hercules, from Spain,
8.267: Arriv'd in triumph, from Geryon slain:
8.268: Thrice liv'd the giant, and thrice liv'd in vain.
8.269: His prize, the lowing herds, Alcides drove
8.270: Near Tiber's bank, to graze the shady grove.
8.271: Allur'd with hope of plunder, and intent
8.272: By force to rob, by fraud to circumvent,
8.273: The brutal Cacus, as by chance they stray'd,
8.274: Four oxen thence, and four fair kine convey'd;
8.275: And, lest the printed footsteps might be seen,
8.276: He dragg'd 'em backwards to his rocky den.
8.277: The tracks averse a lying notice gave,
8.278: And led the searcher backward from the cave.
8.279: "Meantime the herdsman hero shifts his place,
8.280: To find fresh pasture and untrodden grass.
8.281: The beasts, who miss'd their mates, fill'd all around
8.282: With bellowings, and the rocks restor'd the sound.
8.283: One heifer, who had heard her love complain,
8.284: Roar'd from the cave, and made the project vain.
8.285: Alcides found the fraud; with rage he shook,
8.286: And toss'd about his head his knotted oak.
8.287: Swift as the winds, or Scythian arrows' flight,
8.288: He clomb, with eager haste, th' aerial height.
8.289: Then first we saw the monster mend his pace;
8.290: Fear his eyes, and paleness in his face,
8.291: Confess'd the god's approach. Trembling he springs,
8.292: As terror had increas'd his feet with wings;
8.293: Nor stay'd for stairs; but down the depth he threw
8.294: His body, on his back the door he drew
8.295: (The door, a rib of living rock; with pains
8.296: His father hew'd it out, and bound with iron chains):
8.297: He broke the heavy links, the mountain clos'd,
8.298: And bars and levers to his foe oppos'd.
8.299: The wretch had hardly made his dungeon fast;
8.300: The fierce avenger came with bounding haste;
8.301: Survey'd the mouth of the forbidden hold,
8.302: And here and there his raging eyes he roll'd.
8.303: He gnash'd his teeth; and thrice he compass'd round
8.304: With winged speed the circuit of the ground.
8.305: Thrice at the cavern's mouth he pull'd in vain,
8.306: And, panting, thrice desisted from his pain.
8.307: A pointed flinty rock, all bare and black,
8.308: Grew gibbous from behind the mountain's back;
8.309: Owls, ravens, all ill omens of the night,
8.310: Here built their nests, and hither wing'd their
8.311: The leaning head hung threat'ning o'er the flood,
8.312: And nodded to the left. The hero stood
8.313: Adverse, with planted feet, and, from the right,
8.314: Tugg'd at the solid stone with all his might.
8.315: Thus heav'd, the fix'd foundations of the rock
8.316: Gave way; heav'n echo'd at the rattling shock.
8.317: Tumbling, it chok'd the flood: on either side
8.318: The banks leap backward, and the streams divide;
8.319: The sky shrunk upward with unusual dread,
8.320: And trembling Tiber div'd beneath his bed.
8.321: The court of Cacus stands reveal'd to sight;
8.322: The cavern glares with new-admitted light.
8.323: So the pent vapors, with a rumbling sound,
8.324: Heave from below, and rend the hollow ground;
8.325: A sounding flaw succeeds; and, from on high,
8.326: The gods with hate beheld the nether sky:
8.327: The ghosts repine at violated night,
8.328: And curse th' invading sun, and sicken at the sight.
8.329: The graceless monster, caught in open day,
8.330: Inclos'd, and in despair to fly away,
8.331: Howls horrible from underneath, and fills
8.332: His hollow palace with unmanly yells.
8.333: The hero stands above, and from afar
8.334: Plies him with darts, and stones, and distant war.
8.335: He, from his nostrils huge mouth, expires
8.336: Black clouds of smoke, amidst his father's fires,
8.337: Gath'ring, with each repeated blast, the night,
8.338: To make uncertain aim, and erring sight.
8.339: The wrathful god then plunges from above,
8.340: And, where in thickest waves the sparkles drove,
8.341: There lights; and wades thro' fumes, and gropes his
8.342: Half sing'd, half stifled, till he grasps his prey.
8.343: The monster, spewing fruitless flames, he found;
8.344: He squeez'd his throat; he writh'd his neck around,
8.345: And in a knot his crippled members bound;
8.346: Then from their sockets tore his burning eyes:
8.347: Roll'd on a heap, the breathless robber lies.
8.348: The doors, unbarr'd, receive the rushing day,
8.349: And thoro' lights disclose the ravish'd prey.
8.350: The bulls, redeem'd, breathe open air again.
8.351: Next, by the feet, they drag him from his den.
8.352: The wond'ring neighborhood, with glad surprise,
8.353: Behold his shagged breast, his giant size,
8.354: His mouth that flames no more, and his extinguish'd
8.355: From that auspicious day, with rites divine,
8.356: We worship at the hero's holy shrine.
8.357: Potitius first ordain'd these annual vows:
8.358: As priests, were added the Pinarian house,
8.359: Who rais'd this altar in the sacred shade,
8.360: Where honors, ever due, for ever shall be paid.
8.361: For these deserts, and this high virtue shown,
8.362: Ye warlike youths, your heads with garlands crown:
8.363: Fill high the goblets with a sparkling flood,
8.364: And with deep draughts invoke our common god."
8.365: This said, a double wreath Evander twin'd,
8.366: And poplars black and white his temples bind.
8.367: Then brims his ample bowl. With like design
8.368: The rest invoke the gods, with sprinkled wine.
8.369: Meantime the sun descended from the skies,
8.370: And the bright evening star began to rise.
8.371: And now the priests, Potitius at their head,
8.372: In skins of beasts involv'd, the long procession
8.373: Held high the flaming tapers in their hands,
8.374: As custom had prescrib'd their holy bands;
8.375: Then with a second course the tables load,
8.376: And with full chargers offer to the god.
8.377: The Salii sing, and cense his altars round
8.378: With Saban smoke, their heads with poplar bound-
8.379: One choir of old, another of the young,
8.380: To dance, and bear the burthen of the song.
8.381: The lay records the labors, and the praise,
8.382: And all th' immortal acts of Hercules:
8.383: First, how the mighty babe, when swath'd in bands,
8.384: The serpents strangled with his infant hands;
8.385: Then, as in years and matchless force he grew,
8.386: Th' Oechalian walls, and Trojan, overthrew.
8.387: Besides, a thousand hazards they relate,
8.388: Procur'd by Juno's and Eurystheus' hate:
8.390: The cloud-born Centaurs, and the monster crew:
8.391: Nor thy resistless arm the bull withstood,
8.392: Nor he, the roaring terror of the wood.
8.393: The triple porter of the Stygian seat,
8.394: With lolling tongue, lay fawning at thy feet,
8.395: And, seiz'd with fear, forgot his mangled meat.
8.396: Th' infernal waters trembled at thy sight;
8.397: Thee, god, no face of danger could affright;
8.398: Not huge Typhoeus, nor th' unnumber'd snake,
8.399: Increas'd with hissing heads, in Lerna's lake.
8.400: Hail, Jove's undoubted son! an added grace
8.401: To heav'n and the great author of thy race!
8.402: Receive the grateful off'rings which we pay,
8.403: And smile propitious on thy solemn day!"
8.404: In numbers thus they sung; above the rest,
8.405: The den and death of Cacus crown the feast.
8.406: The woods to hollow vales convey the sound,
8.407: The vales to hills, and hills the notes rebound.
8.408: The rites perform'd, the cheerful train retire.
8.409: Betwixt young Pallas and his aged sire,
8.410: The Trojan pass'd, the city to survey,
8.411: And pleasing talk beguil'd the tedious way.
8.412: The stranger cast around his curious eyes,
8.413: New objects viewing still, with new surprise;
8.414: With greedy joy enquires of various things,
8.415: And acts and monuments of ancient kings.
8.416: Then thus the founder of the Roman tow'rs:
8.417: "These woods were first the seat of sylvan pow'rs,
8.418: Of Nymphs and Fauns, and salvage men, who took
8.419: Their birth from trunks of trees and stubborn oak.
8.420: Nor laws they knew, nor manners, nor the care
8.421: Of lab'ring oxen, or the shining share,
8.422: Nor arts of gain, nor what they gain'd to spare.
8.423: Their exercise the chase; the running flood
8.424: Supplied their thirst, the trees supplied their

8.907: Rang'd on the line oppos'd, Antonius brings
8.908: Barbarian aids, and troops of Eastern kings;
8.909: Th' Arabians near, and Bactrians from afar,
8.910: Of tongues discordant, and a mingled war:
8.911: And, rich in gaudy robes, amidst the strife,
8.912: His ill fate follows him- th' Egyptian wife.
8.913: Moving they fight; with oars and forky prows
8.914: The froth is gather'd, and the water glows.
8.915: It seems, as if the Cyclades again
8.916: Were rooted up, and justled in the main;
8.917: Or floating mountains floating mountains meet;
8.918: Such is the fierce encounter of the fleet.
8.919: Fireballs are thrown, and pointed jav'lins fly;
8.920: The fields of Neptune take a purple dye.
8.921: The queen herself, amidst the loud alarms,
8.922: With cymbals toss'd her fainting soldiers warms-
8.923: Fool as she was! who had not yet divin'd
8.924: Her cruel fate, nor saw the snakes behind.
8.925: Her country gods, the monsters of the sky,
8.926: Great Neptune, Pallas, and Love's Queen defy:
8.927: The dog Anubis barks, but barks in vain,
8.928: Nor longer dares oppose th' ethereal train.
8.929: Mars in the middle of the shining shield
8.930: Is grav'd, and strides along the liquid field.
8.931: The Dirae souse from heav'n with swift descent;
8.932: And Discord, dyed in blood, with garments rent,
8.933: Divides the prease: her steps Bellona treads,
8.934: And shakes her iron rod above their heads.
8.935: This seen, Apollo, from his Actian height,
8.936: Pours down his arrows; at whose winged flight
8.937: The trembling Indians and Egyptians yield,
8.938: And soft Sabaeans quit the wat'ry field.
8.939: The fatal mistress hoists her silken sails,
8.940: And, shrinking from the fight, invokes the gales.
8.941: Aghast she looks, and heaves her breast for breath,
8.942: Panting, and pale with fear of future death.
8.943: The god had figur'd her as driv'n along
8.944: By winds and waves, and scudding thro' the throng.
8.945: Just opposite, sad Nilus opens wide
8.946: His arms and ample bosom to the tide,
8.947: And spreads his mantle o'er the winding coast,
8.948: In which he wraps his queen, and hides the flying
8.949: The victor to the gods his thanks express'd,
8.950: And Rome, triumphant, with his presence bless'd.
8.951: Three hundred temples in the town he plac'd;
8.952: With spoils and altars ev'ry temple grac'd.
8.953: Three shining nights, and three succeeding days,
8.954: The fields resound with shouts, the streets with
8.955: The domes with songs, the theaters with plays.
8.956: All altars flame: before each altar lies,
8.957: Drench'd in his gore, the destin'd sacrifice.
8.958: Great Caesar sits sublime upon his throne,
8.959: Before Apollo's porch of Parian stone;
8.960: Accepts the presents vow'd for victory,
8.961: And hangs the monumental crowns on high.
8.962: Vast crowds of vanquish'd nations march along,
8.963: Various in arms, in habit, and in tongue.
8.964: Here, Mulciber assigns the proper place
8.965: For Carians, and th' ungirt Numidian race;
8.966: Then ranks the Thracians in the second row,
8.967: With Scythians, expert in the dart and bow.
8.968: And here the tam'd Euphrates humbly glides,
8.969: And there the Rhine submits her swelling tides,
8.970: And proud Araxes, whom no bridge could bind;
8.971: The Danes' unconquer'd offspring march behind,
8.972: And Morini, the last of humankind.
8.973: These figures, on the shield divinely wrought,
8.974: By Vulcan labor'd, and by Venus brought,
8.975: With joy and wonder fill the hero's thought.
8.976: Unknown the names, he yet admires the grace,
8.977: And bears aloft the fame and fortune of his race.

9.1: While these affairs in distant places pass'd,
9.2: The various Iris Juno sends with haste,
9.3: To find bold Turnus, who, with anxious thought,
9.4: The secret shade of his great grandsire sought.
9.5: Retir'd alone she found the daring man,
9.6: And op'd her rosy lips, and thus began:
9.7: "What none of all the gods could grant thy vows,
9.8: That, Turnus, this auspicious day bestows.
9.9: Aeneas, gone to seek th' Arcadian prince,
9.10: Has left the Trojan camp without defense;
9.11: And, short of succors there, employs his pains
9.12: In parts remote to raise the Tuscan swains.
9.13: Now snatch an hour that favors thy designs;
9.14: Unite thy forces, and attack their lines."
9.15: This said, on equal wings she pois'd her weight,
9.16: And form'd a radiant rainbow in her flight.
9.17: The Daunian hero lifts his hands eyes,
9.18: And thus invokes the goddess as she flies:
9.19: "Iris, the grace of heav'n, what pow'r divine
9.20: Has sent thee down, thro' dusky clouds to shine?
9.21: See, they divide; immortal day appears,
9.22: And glitt'ring planets dancing in their spheres!
9.23: With joy, these happy omens I obey,
9.24: And follow to the war the god that leads the way."
9.25: Thus having said, as by the brook he stood,
9.26: He scoop'd the water from the crystal flood;
9.27: Then with his hands the drops to heav'n he throws,
9.28: And loads the pow'rs above with offer'd vows.
9.29: Now march the bold confed'rates thro' the plain,
9.30: Well hors'd, well clad; a rich and shining train.
9.31: Messapus leads the van; and, in the rear,
9.32: The sons of Tyrrheus in bright arms appear.
9.33: In the main battle, with his flaming crest,
9.34: The mighty Turnus tow'rs above the rest.
9.36: Like ebbing Nile, or Ganges in his flow.
9.37: The Trojans view the dusty cloud from far,
9.38: And the dark menace of the distant war.
9.39: Caicus from the rampire saw it rise,
9.40: Black'ning the fields, and thick'ning thro' the
9.41: Then to his fellows thus aloud he calls:
9.42: "What rolling clouds, my friends, approach the walls?
9.43: Arm! arm! and man the works! prepare your spears
9.44: And pointed darts! the Latian host appears."
9.45: Thus warn'd, they shut their gates; with shouts
9.46: The bulwarks, and, secure, their foes attend:
9.47: For their wise gen'ral, with foreseeing care,
9.48: Had charg'd them not to tempt the doubtful war,
9.49: Nor, tho' provok'd, in open fields advance,
9.50: But close within their lines attend their chance.
9.51: Unwilling, yet they keep the strict command,
9.52: And sourly wait in arms the hostile band.
9.53: The fiery Turnus flew before the rest:
9.54: A piebald steed of Thracian strain he press'd;
9.55: His helm of massy gold, and crimson was his crest.
9.56: With twenty horse to second his designs,
9.57: An unexpected foe, he fac'd the lines.
9.58: "Is there," he said, "in arms, who bravely dare
9.59: His leader's honor and his danger share?"
9.60: Then spurring on, his brandish'd dart he threw,
9.61: In sign of war: applauding shouts ensue.
9.62: Amaz'd to find a dastard race, that run
9.63: Behind the rampires and the battle shun,
9.64: He rides around the camp, with rolling eyes,
9.65: And stops at ev'ry post, and ev'ry passage tries.
9.66: So roams the nightly wolf about the fold:
9.67: Wet with descending show'rs, and stiff with cold,
9.68: He howls for hunger, and he grins for pain,
9.69: (His gnashing teeth are exercis'd in vain,)
9.70: And, impotent of anger, finds no way
9.71: In his distended paws to grasp the prey.
9.72: The mothers listen; but the bleating lambs
9.73: Securely swig the dug, beneath the dams.
9.74: Thus ranges eager Turnus o'er the plain.
9.75: Sharp with desire, and furious with disdain;
9.76: Surveys each passage with a piercing sight,
9.77: To force his foes in equal field to fight.
9.78: Thus while he gazes round, at length he spies,
9.79: Where, fenc'd with strong redoubts, their navy lies,
9.80: Close underneath the walls; the washing tide
9.81: Secures from all approach this weaker side.
9.82: He takes the wish'd occasion, fills his hand
9.83: With ready fires, and shakes a flaming brand.
9.84: Urg'd by his presence, ev'ry soul is warm'd,
9.85: And ev'ry hand with kindled firs is arm'd.
9.86: From the fir'd pines the scatt'ring sparkles fly;
9.87: Fat vapors, mix'd with flames, involve the sky.
9.88: What pow'r, O Muses, could avert the flame
9.89: Which threaten'd, in the fleet, the Trojan name?
9.90: Tell: for the fact, thro' length of time obscure,
9.91: Is hard to faith; yet shall the fame endure.
9.92: 'T is said that, when the chief prepar'd his flight,
9.93: And fell'd his timber from Mount Ida's height,
9.94: The grandam goddess then approach'd her son,
9.95: And with a mother's majesty begun:
9.96: "Grant me," she said, "the sole request I bring,
9.97: Since conquer'd heav'n has own'd you for its king.
9.98: On Ida's brows, for ages past, there stood,
9.99: With firs and maples fill'd, a shady wood;
9.100: And on the summit rose a sacred grove,
9.101: Where I was worship'd with religious love.
9.102: Those woods, that holy grove, my long delight,
9.103: I gave the Trojan prince, to speed his flight.
9.104: Now, fill'd with fear, on their behalf I come;
9.105: Let neither winds o'erset, nor waves intomb
9.106: The floating forests of the sacred pine;
9.107: But let it be their safety to be mine."
9.108: Then thus replied her awful son, who rolls
9.109: The radiant stars, and heav'n and earth controls:
9.110: "How dare you, mother, endless date demand
9.111: For vessels molded by a mortal hand?
9.112: What then is fate? Shall bold Aeneas ride,
9.113: Of safety certain, on th' uncertain tide?
9.114: Yet, what I can, I grant; when, wafted o'er,
9.115: The chief is landed on the Latian shore,
9.116: Whatever ships escape the raging storms,
9.117: At my command shall change their fading forms
9.118: To nymphs divine, and plow the wat'ry way,
9.119: Like Dotis and the daughters of the sea."
9.120: To seal his sacred vow, by Styx he swore,
9.121: The lake of liquid pitch, the dreary shore,
9.123: And the black regions of his brother god.
9.124: He said; and shook the skies with his imperial nod.
9.125: And now at length the number'd hours were come,
9.127: When the great Mother of the Gods was free
9.128: To save her ships, and finish Jove's decree.
9.129: First, from the quarter of the morn, there sprung
9.130: A light that sign'd the heav'ns, and shot along;
9.131: Then from a cloud, fring'd round with golden fires,
9.132: Were timbrels heard, and Berecynthian choirs;
9.133: And, last, a voice, with more than mortal sounds,
9.134: Both hosts, in arms oppos'd, with equal horror wounds:
9.135: "O Trojan race, your needless aid forbear,
9.136: And know, my ships are my peculiar care.
9.137: With greater ease the bold Rutulian may,
9.138: With hissing brands, attempt to burn the sea,
9.139: Than singe my sacred pines. But you, my charge,
9.140: Loos'd from your crooked anchors, launch at large,
9.141: Exalted each a nymph: forsake the sand,
9.142: And swim the seas, at Cybele's command."
9.143: No sooner had the goddess ceas'd to speak,
9.144: When, lo! th' obedient ships their haulsers break;
9.145: And, strange to tell, like dolphins, in the main
9.146: They plunge their prows, and dive, and spring again:
9.147: As many beauteous maids the billows sweep,
9.148: As rode before tall vessels on the deep.
9.149: The foes, surpris'd with wonder, stood aghast;
9.150: Messapus curb'd his fiery courser's haste;
9.151: Old Tiber roar'd, and, raising up his head,
9.152: Call'd back his waters to their oozy bed.
9.153: Turnus alone, undaunted, bore the shock,
9.154: And with these words his trembling troops bespoke:
9.155: "These monsters for the Trojans' fate are meant,
9.156: And are by Jove for black presages sent.
9.157: He takes the cowards' last relief away;
9.158: For fly they cannot, and, constrain'd to stay,
9.159: Must yield unfought, a base inglorious prey.
9.160: The liquid half of all the globe is lost;
9.161: Heav'n shuts the seas, and we secure the coast.
9.162: Theirs is no more than that small spot of ground
9.163: Which myriads of our martial men surround.
9.164: Their fates I fear not, or vain oracles.
9.165: 'T was giv'n to Venus they should cross the seas,
9.166: And land secure upon the Latian plains:
9.167: Their promis'd hour is pass'd, and mine remains.
9.168: 'T is in the fate of Turnus to destroy,
9.169: With sword and fire, the faithless race of Troy.
9.170: Shall such affronts as these alone inflame
9.171: The Grecian brothers, and the Grecian name?
9.172: My cause and theirs is one; a fatal strife,
9.173: And final ruin, for a ravish'd wife.
9.174: Was 't not enough, that, punish'd for the crime,
9.175: They fell; but will they fall a second time?
9.176: One would have thought they paid enough before,
9.177: To curse the costly sex, and durst offend no more.
9.178: Can they securely trust their feeble wall,
9.179: A slight partition, a thin interval,
9.180: Betwixt their fate and them; when Troy, tho' built
9.181: By hands divine, yet perish'd by their guilt?
9.182: Lend me, for once, my friends, your valiant hands,
9.183: To force from out their lines these dastard bands.
9.184: Less than a thousand ships will end this war,
9.185: Nor Vulcan needs his fated arms prepare.
9.186: Let all the Tuscans, all th' Arcadians, join!
9.187: Nor these, nor those, shall frustrate my design.
9.188: Let them not fear the treasons of the night,
9.189: The robb'd Palladium, the pretended flight:
9.190: Our onset shall be made in open light.
9.191: No wooden engine shall their town betray;
9.192: Fires they shall have around, but fires by day.
9.193: No Grecian babes before their camp appear,
9.194: Whom Hector's arms detain'd to the tenth tardy year.
9.195: Now, since the sun is rolling to the west,
9.196: Give we the silent night to needful rest:
9.197: Refresh your bodies, and your arms prepare;
9.198: The morn shall end the small remains of war."
9.199: The post of honor to Messapus falls,
9.200: To keep the nightly guard, to watch the walls,
9.201: To pitch the fires at distances around,
9.202: And close the Trojans in their scanty ground.
9.203: Twice seven Rutulian captains ready stand,
9.204: And twice seven hundred horse these chiefs command;
9.205: All clad in shining arms the works invest,
9.206: Each with a radiant helm and waving crest.
9.207: Stretch'd at their length, they press the grassy
9.208: They laugh, they sing, (the jolly bowls go round,)
9.209: With lights and cheerful fires renew the day,
9.210: And pass the wakeful night in feasts and play.
9.211: The Trojans, from above, their foes beheld,
9.212: And with arm'd legions all the rampires fill'd.
9.213: Seiz'd with affright, their gates they first explore;
9.214: Join works to works with bridges, tow'r to tow'r:
9.215: Thus all things needful for defense abound.
9.216: Mnestheus and brave Seresthus walk the round,
9.217: Commission'd by their absent prince to share
9.218: The common danger, and divide the care.
9.219: The soldiers draw their lots, and, as they fall,
9.220: By turns relieve each other on the wall.
9.221: Nigh where the foes their utmost guards advance,
9.222: To watch the gate was warlike Nisus' chance.
9.223: His father Hyrtacus of noble blood;
9.224: His mother was a huntress of the wood,
9.225: And sent him to the wars. Well could he bear
9.226: His lance in fight, and dart the flying spear,
9.227: But better skill'd unerring shafts to send.
9.228: Beside him stood Euryalus, his friend:
9.229: Euryalus, than whom the Trojan host
9.230: No fairer face, or sweeter air, could boast-
9.231: Scarce had the down to shade his cheeks begun.
9.232: One was their care, and their delight was one:
9.233: One common hazard in the war they shar'd,
9.234: And now were both by choice upon the guard.
9.235: Then Nisus thus: "Or do the gods inspire
9.236: This warmth, or make we gods of our desire?
9.237: A gen'rous ardor boils within my breast,
9.238: Eager of action, enemy to rest:
9.239: This urges me to fight, and fires my mind
9.240: To leave a memorable name behind.
9.241: Thou see'st the foe secure; how faintly shine
9.242: Their scatter'd fires! the most, in sleep supine
9.243: Along the ground, an easy conquest lie:
9.244: The wakeful few the fuming flagon ply;
9.245: All hush'd around. Now hear what I revolve-
9.246: A thought unripe- and scarcely yet resolve.
9.247: Our absent prince both camp and council mourn;
9.248: By message both would hasten his return:
9.249: If they confer what I demand on thee,
9.250: (For fame is recompense enough for me,)
9.251: Methinks, beneath yon hill, I have espied
9.252: A way that safely will my passage guide."
9.253: Euryalus stood list'ning while he spoke,
9.254: With love of praise and noble envy struck;
9.255: Then to his ardent friend expos'd his mind:
9.256: "All this, alone, and leaving me behind!
9.257: Am I unworthy, Nisus, to be join'd?
9.258: Thinkist thou I can my share of glory yield,
9.259: Or send thee unassisted to the field?
9.260: Not so my father taught my childhood arms;
9.261: Born in a siege, and bred among alarms!
9.262: Nor is my youth unworthy of my friend,
9.263: Nor of the heav'n-born hero I attend.
9.264: The thing call'd life, with ease I can disclaim,
9.265: And think it over-sold to purchase fame."
9.266: Then Nisus thus: "Alas! thy tender years
9.267: Would minister new matter to my fears.
9.268: So may the gods, who view this friendly strife,
9.269: Restore me to thy lov'd embrace with life,
9.270: Condemn'd to pay my vows, (as sure I trust,)
9.271: This thy request is cruel and unjust.
9.272: But if some chance- as many chances are,
9.273: And doubtful hazards, in the deeds of war-
9.274: If one should reach my head, there let it fall,
9.275: And spare thy life; I would not perish all.
9.276: Thy bloomy youth deserves a longer date:
9.277: Live thou to mourn thy love's unhappy fate;
9.278: To bear my mangled body from the foe,
9.279: Or buy it back, and fun'ral rites bestow.
9.280: Or, if hard fortune shall those dues deny,
9.281: Thou canst at least an empty tomb supply.
9.282: O let not me the widow's tears renew!
9.283: Nor let a mother's curse my name pursue:
9.284: Thy pious parent, who, for love of thee,
9.285: Forsook the coasts of friendly Sicily,
9.286: Her age committing to the seas and wind,
9.287: When ev'ry weary matron stay'd behind."
9.288: To this, Euryalus: "You plead in vain,
9.289: And but protract the cause you cannot gain.
9.290: No more delays, but haste!" With that, he wakes
9.291: The nodding watch; each to his office takes.
9.292: The guard reliev'd, the gen'rous couple went
9.293: To find the council at the royal tent.
9.294: All creatures else forgot their daily care,
9.295: And sleep, the common gift of nature, share;
9.296: Except the Trojan peers, who wakeful sate
9.297: In nightly council for th' indanger'd state.
9.298: They vote a message to their absent chief,
9.299: Shew their distress, and beg a swift relief.
9.300: Amid the camp a silent seat they chose,
9.301: Remote from clamor, and secure from foes.
9.302: On their left arms their ample shields they bear,
9.303: The right reclin'd upon the bending spear.
9.304: Now Nisus and his friend approach the guard,
9.305: And beg admission, eager to be heard:
9.306: Th' affair important, not to be deferr'd.
9.308: Ord'ring the more experienc'd to begin.
9.309: Then Nisus thus: "Ye fathers, lend your ears;
9.310: Nor judge our bold attempt beyond our years.
9.311: The foe, securely drench'd in sleep and wine,
9.312: Neglect their watch; the fires but thinly shine;
9.313: And where the smoke in cloudy vapors flies,
9.314: Cov'ring the plain, and curling to the skies,
9.315: Betwixt two paths, which at the gate divide,
9.316: Close by the sea, a passage we have spied,
9.317: Which will our way to great Aeneas guide.
9.318: Expect each hour to see him safe again,
9.319: Loaded with spoils of foes in battle slain.
9.320: Snatch we the lucky minute while we may;
9.321: Nor can we be mistaken in the way;
9.322: For, hunting in the vale, we both have seen
9.323: The rising turrets, and the stream between,
9.324: And know the winding course, with ev'ry ford."
9.325: He ceas'd; and old Alethes took the word:
9.326: "Our country gods, in whom our trust we place,
9.327: Will yet from ruin save the Trojan race,
9.328: While we behold such dauntless worth appear
9.329: In dawning youth, and souls so void of fear."
9.330: Then into tears of joy the father broke;
9.331: Each in his longing arms by turns he took;
9.332: Panted and paus'd; and thus again he spoke:
9.333: "Ye brave young men, what equal gifts can we,
9.334: In recompense of such desert, decree?
9.335: The greatest, sure, and best you can receive,
9.336: The gods and your own conscious worth will give.
9.337: The rest our grateful gen'ral will bestow,
9.338: And young Ascanius till his manhood owe."
9.339: "And I, whose welfare in my father lies,"
9.341: By my dear country, by my household gods,
9.342: By hoary Vesta's rites and dark abodes,
9.343: Adjure you both, (on you my fortune stands;
9.344: That and my faith I plight into your hands,)
9.345: Make me but happy in his safe return,
9.346: Whose wanted presence I can only mourn;
9.347: Your common gift shall two large goblets be
9.348: Of silver, wrought with curious imagery,
9.349: And high emboss'd, which, when old Priam reign'd,
9.350: My conqu'ring sire at sack'd Arisba gain'd;
9.351: And more, two tripods cast in antic mold,
9.352: With two great talents of the finest gold;
9.353: Beside a costly bowl, ingrav'd with art,
9.354: Which Dido gave, when first she gave her heart.
9.355: But, if in conquer'd Italy we reign,
9.356: When spoils by lot the victor shall obtain-
9.357: Thou saw'st the courser by proud Turnus press'd:
9.358: That, Nisus, and his arms, and nodding crest,
9.359: And shield, from chance exempt, shall be thy share:
9.360: Twelve lab'ring slaves, twelve handmaids young and
9.361: All clad in rich attire, and train'd with care;
9.362: And, last, a Latian field with fruitful plains,
9.363: And a large portion of the king's domains.
9.364: But thou, whose years are more to mine allied-
9.365: No fate my vow'd affection shall divide
9.366: From thee, heroic youth! Be wholly mine;
9.367: Take full possession; all my soul is thine.
9.368: One faith, one fame, one fate, shall both attend;
9.369: My life's companion, and my bosom friend:
9.370: My peace shall be committed to thy care,
9.371: And to thy conduct my concerns in war."
9.372: Then thus the young Euryalus replied:
9.374: The same shall be my age, as now my youth;
9.375: No time shall find me wanting to my truth.
9.376: This only from your goodness let me gain
9.377: (And, this ungranted, all rewards are vain)
9.378: Of Priam's royal race my mother came-
9.379: And sure the best that ever bore the name-
9.380: Whom neither Troy nor Sicily could hold
9.381: From me departing, but, o'erspent and old,
9.382: My fate she follow'd. Ignorant of this
9.384: Nor pious blessing taken, her I leave,
9.385: And in this only act of all my life deceive.
9.386: By this right hand and conscious Night I swear,
9.387: My soul so sad a farewell could not bear.
9.388: Be you her comfort; fill my vacant place
9.389: (Permit me to presume so great a grace)
9.390: Support her age, forsaken and distress'd.
9.391: That hope alone will fortify my breast
9.392: Against the worst of fortunes, and of fears."
9.393: He said. The mov'd assistants melt in tears.
9.394: Then thus Ascanius, wonderstruck to see
9.395: That image of his filial piety:
9.396: "So great beginnings, in so green an age,
9.397: Exact the faith which I again ingage.
9.398: Thy mother all the dues shall justly claim,
9.399: Creusa had, and only want the name.
9.400: Whate'er event thy bold attempt shall have,
9.401: 'T is merit to have borne a son so brave.
9.402: Now by my head, a sacred oath, I swear,
9.403: (My father us'd it,) what, returning here
9.404: Crown'd with success, I for thyself prepare,
9.405: That, if thou fail, shall thy lov'd mother share."
9.406: He said, and weeping, while he spoke the word,

10.239: Oft of the stars, and of their wat'ry way;
10.240: And what he suffer'd both by land and sea.
10.241: Now, sacred sisters, open all your spring!
10.242: The Tuscan leaders, and their army sing,
10.243: Which follow'd great Aeneas to the war:
10.244: Their arms, their numbers, and their names declare.
10.245: A thousand youths brave Massicus obey,
10.246: Borne in the Tiger thro' the foaming sea;
10.247: From Asium brought, and Cosa, by his care:
10.248: For arms, light quivers, bows and shafts, they bear.
10.249: Fierce Abas next: his men bright armor wore;
10.250: His stern Apollo's golden statue bore.
10.252: All skill'd in martial exercise, and strong.
10.253: Three hundred more for battle Ilva joins,
10.254: An isle renown'd for steel, and unexhausted mines.
10.255: Asylas on his prow the third appears,
10.256: Who heav'n interprets, and the wand'ring stars;
10.258: And peals of thunder, with presaging sounds.
10.259: A thousand spears in warlike order stand,
10.260: Sent by the Pisans under his command.
10.261: Fair Astur follows in the wat'ry field,
10.262: Proud of his manag'd horse and painted shield.
10.263: Gravisca, noisome from the neighb'ring fen,
10.264: And his own Caere, sent three hundred men;
10.265: With those which Minio's fields and Pyrgi gave,
10.266: All bred in arms, unanimous, and brave.
10.267: Thou, Muse, the name of Cinyras renew,
10.268: And brave Cupavo follow'd but by few;
10.269: Whose helm confess'd the lineage of the man,
10.270: And bore, with wings display'd, a silver swan.
10.271: Love was the fault of his fam'd ancestry,
10.272: Whose forms and fortunes in his ensigns fly.
10.274: And sung his loss in poplar groves, alone,
10.275: Beneath the sister shades, to soothe his grief.
10.276: Heav'n heard his song, and hasten'd his relief,
10.277: And chang'd to snowy plumes his hoary hair,
10.278: And wing'd his flight, to chant aloft in air.
10.279: His son Cupavo brush'd the briny flood:
10.280: Upon his stern a brawny Centaur stood,
10.281: Who heav'd a rock, and, threat'ning still to throw,
10.282: With lifted hands alarm'd the seas below:
10.283: They seem'd to fear the formidable sight,
10.284: And roll'd their billows on, to speed his flight.
10.285: Ocnus was next, who led his native train
10.286: Of hardy warriors thro' the wat'ry plain:
10.287: The son of Manto by the Tuscan stream,
10.288: From whence the Mantuan town derives the name-
10.289: An ancient city, but of mix'd descent:
10.290: Three sev'ral tribes compose the government;
10.291: Four towns are under each; but all obey
10.292: The Mantuan laws, and own the Tuscan sway.
10.293: Hate to Mezentius arm'd five hundred more,
10.294: Whom Mincius from his sire Benacus bore:
10.295: Mincius, with wreaths of reeds his forehead cover'd
10.296: These grave Auletes leads: a hundred sweep
10.297: With stretching oars at once the glassy deep.
10.298: Him and his martial train the Triton bears;
10.299: High on his poop the sea-green god appears:
10.300: Frowning he seems his crooked shell to sound,
10.301: And at the blast the billows dance around.
10.302: A hairy man above the waist he shows;
10.303: A porpoise tail beneath his belly grows;
10.304: And ends a fish: his breast the waves divides,
10.305: And froth and foam augment the murm'ring tides.
10.306: Full thirty ships transport the chosen train
10.307: For Troy's relief, and scour the briny main.
10.308: Now was the world forsaken by the sun,
10.309: And Phoebe half her nightly race had run.
10.310: The careful chief, who never clos'd his eyes,
10.311: Himself the rudder holds, the sails supplies.
10.312: A choir of Nereids meet him on the flood,
10.313: Once his own galleys, hewn from Ida's wood;
10.314: But now, as many nymphs, the sea they sweep,
10.315: As rode, before, tall vessels on the deep.
10.316: They know him from afar; and in a ring
10.317: Inclose the ship that bore the Trojan king.
10.318: Cymodoce, whose voice excell'd the rest,
10.319: Above the waves advanc'd her snowy breast;
10.320: Her right hand stops the stern; her left divides
10.321: The curling ocean, and corrects the tides.
10.322: She spoke for all the choir, and thus began
10.323: With pleasing words to warn th' unknowing man:
10.324: "Sleeps our lov'd lord? O goddess-born, awake!
10.325: Spread ev'ry sail, pursue your wat'ry track,
10.326: And haste your course. Your navy once were we,
10.327: From Ida's height descending to the sea;
10.328: Till Turnus, as at anchor fix'd we stood,
10.329: Presum'd to violate our holy wood.
10.330: Then, loos'd from shore, we fled his fires profane
10.332: And since have sought you thro' the Tuscan main.
10.333: The mighty Mother chang'd our forms to these,
10.334: And gave us life immortal in the seas.
10.335: But young Ascanius, in his camp distress'd,
10.336: By your insulting foes is hardly press'd.
10.337: Th' Arcadian horsemen, and Etrurian host,
10.338: Advance in order on the Latian coast:
10.339: To cut their way the Daunian chief designs,
10.340: Before their troops can reach the Trojan lines.
10.341: Thou, when the rosy morn restores the light,
10.342: First arm thy soldiers for th' ensuing fight:
10.343: Thyself the fated sword of Vulcan wield,
10.344: And bear aloft th' impenetrable shield.
10.345: To-morrow's sun, unless my skill be vain,
10.346: Shall see huge heaps of foes in battle slain."
10.347: Parting, she spoke; and with immortal force
10.348: Push'd on the vessel in her wat'ry course;
10.349: For well she knew the way. Impell'd behind,
10.350: The ship flew forward, and outstripp'd the wind.
10.351: The rest make up. Unknowing of the cause,
10.352: The chief admires their speed, and happy omens draws.
10.353: Then thus he pray'd, and fix'd on heav'n his eyes:
10.354: "Hear thou, great Mother of the deities.
10.355: With turrets crown'd! (on Ida's holy hill
10.356: Fierce tigers, rein'd and curb'd, obey thy will.)
10.357: Firm thy own omens; lead us on to fight;
10.358: And let thy Phrygians conquer in thy right."
10.359: He said no more. And now renewing day
10.360: Had chas'd the shadows of the night away.
10.361: He charg'd the soldiers, with preventing care,
10.362: Their flags to follow, and their arms prepare;
10.363: Warn'd of th' ensuing fight, and bade 'em hope the
10.364: Now, his lofty poop, he view'd below
10.365: His camp incompass'd, and th' inclosing foe.
10.366: His blazing shield, imbrac'd, he held on high;
10.367: The camp receive the sign, and with loud shouts
10.368: Hope arms their courage: from their tow'rs they
10.369: Their darts with double force, and drive the foe.
10.370: Thus, at the signal giv'n, the cranes arise
10.371: Before the stormy south, and blacken all the skies.
10.372: King Turnus wonder'd at the fight renew'd,
10.373: Till, looking back, the Trojan fleet he view'd,
10.374: The seas with swelling canvas cover'd o'er,
10.375: And the swift ships descending on the shore.
10.376: The Latians saw from far, with dazzled eyes,
10.377: The radiant crest that seem'd in flames to rise,
10.378: And dart diffusive fires around the field,
10.379: And the keen glitt'ring the golden shield.
10.380: Thus threat'ning comets, when by night they rise,
10.381: Shoot sanguine streams, and sadden all the skies:
10.382: So Sirius, flashing forth sinister lights,
10.383: Pale humankind with plagues and with dry famine
10.384: Yet Turnus with undaunted mind is bent
10.385: To man the shores, and hinder their descent,
10.386: And thus awakes the courage of his friends:
10.387: "What you so long have wish'd, kind Fortune sends;
10.388: In ardent arms to meet th' invading foe:
10.389: You find, and find him at advantage now.
10.390: Yours is the day: you need but only dare;
10.391: Your swords will make you masters of the war.
10.392: Your sires, your sons, your houses, and your lands,
10.393: And dearest wifes, are all within your hands.
10.394: Be mindful of the race from whence you came,
10.395: And emulate in arms your fathers' fame.
10.396: Now take the time, while stagg'ring yet they stand
10.397: With feet unfirm, and prepossess the strand:
10.398: Fortune befriends the bold." Nor more he said,
10.399: But balanc'd whom to leave, and whom to lead;
10.400: Then these elects, the landing to prevent;
10.401: And those he leaves, to keep the city pent.
10.402: Meantime the Trojan sends his troops ashore:
10.403: Some are by boats expos'd, by bridges more.
10.404: With lab'ring oars they bear along the strand,
10.405: Where the tide languishes, and leap aland.
10.406: Tarchon observes the coast with careful eyes,
10.407: And, where no ford he finds, no water fries,
10.408: Nor billows with unequal murmurs roar,
10.409: But smoothly slide along, and swell the shore,
10.410: That course he steer'd, and thus he gave command:
10.411: "Here ply your oars, and at all hazard land:
10.412: Force on the vessel, that her keel may wound
10.413: This hated soil, and furrow hostile ground.
10.414: Let me securely land- I ask no more;
10.415: Then sink my ships, or shatter on the shore."
10.416: This fiery speech inflames his fearful friends:
10.417: They tug at ev'ry oar, and ev'ry stretcher bends;
10.418: They run their ships aground; the vessels knock,
10.419: (Thus forc'd ashore,) and tremble with the shock.
10.420: Tarchon's alone was lost, that stranded stood,
10.421: Stuck on a bank, and beaten by the flood:
10.422: She breaks her back; the loosen'd sides give way,
10.423: And plunge the Tuscan soldiers in the sea.
10.424: Their broken oars and floating planks withstand
10.425: Their passage, while they labor to the land,
10.426: And ebbing tides bear back upon th' uncertain sand.
10.427: Now Turnus leads his troops without delay,
10.428: Advancing to the margin of the sea.
10.429: The trumpets sound: Aeneas first assail'd
10.430: The clowns new-rais'd and raw, and soon prevail'd.
10.431: Great Theron fell, an omen of the fight;
10.432: Great Theron, large of limbs, of giant height.
10.433: He first in open field defied the prince:
10.434: But armor scal'd with gold was no defense
10.435: Against the fated sword, which open'd wide
10.436: His plated shield, and pierc'd his naked side.
10.437: Next, Lichas fell, who, not like others born,
10.438: Was from his wretched mother ripp'd and torn;
10.439: Sacred, O Phoebus, from his birth to thee;
10.440: For his beginning life from biting steel was free.
10.441: Not far from him was Gyas laid along,
10.442: Of monstrous bulk; with Cisseus fierce and strong:
10.443: Vain bulk and strength! for, when the chief assail'd,
10.444: Nor valor nor Herculean arms avail'd,
10.445: Nor their fam'd father, wont in war to go
10.446: With great Alcides, while he toil'd below.
10.447: The noisy Pharos next receiv'd his death:
10.448: Aeneas writh'd his dart, and stopp'd his bawling
10.449: Then wretched Cydon had receiv'd his doom,
10.450: Who courted Clytius in his beardless bloom,
10.451: And sought with lust obscene polluted joys:
10.452: The Trojan sword had curd his love of boys,
10.453: Had not his sev'n bold brethren stopp'd the course
10.454: Of the fierce champions, with united force.
10.455: Sev'n darts were thrown at once; and some rebound
10.456: From his bright shield, some on his helmet sound:
10.457: The rest had reach'd him; but his mother's care
10.458: Prevented those, and turn'd aside in air.
10.459: The prince then call'd Achates, to supply
10.460: The spears that knew the way to victory-
10.461: "Those fatal weapons, which, inur'd to blood,
10.462: In Grecian bodies under Ilium stood:
10.463: Not one of those my hand shall toss in vain
10.464: Against our foes, on this contended plain."
10.465: He said; then seiz'd a mighty spear, and threw;
10.466: Which, wing'd with fate, thro' Maeon's buckler flew,
10.467: Pierc'd all the brazen plates, and reach'd his heart:
10.469: Alcanor saw; and reach'd, but reach'd in vain,
10.470: His helping hand, his brother to sustain.
10.471: A second spear, which kept the former course,
10.472: From the same hand, and sent with equal force,
10.473: His right arm pierc'd, and holding on, bereft
10.474: His use of both, and pinion'd down his left.
10.475: Then Numitor from his dead brother drew
10.476: Th' ill-omen'd spear, and at the Trojan threw:
10.477: Preventing fate directs the lance awry,
10.478: Which, glancing, only mark'd Achates' thigh.
10.479: In pride of youth the Sabine Clausus came,
10.480: And, from afar, at Dryops took his aim.
10.481: The spear flew hissing thro' the middle space,
10.482: And pierc'd his throat, directed at his face;
10.483: It stopp'd at once the passage of his wind,
10.484: And the free soul to flitting air resign'd:
10.485: His forehead was the first that struck the ground;
10.486: Lifeblood and life rush'd mingled thro' the wound.
10.487: He slew three brothers of the Borean race,
10.488: And three, whom Ismarus, their native place,
10.489: Had sent to war, but all the sons of Thrace.
10.490: Halesus, next, the bold Aurunci leads:
10.491: The son of Neptune to his aid succeeds,
10.492: Conspicuous on his horse. On either hand,
10.493: These fight to keep, and those to win, the land.
10.494: With mutual blood th' Ausonian soil is dyed,
10.495: While on its borders each their claim decide.
10.496: As wintry winds, contending in the sky,
10.497: With equal force of lungs their titles try:
10.498: They rage, they roar; the doubtful rack of heav'n
10.499: Stands without motion, and the tide undriv'n:
10.500: Each bent to conquer, neither side to yield,
10.501: They long suspend the fortune of the field.
10.502: Both armies thus perform what courage can;
10.503: Foot set to foot, and mingled man to man.
10.504: But, in another part, th' Arcadian horse
10.505: With ill success ingage the Latin force:
10.506: For, where th' impetuous torrent, rushing down,
10.507: Huge craggy stones and rooted trees had thrown,
10.508: They left their coursers, and, unus'd to fight
10.509: On foot, were scatter'd in a shameful flight.
10.510: Pallas, who with disdain and grief had view'd
10.511: His foes pursuing, and his friends pursued,
10.512: Us'd threat'nings mix'd with pray'rs, his last resource,
10.513: With these to move their minds, with those to fire their
10.514: "Which way, companions? whether would you run?
10.515: By you yourselves, and mighty battles won,
10.516: By my great sire, by his establish'd name,
10.517: And early promise of my future fame;
10.518: By my youth, emulous of equal right
10.519: To share his honors- shun ignoble flight!
10.520: Trust not your feet: your hands must hew way
10.521: Thro' yon black body, and that thick array:
10.522: 'T is thro' that forward path that we must come;
10.523: There lies our way, and that our passage home.
10.524: Nor pow'rs above, nor destinies below
10.525: Oppress our arms: with equal strength we go,
10.526: With mortal hands to meet a mortal foe.
10.527: See on what foot we stand: a scanty shore,
10.528: The sea behind, our enemies before;
10.529: No passage left, unless we swim the main;
10.530: Or, forcing these, the Trojan trenches gain."
10.531: This said, he strode with eager haste along,
10.532: And bore amidst the thickest of the throng.
10.533: Lagus, the first he met, with fate to foe,
10.534: Had heav'd a stone of mighty weight, to throw:
10.535: Stooping, the spear descended on his chine,
10.536: Just where the bone distinguished either loin:
10.537: It stuck so fast, so deeply buried lay,
10.538: That scarce the victor forc'd the steel away.
10.539: Hisbon came on: but, while he mov'd too slow
10.540: To wish'd revenge, the prince prevents his blow;
10.541: For, warding his at once, at once he press'd,
10.542: And plung'd the fatal weapon in his breast.
10.543: Then lewd Anchemolus he laid in dust,
10.544: Who stain'd his stepdam's bed with impious lust.
10.545: And, after him, the Daucian twins were slain,
10.546: Laris and Thymbrus, on the Latian plain;
10.547: So wondrous like in feature, shape, and size,
10.548: As caus'd an error in their parents' eyes-
10.549: Grateful mistake! but soon the sword decides
10.550: The nice distinction, and their fate divides:
10.551: For Thymbrus' head was lopp'd; and Laris' hand,
10.552: Dismember'd, sought its owner on the strand:
10.553: The trembling fingers yet the fauchion strain,
10.554: And threaten still th' intended stroke in vain.
10.555: Now, to renew the charge, th' Arcadians came:
10.556: Sight of such acts, and sense of honest shame,
10.557: And grief, with anger mix'd, their minds inflame.
10.558: Then, with a casual blow was Rhoeteus slain,
10.559: Who chanc'd, as Pallas threw, to cross the plain:
10.560: The flying spear was after Ilus sent;
10.561: But Rhoeteus happen'd on a death unmeant:
10.562: From Teuthras and from Tyres while he fled,
10.563: The lance, athwart his body, laid him dead:
10.564: Roll'd from his chariot with a mortal wound,
10.565: And intercepted fate, he spurn'd the ground.

10.567: The watchful shepherd to the forest flies,
10.568: And fires the midmost plants; contagion spreads,

10.570: Around the forest flies the furious blast,

10.576: And, pouring on their foes, their prince delight.
10.577: Halesus came, fierce with desire of blood;
10.578: But first collected in his arms he stood:
10.579: Advancing then, he plied the spear so well,
10.581: Around his head he toss'd his glitt'ring brand,
10.582: And from Strymonius hew'd his better hand,
10.583: Held up to guard his throat; then hurl'd a stone
10.584: At Thoas' ample front, and pierc'd the bone:
10.585: It struck beneath the space of either eye;
10.586: And blood, and mingled brains, together fly.
10.587: Deep skill'd in future fates, Halesus' sire
10.588: Did with the youth to lonely groves retire:
10.589: But, when the father's mortal race was run,
10.590: Dire destiny laid hold upon the son,
10.591: And haul'd him to the war, to find, beneath
10.592: Th' Evandrian spear, a memorable death.
10.593: Pallas th' encounter seeks, but, ere he throws,
10.594: To Tuscan Tiber thus address'd his vows:
10.595: "O sacred stream, direct my flying dart,
10.596: And give to pass the proud Halesus' heart!
10.597: His arms and spoils thy holy oak shall bear."
10.598: Pleas'd with the bribe, the god receiv'd his pray'r:
10.599: For, while his shield protects a friend distress'd,
10.600: The dart came driving on, and pierc'd his breast.
10.601: But Lausus, no small portion of the war,
10.602: Permits not panic fear to reign too far,
10.603: Caus'd by the death of so renown'd a knight;
10.604: But by his own example cheers the fight.
10.605: Fierce Abas first he slew; Abas, the stay
10.606: Of Trojan hopes, and hindrance of the day.
10.607: The Phrygian troops escap'd the Greeks in vain:
10.608: They, and their mix'd allies, now load the plain.
10.609: To the rude shock of war both armies came;
10.610: Their leaders equal, and their strength the same.
10.611: The rear so press'd the front, they could not wield
10.612: Their angry weapons, to dispute the field.
10.613: Here Pallas urges on, and Lausus there:
10.614: Of equal youth and beauty both appear,
10.615: But both by fate forbid to breathe their native
10.616: Their congress in the field great Jove withstands:
10.617: Both doom'd to fall, but fall by greater hands.
10.618: Meantime Juturna warns the Daunian chief
10.619: Of Lausus' danger, urging swift relief.
10.620: With his driv'n chariot he divides the crowd,
10.621: And, making to his friends, thus calls aloud:
10.622: "Let none presume his needless aid to join;
10.623: Retire, and clear the field; the fight is mine:
10.624: To this right hand is Pallas only due;
10.625: O were his father here, my just revenge to view!"
10.626: From the forbidden space his men retir'd.
10.627: Pallas their awe, and his stern words, admir'd;
10.628: Survey'd him o'er and o'er with wond'ring sight,
10.629: Struck with his haughty mien, and tow'ring height.
10.630: Then to the king: "Your empty vaunts forbear;
10.631: Success I hope, and fate I cannot fear;
10.632: Alive or dead, I shall deserve a name;
10.633: Jove is impartial, and to both the same."
10.634: He said, and to the void advanc'd his pace:
10.635: Pale horror sate on each Arcadian face.
10.636: Then Turnus, from his chariot leaping light,
10.637: Address'd himself on foot to single fight.
10.638: And, as a lion- when he spies from far
10.639: A bull that seems to meditate the war,
10.640: Bending his neck, and spurning back the sand-
10.641: Runs roaring downward from his hilly stand:
10.642: Imagine eager Turnus not more slow,
10.643: To rush from high on his unequal foe.
10.644: Young Pallas, when he saw the chief advance
10.645: Within due distance of his flying lance,
10.646: Prepares to charge him first, resolv'd to try
10.647: If fortune would his want of force supply;
10.648: And thus to Heav'n and Hercules address'd:
10.650: His son adjures you by those holy rites,
10.651: That hospitable board, those genial nights;
10.652: Assist my great attempt to gain this prize,
10.653: And let proud Turnus view, with dying eyes,
10.654: His ravish'd spoils." 'T was heard, the vain request;
10.655: Alcides mourn'd, and stifled sighs within his breast.
10.656: Then Jove, to soothe his sorrow, thus began:
10.657: "Short bounds of life are set to mortal man.
10.658: 'T is virtue's work alone to stretch the narrow
10.659: So many sons of gods, in bloody fight,
10.660: Around the walls of Troy, have lost the light:
10.661: My own Sarpedon fell beneath his foe;
10.662: Nor I, his mighty sire, could ward the blow.
10.663: Ev'n Turnus shortly shall resign his breath,
10.664: And stands already on the verge of death."
10.665: This said, the god permits the fatal fight,
10.666: But from the Latian fields averts his sight.
10.667: Now with full force his spear young Pallas threw,
10.668: And, having thrown, his shining fauchion drew
10.669: The steel just graz'd along the shoulder joint,
10.670: And mark'd it slightly with the glancing point,
10.671: Fierce Turnus first to nearer distance drew,
10.672: And pois'd his pointed spear, before he threw:
10.673: Then, as the winged weapon whizz'd along,
10.674: "See now," said he, "whose arm is better strung."
10.675: The spear kept on the fatal course, unstay'd
10.676: By plates of ir'n, which o'er the shield were laid:

10.678: His corslet pierc'd, and reach'd his heart at last.
10.679: In vain the youth tugs at the broken wood;
10.680: The soul comes issuing with the vital blood:
10.681: He falls; his arms upon his body sound;
10.682: And with his bloody teeth he bites the ground.
10.684: Said he; "my message to your master bear:
10.685: Such as the sire deserv'd, the son I send;
10.686: It costs him dear to be the Phrygians' friend.
10.687: The lifeless body, tell him, I bestow,
10.688: Unask'd, to rest his wand'ring ghost below."
10.689: He said, and trampled down with all the force
10.690: Of his left foot, and spurn'd the wretched corse;
10.691: Then snatch'd the shining belt, with gold inlaid;
10.692: The belt Eurytion's artful hands had made,
10.693: Where fifty fatal brides, express'd to sight,
10.694: All in the compass of one mournful night,
10.695: Depriv'd their bridegrooms of returning light.
10.696: In an ill hour insulting Turnus tore
10.697: Those golden spoils, and in a worse he wore.
10.698: O mortals, blind in fate, who never know
10.699: To bear high fortune, or endure the low!
10.700: The time shall come, when Turnus, but in vain,
10.701: Shall wish untouch'd the trophies of the slain;
10.702: Shall wish the fatal belt were far away,
10.703: And curse the dire remembrance of the day.
10.704: The sad Arcadians, from th' unhappy field,
10.705: Bear back the breathless body on a shield.
10.706: O grace and grief of war! at once restor'd,
10.707: With praises, to thy sire, at once deplor'd!
10.708: One day first sent thee to the fighting field,
