10.1166: He griev'd; he wept; the sight an image brought
10.1167: Of his own filial love, a sadly pleasing thought:
10.1168: Then stretch'd his hand to hold him up, and said:
10.1169: "Poor hapless youth! what praises can be paid
10.1170: To love so great, to such transcendent store
10.1171: Of early worth, and sure presage of more?
10.1173: Untouch'd thy arms, untaken be thy sword;
10.1174: And all that pleas'd thee living, still remain
10.1175: Inviolate, and sacred to the slain.
10.1176: Thy body on thy parents I bestow,
10.1177: To rest thy soul, at least, if shadows know,
10.1178: Or have a sense of human things below.
10.1179: There to thy fellow ghosts with glory tell:
10.1180: ''T was by the great Aeneas hand I fell.'"
10.1181: With this, his distant friends he beckons near,
10.1182: Provokes their duty, and prevents their fear:
10.1183: Himself assists to lift him from the ground,
10.1184: With clotted locks, and blood that well'd from out the
10.1185: Meantime, his father, now no father, stood,
10.1186: And wash'd his wounds by Tiber's yellow flood:
10.1187: Oppress'd with anguish, panting, and o'erspent,
10.1188: His fainting limbs against an oak he leant.
10.1189: A bough his brazen helmet did sustain;
10.1190: His heavier arms lay scatter'd on the plain:
10.1191: A chosen train of youth around him stand;
10.1192: His drooping head was rested on his hand:
10.1193: His grisly beard his pensive bosom sought;
10.1194: And all on Lausus ran his restless thought.
10.1195: Careful, concern'd his danger to prevent,
10.1196: He much enquir'd, and many a message sent
10.1197: To warn him from the field- alas! in vain!
10.1198: Behold, his mournful followers bear him slain!
10.1199: O'er his broad shield still gush'd the yawning wound,
10.1200: And drew a bloody trail along the ground.
10.1201: Far off he heard their cries, far off divin'd
10.1202: The dire event, with a foreboding mind.
10.1203: With dust he sprinkled first his hoary head;
10.1204: Then both his lifted hands to heav'n he spread;
10.1205: Last, the dear corpse embracing, thus he said:
10.1206: "What joys, alas! could this frail being give,
10.1207: That I have been so covetous to live?
10.1208: To see my son, and such a son, resign
10.1209: His life, a ransom for preserving mine!
10.1210: And am I then preserv'd, and art thou lost?
10.1211: How much too dear has that redemption cost!
10.1212: 'T is now my bitter banishment I feel:
10.1213: This is a wound too deep for time to heal.
10.1214: My guilt thy growing virtues did defame;
10.1215: My blackness blotted thy unblemish'd name.
10.1216: Chas'd from a throne, abandon'd, and exil'd
10.1217: For foul misdeeds, were punishments too mild:
10.1218: I ow'd my people these, and, from their hate,
10.1219: With less resentment could have borne my fate.
10.1220: And yet I live, and yet sustain the sight
10.1221: Of hated men, and of more hated light:
10.1222: But will not long." With that he rais'd from ground
10.1223: His fainting limbs, that stagger'd with his wound;
10.1224: Yet, with a mind resolv'd, and unappall'd
10.1225: With pains or perils, for his courser call'd
10.1226: Well-mouth'd, well-manag'd, whom himself did dress
10.1227: With daily care, and mounted with success;
10.1228: His aid in arms, his ornament in peace.
10.1229: Soothing his courage with a gentle stroke,
10.1230: The steed seem'd sensible, while thus he spoke:
10.1231: "O Rhoebus, we have liv'd too long for me-
10.1232: If life and long were terms that could agree!
10.1233: This day thou either shalt bring back the head
10.1234: And bloody trophies of the Trojan dead;
10.1235: This day thou either shalt revenge my woe,
10.1236: For murther'd Lausus, on his cruel foe;
10.1238: Our conquest, with thy conquer'd master die:
10.1239: For, after such a lord, rest secure,
10.1240: Thou wilt no foreign reins, or Trojan load endure."
10.1241: He said; and straight th' officious courser kneels,
10.1242: To take his wonted weight. His hands he fills
10.1243: With pointed jav'lins; on his head he lac'd
10.1244: His glitt'ring helm, which terribly was grac'd
10.1245: With waving horsehair, nodding from afar;
10.1246: Then spurr'd his thund'ring steed amidst the war.
10.1247: Love, anguish, wrath, and grief, to madness wrought,
10.1248: Despair, and secret shame, and conscious thought
10.1249: Of inborn worth, his lab'ring soul oppress'd,
10.1250: Roll'd in his eyes, and rag'd within his breast.
10.1251: Then loud he call'd Aeneas thrice by name:
10.1252: The loud repeated voice to glad Aeneas came.
10.1253: "Great Jove," he said, "and the far-shooting god,
10.1254: Inspire thy mind to make thy challenge good!"
10.1255: He spoke no more; but hasten'd, void of fear,
10.1256: And threaten'd with his long protended spear.
10.1257: To whom Mezentius thus: "Thy vaunts are vain.
10.1258: My Lausus lies extended on the plain:
10.1259: He's lost! thy conquest is already won;
10.1260: The wretched sire is murther'd in the son.
10.1261: Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy.
10.1262: Forbear thy threats: my bus'ness is to die;
10.1263: But first receive this parting legacy."
10.1264: He said; and straight a whirling dart he sent;
10.1266: Round in a spacious ring he rides the field,
10.1267: And vainly plies th' impenetrable shield.
10.1268: Thrice rode he round; and thrice Aeneas wheel'd,
10.1269: Turn'd as he turn'd: the golden orb withstood
10.1270: The strokes, and bore about an iron wood.
10.1271: Impatient of delay, and weary grown,
10.1272: Still to defend, and to defend alone,
10.1273: To wrench the darts which in his buckler light,
10.1274: Urg'd and o'er-labor'd in unequal fight;
10.1275: At length resolv'd, he throws with all his force
10.1276: Full at the temples of the warrior horse.
10.1277: Just where the stroke was aim'd, th' unerring spear
10.1278: Made way, and stood transfix'd thro' either ear.
10.1279: Seiz'd with unwonted pain, surpris'd with fright,
10.1280: The wounded steed curvets, and, rais'd upright,
10.1281: Lights on his feet before; his hoofs behind
10.1282: Spring up in air aloft, and lash the wind.
10.1283: Down comes the rider headlong from his height:
10.1284: His horse came after with unwieldy weight,
10.1285: And, flound'ring forward, pitching on his head,
10.1287: From either host, the mingled shouts and cries
10.1288: Of Trojans and Rutulians rend the skies.
10.1289: Aeneas, hast'ning, wav'd his fatal sword
10.1290: High o'er his head, with this reproachful word:
10.1291: "Now; where are now thy vaunts, the fierce disdain
10.1292: Of proud Mezentius, and the lofty strain?"
10.1293: Struggling, and wildly staring on the skies,
10.1294: With scarce recover'd sight he thus replies:
10.1295: "Why these insulting words, this waste of breath,
10.1296: To souls undaunted, and secure of death?
10.1297: 'T is no dishonor for the brave to die,
10.1298: Nor came I here with hope victory;
10.1299: Nor ask I life, nor fought with that design:
10.1300: As I had us'd my fortune, use thou thine.
10.1301: My dying son contracted no such band;
10.1302: The gift is hateful from his murd'rer's hand.
10.1303: For this, this only favor let me sue,
10.1304: If pity can to conquer'd foes be due:
10.1305: Refuse it not; but let my body have
10.1306: The last retreat of humankind, a grave.
10.1307: Too well I know th' insulting people's hate;
10.1308: Protect me from their vengeance after fate:
10.1309: This refuge for my poor remains provide,
10.1310: And lay my much-lov'd Lausus by my side."
10.1311: He said, and to the sword his throat applied.
10.1312: The crimson stream distain'd his arms around,
10.1313: And the disdainful soul came rushing thro' the wound.

11.1: Scarce had the rosy Morning rais'd her head
11.2: Above the waves, and left her wat'ry bed;
11.3: The pious chief, whom double cares attend
11.4: For his unburied soldiers and his friend,
11.5: Yet first to Heav'n perform'd a victor's vows:
11.6: He bar'd an ancient oak of all her boughs;
11.7: Then on a rising ground the trunk he plac'd,
11.8: Which with the spoils of his dead foe he grac'd.
11.9: The coat of arms by proud Mezentius worn,
11.10: Now on a naked snag in triumph borne,
11.11: Was hung on high, and glitter'd from afar,
11.12: A trophy sacred to the God of War.
11.13: Above his arms, fix'd on the leafless wood,
11.14: Appear'd his plumy crest, besmear'd with blood:
11.15: His brazen buckler on the left was seen;
11.16: Truncheons of shiver'd lances hung between;
11.17: And on the right was placed his corslet, bor'd;
11.18: And to the neck was tied his unavailing sword.
11.19: A crowd of chiefs inclose the godlike man,
11.20: Who thus, conspicuous in the midst, began:
11.21: "Our toils, my friends, are crown'd with sure success;
11.22: The greater part perform'd, achieve the less.
11.23: Now follow cheerful to the trembling town;
11.24: Press but an entrance, and presume it won.
11.25: Fear is no more, for fierce Mezentius lies,
11.26: As the first fruits of war, a sacrifice.
11.27: Turnus shall fall extended on the plain,
11.28: And, in this omen, is already slain.
11.29: Prepar'd in arms, pursue your happy chance;
11.30: That none unwarn'd may plead his ignorance,
11.31: And I, at Heav'n's appointed hour, may find
11.32: Your warlike ensigns waving in the wind.
11.33: Meantime the rites and fun'ral pomps prepare,
11.34: Due to your dead companions of the war:
11.35: The last respect the living can bestow,
11.36: To shield their shadows from contempt below.
11.37: That conquer'd earth be theirs, for which they fought,
11.38: And which for us with their own blood they bought;
11.39: But first the corpse of our unhappy friend
11.40: To the sad city of Evander send,
11.41: Who, not inglorious, in his age's bloom,
11.42: Was hurried hence by too severe a doom."
11.43: Thus, weeping while he spoke, he took his way,
11.44: Where, new in death, lamented Pallas lay.
11.45: Acoetes watch'd the corpse; whose youth deserv'd
11.46: The father's trust; and now the son he serv'd
11.47: With equal faith, but less auspicious care.
11.48: Th' attendants of the slain his sorrow share.
11.49: A troop of Trojans mix'd with these appear,
11.50: And mourning matrons with dishevel'd hair.
11.51: Soon as the prince appears, they raise a cry;
11.52: All beat their breasts, and echoes rend the sky.
11.53: They rear his drooping forehead from the ground;
11.54: But, when Aeneas view'd the grisly wound
11.55: Which Pallas in his manly bosom bore,
11.56: And the fair flesh distain'd with purple gore;
11.57: First, melting into tears, the pious man
11.58: Deplor'd so sad a sight, then thus began:
11.59: "Unhappy youth! when Fortune gave the rest
11.60: Of my full wishes, she refus'd the best!
11.61: She came; but brought not thee along, to bless
11.62: My longing eyes, and share in my success:
11.63: She grudg'd thy safe return, the triumphs due
11.64: To prosp'rous valor, in the public view.
11.65: Not thus I promis'd, when thy father lent
11.66: Thy needless succor with a sad consent;
11.67: Embrac'd me, parting for th' Etrurian land,
11.68: And sent me to possess a large command.
11.69: He warn'd, and from his own experience told,
11.70: Our foes were warlike, disciplin'd, and bold.
11.71: And now perhaps, in hopes of thy return,
11.72: Rich odors on his loaded altars burn,
11.73: While we, with vain officious pomp, prepare
11.74: To send him back his portion of the war,
11.75: A bloody breathless body, which can owe
11.76: No farther debt, but to the pow'rs below.
11.77: The wretched father, ere his race is run,
11.78: Shall view the fun'ral honors of his son.
11.79: These are my triumphs of the Latian war,
11.80: Fruits of my plighted faith and boasted care!
11.81: And yet, unhappy sire, thou shalt not see
11.82: A son whose death disgrac'd his ancestry;
11.83: Thou shalt not blush, old man, however griev'd:
11.84: Thy Pallas no dishonest wound receiv'd.
11.85: He died no death to make thee wish, too late,
11.86: Thou hadst not liv'd to see his shameful fate:
11.87: But what a champion has th' Ausonian coast,
11.88: And what a friend hast thou, Ascanius, lost!"
11.89: Thus having mourn'd, he gave the word around,
11.90: To raise the breathless body from the ground;
11.91: And chose a thousand horse, the flow'r of all
11.92: His warlike troops, to wait the funeral,
11.93: To bear him back and share Evander's grief:
11.94: A well-becoming, but a weak relief.
11.95: Of oaken twigs they twist an easy bier,
11.96: Then on their shoulders the sad burden rear.
11.97: The body on this rural hearse is borne:
11.98: Strew'd leaves and funeral greens the bier adorn.
11.99: All pale he lies, and looks a lovely flow'r,
11.100: New cropp'd by virgin hands, to dress the bow'r:
11.101: Unfaded yet, but yet unfed below,
11.102: No more to mother earth or the green stern shall
11.103: Then two fair vests, of wondrous work and cost,
11.104: Of purple woven, and with gold emboss'd,
11.105: For ornament the Trojan hero brought,
11.106: Which with her hands Sidonian Dido wrought.
11.107: One vest array'd the corpse; and one they spread
11.108: O'er his clos'd eyes, and wrapp'd around his head,
11.109: That, when the yellow hair in flame should fall,
11.110: The catching fire might burn the golden caul.
11.111: Besides, the spoils of foes in battle slain,
11.112: When he descended on the Latian plain;
11.113: Arms, trappings, horses, by the hearse are led
11.114: In long array- th' achievements of the dead.
11.115: Then, pinion'd with their hands behind, appear
11.116: Th' unhappy captives, marching in the rear,
11.117: Appointed off'rings in the victor's name,
11.118: To sprinkle with their blood the fun'ral flame.
11.119: Inferior trophies by the chiefs are borne;
11.120: Gauntlets and helms their loaded hands adorn;
11.121: And fair inscriptions fix'd, and titles read
11.122: Of Latian leaders conquer'd by the dead.
11.123: Acoetes on his pupil's corpse attends,
11.124: With feeble steps, supported by his friends.
11.125: Pausing at ev'ry pace, in sorrow drown'd,
11.126: Betwixt their arms he sinks upon the ground;
11.127: Where grov'ling while he lies in deep despair,
11.128: He beats his breast, and rends his hoary hair.
11.129: The champion's chariot next is seen to roll,
11.130: Besmear'd with hostile blood, and honorably foul.
11.131: To close the pomp, Aethon, the steed of state,
11.132: Is led, the fun'rals of his lord to wait.
11.133: Stripp'd of his trappings, with a sullen pace
11.134: He walks; and the big tears run rolling down his
11.135: The lance of Pallas, and the crimson crest,
11.136: Are borne behind: the victor seiz'd the rest.
11.137: The march begins: the trumpets hoarsely sound;
11.138: The pikes and lances trail along the ground.
11.139: Thus while the Trojan and Arcadian horse
11.140: To Pallantean tow'rs direct their course,
11.141: In long procession rank'd, the pious chief
11.142: Stopp'd in the rear, and gave a vent to grief:
11.143: "The public care," he said, "which war attends,
11.144: Diverts our present woes, at least suspends.
11.145: Peace with the manes of great Pallas dwell!
11.146: Hail, holy relics! and a last farewell!"
11.147: He said no more, but, inly thro' he mourn'd,
11.148: Restrained his tears, and to the camp return'd.
11.149: Now suppliants, from Laurentum sent, demand
11.150: A truce, with olive branches in their hand;
11.151: Obtest his clemency, and from the plain
11.152: Beg leave to draw the bodies of their slain.
11.153: They plead, that none those common rites deny
11.154: To conquer'd foes that in fair battle die.
11.155: All cause of hate was ended in their death;
11.156: Nor could he war with bodies void of breath.
11.157: A king, they hop'd, would hear a king's request,
11.158: Whose son he once was call'd, and once his guest.
11.159: Their suit, which was too just to be denied,
11.160: The hero grants, and farther thus replied:
11.161: "O Latian princes, how severe a fate
11.162: In causeless quarrels has involv'd your state,
11.163: And arm'd against an unoffending man,
11.164: Who sought your friendship ere the war began!
11.165: You beg a truce, which I would gladly give,
11.166: Not only for the slain, but those who live.
11.167: I came not hither but by Heav'n's command,
11.168: And sent by fate to share the Latian land.
11.169: Nor wage I wars unjust: your king denied
11.170: My proffer'd friendship, and my promis'd bride;
11.171: Left me for Turnus. Turnus then should try
11.172: His cause in arms, to conquer or to die.
11.173: My right and his are in dispute: the slain
11.174: Fell without fault, our quarrel to maintain.
11.175: In equal arms let us alone contend;
11.176: And let him vanquish, whom his fates befriend.
11.177: This is the way (so tell him) to possess
11.178: The royal virgin, and restore the peace.
11.179: Bear this message back, with ample leave,
11.180: That your slain friends may fun'ral rites receive."
11.181: Thus having said- th' embassadors, amaz'd,
11.182: Stood mute a while, and on each other gaz'd.
11.183: Drances, their chief, who harbor'd in his breast
11.184: Long hate to Turnus, as his foe profess'd,
11.185: Broke silence first, and to the godlike man,
11.186: With graceful action bowing, thus began:
11.187: "Auspicious prince, in arms a mighty name,
11.188: But yet whose actions far transcend your fame;
11.189: Would I your justice or your force express,
11.190: Thought can but equal; and all words are less.
11.191: Your answer we shall thankfully relate,
11.192: And favors granted to the Latian state.
11.193: If wish'd success our labor shall attend,
11.194: Think peace concluded, and the king your friend:
11.195: Let Turnus leave the realm to your command,
11.196: And seek alliance in some other land:
11.197: Build you the city which your fates assign;
11.198: We shall be proud in the great work to join."
11.199: Thus Drances; and his words so well persuade
11.200: The rest impower'd, that soon a truce is made.
11.201: Twelve days the term allow'd: and, during those,
11.202: Latians and Trojans, now no longer foes,
11.203: Mix'd in the woods, for fun'ral piles prepare
11.204: To fell the timber, and forget the war.
11.205: Loud axes thro' the groaning groves resound;
11.206: Oak, mountain ash, and poplar spread the ground;
11.207: First fall from high; and some the trunks receive
11.208: In loaden wains; with wedges some they cleave.
11.209: And now the fatal news by Fame is blown
11.210: Thro' the short circuit of th' Arcadian town,
11.211: Of Pallas slain- by Fame, which just before
11.212: His triumphs on distended pinions bore.
11.213: Rushing from out the gate, the people stand,
11.214: Each with a fun'ral flambeau in his hand.
11.215: Wildly they stare, distracted with amaze:
11.216: The fields are lighten'd with a fiery blaze,
11.217: That cast a sullen splendor on their friends,
11.218: The marching troop which their dead prince attends.
11.219: Both parties meet: they raise a doleful cry;
11.220: The matrons from the walls with shrieks reply,
11.221: And their mix'd mourning rends the vaulted sky.
11.222: The town is fill'd with tumult and with tears,
11.223: Till the loud clamors reach Evander's ears:
11.224: Forgetful of his state, he runs along,
11.225: With a disorder'd pace, and cleaves the throng;
11.226: Falls on the corpse; and groaning there he lies,
11.227: With silent grief, that speaks but at his eyes.
11.228: Short sighs and sobs succeed; till sorrow breaks
11.229: A passage, and at once he weeps and speaks:
11.230: "O Pallas! thou hast fail'd thy plighted word,
11.231: To fight with caution, not to tempt the sword!
11.232: I warn'd thee, but in vain; for well I knew
11.233: What perils youthful ardor would pursue,
11.234: That boiling blood would carry thee too far,
11.235: Young as thou wert in dangers, raw to war!
11.236: O curst essay of arms, disastrous doom,
11.237: Prelude of bloody fields, and fights to come!
11.239: Vain vows to Heav'n, and unavailing care!
11.240: Thrice happy thou, dear partner of my bed,
11.241: Whose holy soul the stroke of Fortune fled,
11.242: Praescious of ills, and leaving me behind,
11.243: To drink the dregs of life by fate assign'd!
11.244: Beyond the goal of nature I have gone:
11.245: My Pallas late set out, but reach'd too soon.
11.246: If, for my league against th' Ausonian state,
11.247: Amidst their weapons I had found my fate,
11.248: (Deserv'd from them,) then I had been return'd
11.249: A breathless victor, and my son had mourn'd.
11.250: Yet will I not my Trojan friend upbraid,
11.251: Nor grudge th' alliance I so gladly made.
11.252: 'T was not his fault, my Pallas fell so young,
11.253: But my own crime, for having liv'd too long.
11.254: Yet, since the gods had destin'd him to die,
11.255: At least he led the way to victory:
11.256: First for his friends he won the fatal shore,
11.257: And sent whole herds of slaughter'd foes before;
11.258: A death too great, too glorious to deplore.
11.259: Nor will I add new honors to thy grave,
11.260: Content with those the Trojan hero gave:
11.261: That funeral pomp thy Phrygian friends design'd,
11.262: In which the Tuscan chiefs and army join'd.
11.263: Great spoils and trophies, gain'd by thee, they
11.264: Then let thy own achievements be thy share.
11.265: Even thou, O Turnus, hadst a trophy stood,
11.266: Whose mighty trunk had better grac'd the wood,
11.267: If Pallas had arriv'd, with equal length
11.268: Of years, to match thy bulk with equal strength.
11.269: But why, unhappy man, dost thou detain
11.270: These troops, to view the tears thou shedd'st in
11.271: Go, friends, this message to your lord relate:
11.272: Tell him, that, if I bear my bitter fate,
11.273: And, after Pallas' death, live ling'ring on,
11.274: 'T is to behold his vengeance for my son.
11.275: I stay for Turnus, whose devoted head
11.276: Is owing to the living and the dead.
11.277: My son and I expect it from his hand;
11.278: 'T is all that he can give, or we demand.
11.279: Joy is no more; but I would gladly go,
11.280: To greet my Pallas with such news below."
11.281: The morn had now dispell'd the shades of night,
11.282: Restoring toils, when she restor'd the light.
11.283: The Trojan king and Tuscan chief command
11.284: To raise the piles along the winding strand.
11.285: Their friends convey the dead fun'ral fires;
11.286: Black smold'ring smoke from the green wood expires;
11.287: The light of heav'n is chok'd, and the new day retires.
11.288: Then thrice around the kindled piles they go
11.289: (For ancient custom had ordain'd it so)
11.290: Thrice horse and foot about the fires are led;
11.291: And thrice, with loud laments, they hail the dead.
11.292: Tears, trickling down their breasts, bedew the ground,
11.293: And drums and trumpets mix their mournful sound.
11.294: Amid the blaze, their pious brethren throw
11.295: The spoils, in battle taken from the foe:
11.296: Helms, bits emboss'd, and swords of shining steel;
11.297: One casts a target, one a chariot wheel;
11.298: Some to their fellows their own arms restore:
11.299: The fauchions which in luckless fight they bore,
11.300: Their bucklers pierc'd, their darts bestow'd in
11.301: And shiver'd lances gather'd from the plain.
11.302: Whole herds of offer'd bulls, about the fire,
11.303: And bristled boars, and woolly sheep expire.
11.304: Around the piles a careful troop attends,
11.305: To watch the wasting flames, and weep their burning
11.306: Ling'ring along the shore, till dewy night
11.307: New decks the face of heav'n with starry light.
11.308: The conquer'd Latians, with like pious care,
11.309: Piles without number for their dead prepare.
11.310: Part in the places where they fell are laid;
11.311: And part are to the neighb'ring fields convey'd.
11.312: The corps of kings, and captains of renown,
11.313: Borne off in state, are buried in the town;
11.314: The rest, unhonor'd, and without a name,
11.315: Are cast a common heap to feed the flame.
11.316: Trojans and Latians vie with like desires
11.317: To make the field of battle shine with fires,
11.318: And the promiscuous blaze to heav'n aspires.
11.319: Now had the morning thrice renew'd the light,
11.320: And thrice dispell'd the shadows of the night,
11.321: When those who round the wasted fires remain,
11.322: Perform the last sad office to the slain.
11.323: They rake the yet warm ashes from below;
11.324: These, and the bones unburn'd, in earth bestow;
11.325: These relics with their country rites they grace,
11.326: And raise a mount of turf to mark the place.
11.327: But, in the palace of the king, appears
11.328: A scene more solemn, and a pomp of tears.
11.329: Maids, matrons, widows, mix their common moans;
11.330: Orphans their sires, and sires lament their sons.
11.331: All in that universal sorrow share,
11.332: And curse the cause of this unhappy war:
11.333: A broken league, a bride unjustly sought,
11.334: A crown usurp'd, which with their blood is bought!
11.335: These are the crimes with which they load the name
11.336: Of Turnus, and on him alone exclaim:
11.337: "Let him who lords it o'er th' Ausonian land
11.338: Engage the Trojan hero hand to hand:
11.339: His is the gain; our lot is but to serve;
11.340: 'T is just, the sway he seeks, he should deserve."
11.341: This Drances aggravates; and adds, with spite:
11.342: "His foe expects, and dares him to the fight."
11.343: Nor Turnus wants a party, to support
11.344: His cause and credit in the Latian court.
11.345: His former acts secure his present fame,
11.346: And the queen shades him with her mighty name.
11.347: While thus their factious minds with fury burn,
11.348: The legates from th' Aetolian prince return:
11.349: Sad news they bring, that, after all the cost
11.350: And care employ'd, their embassy is lost;
11.351: That Diomedes refus'd his aid in war,
11.352: Unmov'd with presents, and as deaf to pray'r.
11.353: Some new alliance must elsewhere be sought,
11.354: Or peace with Troy on hard conditions bought.
11.355: Latinus, sunk in sorrow, finds too late,
11.356: A foreign son is pointed out by fate;
11.357: And, till Aeneas shall Lavinia wed,
11.358: The wrath of Heav'n is hov'ring o'er his head.
11.359: The gods, he saw, espous'd the juster side,
11.360: When late their titles in the field were tried:
11.361: Witness the fresh laments, and fun'ral tears undried.
11.362: Thus, full of anxious thought, he summons all
11.363: The Latian senate to the council hall.
11.364: The princes come, commanded by their head,
11.365: And crowd the paths that to the palace lead.
11.366: Supreme in pow'r, and reverenc'd for his years,
11.367: He takes the throne, and in the midst appears.
11.368: Majestically sad, he sits in state,
11.369: And bids his envoys their success relate.
11.370: When Venulus began, the murmuring sound
11.371: Was hush'd, and sacred silence reign'd around.
11.372: "We have," said he, "perform'd your high command,
11.373: And pass'd with peril a long tract of land:
11.374: We reach'd the place desir'd; with wonder fill'd,
11.375: The Grecian tents and rising tow'rs beheld.
11.376: Great Diomede has compass'd round with walls
11.377: The city, which Argyripa he calls,
11.378: From his own Argos nam'd. We touch'd, with joy,
11.379: The royal hand that raz'd unhappy Troy.
11.380: When introduc'd, our presents first we bring,
11.381: Then crave an instant audience from the king.
11.382: His leave obtain'd, our native soil we name,
11.383: And tell th' important cause for which we came.
11.384: Attentively he heard us, while we spoke;
11.385: Then, with soft accents, and a pleasing look,
11.386: Made this return: 'Ausonian race, of old
11.387: Renown'd for peace, and for an age of gold,
11.388: What madness has your alter'd minds possess'd,
11.389: To change for war hereditary rest,
11.390: Solicit arms unknown, and tempt the sword,
11.391: A needless ill your ancestors abhorr'd?
11.392: We- for myself I speak, and all the name
11.393: Of Grecians, who to Troy's destruction came,
11.394: Omitting those who were in battle slain,
11.395: Or borne by rolling Simois to the main-
11.396: Not one but suffer'd, and too dearly bought
11.397: The prize of honor which in arms he sought;
11.398: Some doom'd to death, and some in exile driv'n.
11.399: Outcasts, abandon'd by the care of Heav'n;
11.400: So worn, so wretched, so despis'd a crew,
11.401: As ev'n old Priam might with pity view.
11.402: Witness the vessels by Minerva toss'd
11.403: In storms; the vengeful Capharean coast;
11.404: Th' Euboean rocks! the prince, whose brother led
11.405: Our armies to revenge his injur'd bed,
11.406: In Egypt lost! Ulysses with his men
11.407: Have seen Charybdis and the Cyclops' den.
11.408: Why should I name Idomeneus, in vain
11.409: Restor'd to scepters, and expell'd again?
11.410: Or young Achilles, by his rival slain?
11.411: Ev'n he, the King of Men, the foremost name
11.412: Of all the Greeks, and most renown'd by fame,
11.413: The proud revenger of another's wife,
11.414: Yet by his own adult'ress lost his life;
11.415: Fell at his threshold; and the spoils of Troy
11.416: The foul polluters of his bed enjoy.
11.417: The gods have envied me the sweets of life,
11.418: My much lov'd country, and my more lov'd wife:
11.419: Banish'd from both, I mourn; while in the sky,
11.420: Transform'd to birds, my lost companions fly:
11.421: Hov'ring about the coasts, they make their moan,
11.422: And cuff the cliffs with pinions not their own.
11.423: What squalid specters, in the dead of night,
11.424: Break my short sleep, and skim before my sight!
11.425: I might have promis'd to myself those harms,
11.426: Mad as I was, when I, with mortal arms,
11.427: Presum'd against immortal pow'rs to move,
11.428: And violate with wounds the Queen of Love.
11.429: Such arms this hand shall never more employ;
11.430: No hate remains with me to ruin'd Troy.
11.431: I war not with its dust; nor am I glad
11.432: To think of past events, or good or bad.
11.433: Your presents I return: whate'er you bring
11.434: To buy my friendship, send the Trojan king.
11.435: We met in fight; I know him, to my cost:
11.436: With what a whirling force his lance he toss'd!
11.437: Heav'ns! what a spring was in his arm, to throw!
11.438: How high he held his shield, and rose at ev'ry blow!
11.439: Had Troy produc'd two more his match in might,
11.440: They would have chang'd the fortune of the fight:
11.441: Th' invasion of the Greeks had been return'd,
11.442: Our empire wasted, and our cities burn'd.
11.443: The long defense the Trojan people made,
11.444: The war protracted, and the siege delay'd,
11.445: Were due to Hector's and this hero's hand:
11.446: Both brave alike, and equal in command;
11.447: Aeneas, not inferior in the field,
11.448: In pious reverence to the gods excell'd.
11.449: Make peace, ye Latians, and avoid with care
11.450: Th' impending dangers of a fatal war.'
11.451: He said no more; but, with this cold excuse,
11.452: Refus'd th' alliance, and advis'd a truce."
11.454: A jarring murmur fill'd the factious court:
11.455: As, when a torrent rolls with rapid force,
11.456: And dashes o'er the stones that stop the course,
11.457: The flood, constrain'd within a scanty space,
11.458: Roars horrible along th' uneasy race;
11.459: White foam in gath'ring eddies floats around;
11.460: The rocky shores rebellow to the sound.
11.461: The murmur ceas'd: then from his lofty throne
11.462: The king invok'd the gods, and thus begun:
11.463: "I wish, ye Latins, what we now debate
11.464: Had been resolv'd before it was too late.
11.465: Much better had it been for you and me,
11.466: Unforc'd by this our last necessity,
11.467: To have been earlier wise, than now to call
11.468: A council, when the foe surrounds the wall.
11.469: O citizens, we wage unequal war,
11.470: With men not only Heav'n's peculiar care,
11.471: But Heav'n's own race; unconquer'd in the field,
11.472: Or, conquer'd, yet unknowing how to yield.
11.473: What hopes you had in Diomedes, lay down:
11.474: Our hopes must center on ourselves alone.
11.475: Yet those how feeble, and, indeed, how vain,
11.476: You see too well; nor need my words explain.
11.477: Vanquish'd without resource; laid flat by fate;
11.478: Factions within, a foe without the gate!
11.479: Not but I grant that all perform'd their parts
11.480: With manly force, and with undaunted hearts:
11.481: With our united strength the war we wag'd;
11.482: With equal numbers, equal arms, engag'd.
11.483: You see th' event.- Now hear what I propose,
11.484: To save our friends, and satisfy our foes.
11.485: A tract of land the Latins have possess'd
11.486: Along the Tiber, stretching to the west,
11.487: Which now Rutulians and Auruncans till,
11.488: And their mix'd cattle graze the fruitful hill.
11.489: Those mountains fill'd with firs, that lower land,
11.490: If you consent, the Trojan shall command,
11.491: Call'd into part of what is ours; and there,
11.492: On terms agreed, the common country share.
11.493: There let'em build and settle, if they please;
11.494: Unless they choose once more to cross the seas,
11.495: In search of seats remote from Italy,
11.496: And from unwelcome inmates set us free.
11.497: Then twice ten galleys let us build with speed,
11.498: Or twice as many more, if more they need.
11.499: Materials are at hand; a well-grown wood
11.500: Runs equal with the margin of the flood:
11.501: Let them the number and the form assign;
11.502: The care and cost of all the stores be mine.
11.503: To treat the peace, a hundred senators
11.504: Shall be commission'd hence with ample pow'rs,
11.505: With olive the presents they shall bear,
11.506: A purple robe, a royal iv'ry chair,
11.507: And all the marks of sway that Latian monarchs wear,
11.508: And sums of gold. Among yourselves debate
11.509: This great affair, and save the sinking state."
11.510: Then Drances took the word, who grudg'd, long since,
11.511: The rising glories of the Daunian prince.
11.512: Factious and rich, bold at the council board,
11.513: But cautious in the field, he shunn'd the sword;
11.514: A close caballer, and tongue-valiant lord.
11.515: Noble his mother was, and near the throne;
11.516: But, what his father's parentage, unknown.
11.517: He rose, and took th' advantage of the times,
11.518: To load young Turnus with invidious crimes.
11.519: "Such truths, O king," said he, "your words contain,
11.520: As strike the sense, and all replies are vain;
11.521: Nor are your loyal subjects now to seek
11.522: What common needs require, but fear to speak.
11.523: Let him give leave of speech, that haughty man,
11.524: Whose pride this unauspicious war began;
11.525: For whose ambition (let me dare to say,
11.526: Fear set apart, tho' death is in my way)
11.527: The plains of Latium run with blood around.
11.528: So many valiant heroes bite the ground;
11.529: Dejected grief in ev'ry face appears;
11.530: A town in mourning, and a land in tears;
11.531: While he, th' undoubted author of our harms,
11.532: The man who menaces the gods with arms,
11.533: Yet, after all his boasts, forsook the fight,
11.534: And sought his safety in ignoble flight.
11.535: Now, best of kings, since you propose to send
11.536: Such bounteous presents to your Trojan friend;
11.537: Add yet a greater at our joint request,
11.538: One which he values more than all the rest:
11.539: Give him the fair Lavinia for his bride;
11.540: With that alliance let the league be tied,
11.541: And for the bleeding land a lasting peace provide.
11.542: Let insolence no longer awe the throne;
11.543: But, with a father's right, bestow your own.
11.544: For this maligner of the general good,
11.545: If still we fear his force, he must be woo'd;
11.546: His haughty godhead we with pray'rs implore,
11.547: Your scepter to release, and our just rights restore.
11.548: O cursed cause of all our ills, must we
11.549: Wage wars unjust, and fall in fight, for thee!
11.550: What right hast thou to rule the Latian state,
11.551: And send us out to meet our certain fate?
11.552: 'T is a destructive war: from Turnus' hand
11.553: Our peace and public safety we demand.
11.554: Let the fair bride to the brave chief remain;
11.555: If not, the peace, without the pledge, is vain.
11.556: Turnus, I know you think me not your friend,
11.557: Nor will I much with your belief contend:
11.558: I beg your greatness not to give the law
11.559: In others' realms, but, beaten, to withdraw.
11.560: Pity your own, or pity our estate;
11.561: Nor twist our fortunes with your sinking fate.
11.562: Your interest is, the war should never cease;
11.563: But we have felt enough to wish the peace:
11.564: A land exhausted to the last remains,
11.566: Yet, if desire of fame, and thirst of pow'r,
11.567: A beauteous princess, with a crown in dow'r,
11.568: So fire your mind, in arms assert your right,
11.569: And meet your foe, who dares you to the fight.
11.570: Mankind, it seems, is made for you alone;
11.571: We, but the slaves who mount you to the throne:
11.572: A base ignoble crowd, without a name,
11.573: Unwept, unworthy, of the fun'ral flame,
11.574: By duty bound to forfeit each his life,
11.575: That Turnus may possess a royal wife.
11.576: Permit not, mighty man, so mean a crew
11.577: Should share such triumphs, and detain from you
11.578: The post of honor, your undoubted due.
11.579: Rather alone your matchless force employ,
11.580: To merit what alone you must enjoy."
11.581: These words, so full of malice mix'd with art,
11.582: Inflam'd with rage the youthful hero's heart.
11.583: Then, groaning from the bottom of his breast,
11.584: He heav'd for wind, and thus his wrath express'd:
11.585: "You, Drances, never want a stream of words,
11.586: Then, when the public need requires our swords.
11.587: First in the council hall to steer the state,
11.588: And ever foremost in a tongue-debate,
11.589: While our strong walls secure us from the foe,
11.590: Ere yet with blood our ditches overflow:
11.591: But let the potent orator declaim,
11.592: And with the brand of coward blot my name;
11.593: Free leave is giv'n him, when his fatal hand
11.594: Has cover'd with more corps the sanguine strand,
11.595: And high as mine his tow'ring trophies stand.
11.596: If any doubt remains, who dares the most,
11.597: Let us decide it at the Trojan's cost,
11.598: And issue both abreast, where honor calls-
11.599: Foes are not far to seek without the walls-
11.600: Unless his noisy tongue can only fight,
11.601: And feet were giv'n him but to speed his flight.
11.602: I beaten from the field? I forc'd away?
11.603: Who, but so known a dastard, dares to say?
11.604: Had he but ev'n beheld the fight, his eyes
11.605: Had witness'd for me what his tongue denies:
11.606: What heaps of Trojans by this hand were slain,
11.607: And how the bloody Tiber swell'd the main.
11.608: All saw, but he, th' Arcadian troops retire
11.609: In scatter'd squadrons, and their prince expire.
11.610: The giant brothers, in their camp, have found,
11.611: I was not forc'd with ease to quit my ground.
11.612: Not such the Trojans tried me, when, inclos'd,
11.613: I singly their united arms oppos'd:
11.614: First forc'd an entrance thro' their thick array;
11.615: Then, glutted with their slaughter, freed my way.
11.616: 'T is a destructive war? So let it be,
11.617: But to the Phrygian pirate, and to thee!
11.618: Meantime proceed to fill the people's ears
11.619: With false reports, their minds with panic fears:
11.620: Extol the strength of a twice-conquer'd race;
11.621: Our foes encourage, and our friends debase.
11.622: Believe thy fables, and the Trojan town
11.623: Triumphant stands; the Grecians are o'erthrown;
11.624: Suppliant at Hector's feet Achilles lies,
11.625: And Diomede from fierce Aeneas flies.
11.626: Say rapid Aufidus with awful dread
11.627: Runs backward from the sea, and hides his head,
11.628: When the great Trojan on his bank appears;
11.629: For that's as true as thy dissembled fears
11.630: Of my revenge. Dismiss that vanity:
11.631: Thou, Drances, art below a death from me.
11.632: Let that vile soul in that vile body rest;
11.633: The lodging is well worthy of the guest.
11.634: "Now, royal father, to the present state
11.635: Of our affairs, and of this high debate:
11.636: If in your arms thus early you diffide,
11.637: And think your fortune is already tried;
11.638: If one defeat has brought us down so low,
11.639: As never more in fields to meet the foe;
11.640: Then I conclude for peace: 't is time to treat,
11.641: And lie like vassals at the victor's feet.
11.642: But, O! if any ancient blood remains,
11.643: One drop of all our fathers', in our veins,
11.644: That man would I prefer before the rest,
11.645: Who dar'd his death with an undaunted breast;
11.646: Who comely fell, by no dishonest wound,
11.647: To shun that sight, and, dying, gnaw'd the ground.
11.648: But, if we still have fresh recruits in store,
11.649: If our confederates can afford us more;
11.650: If the contended field we bravely fought,
11.651: And not a bloodless victory was bought;
11.652: Their losses equal'd ours; and, for their slain,
11.653: With equal fires they fill'd the shining plain;
11.654: Why thus, unforc'd, should we so tamely yield,
11.655: And, ere the trumpet sounds, resign the field?
11.657: Appear by turns, as fortune shifts the scene:
11.658: Some, rais'd aloft, come tumbling down amain;
11.659: Then fall so hard, they bound and rise again.
11.660: If Diomede refuse his aid to lend,
11.661: The great Messapus yet remains our friend:
11.662: Tolumnius, who foretells events, is ours;
11.663: Th' Italian chiefs and princes join their pow'rs:
11.664: Nor least in number, nor in name the last,
11.665: Your own brave subjects have your cause embrac'd
11.666: Above the rest, the Volscian Amazon
11.667: Contains an army in herself alone,
11.668: And heads a squadron, terrible to sight,
11.669: With glitt'ring shields, in brazen armor bright.
11.670: Yet, if the foe a single fight demand,
11.671: And I alone the public peace withstand;
11.672: If you consent, he shall not be refus'd,
11.673: Nor find a hand to victory unus'd.
11.674: This new Achilles, let him take the field,
11.675: With fated armor, and Vulcanian shield!
11.676: For you, my royal father, and my fame,
11.677: I, Turnus, not the least of all my name,
11.678: Devote my soul. He calls me hand to hand,
11.679: And I alone will answer his demand.
11.680: Drances shall rest secure, and neither share
11.681: The danger, nor divide the prize of war."
11.682: While they debate, nor these nor those will yield,
11.683: Aeneas draws his forces to the field,
11.684: And moves his camp. The scouts with flying speed
11.685: Return, and thro' the frighted city spread
11.686: Th' unpleasing news, the Trojans are descried,
11.687: In battle marching by the river side,
11.688: And bending to the town. They take th' alarm:
11.689: Some tremble, some are bold; all in confusion arm.
11.690: Th' impetuous youth press forward to the field;
11.691: They clash the sword, and clatter on the shield:
11.692: The fearful matrons raise a screaming cry;
11.693: Old feeble men with fainter groans reply;
11.694: A jarring sound results, and mingles in the sky,
11.695: Like that of swans remurm'ring to the floods,
11.696: Or birds of diff'ring kinds in hollow woods.
11.697: Turnus th' occasion takes, and cries aloud:
11.698: "Talk on, ye quaint haranguers of the crowd:
11.699: Declaim in praise of peace, when danger calls,
11.700: And the fierce foes in arms approach the walls."
11.701: He said, and, turning short, with speedy pace,
11.702: Casts back a scornful glance, and quits the place:
11.704: To mount; and lead thyself our Ardean band.
11.705: Messapus and Catillus, post your force
11.706: Along the fields, to charge the Trojan horse.
11.707: Some guard the passes, others man the wall;
11.708: Drawn up in arms, the rest attend my call."
11.709: They swarm from ev'ry quarter of the town,
11.710: And with disorder'd haste the rampires crown.
11.711: Good old Latinus, when he saw, too late,
11.712: The gath'ring storm just breaking on the state,
11.713: Dismiss'd the council till a fitter time,
11.714: And own'd his easy temper as his crime,
11.715: Who, forc'd against his reason, had complied
11.716: To break the treaty for the promis'd bride.
11.717: Some help to sink new trenches; others aid
11.718: To ram the stones, or raise the palisade.
11.719: Hoarse trumpets sound th' alarm; around the walls
11.720: Runs a distracted crew, whom their last labor calls.
11.721: A sad procession in the streets is seen,
11.722: Of matrons, that attend the mother queen:
11.723: High in her chair she sits, and, at her side,
11.724: With downcast eyes, appears the fatal bride.
11.725: They mount the cliff, where Pallas' temple stands;
11.726: Pray'rs in their mouths, and presents in their hands,
11.727: With censers first they fume the sacred shrine,
11.728: Then in this common supplication join:
11.730: Propitious hear, and lend thy Latins aid!
11.731: Break short the pirate's lance; pronounce his fate,
11.732: And lay the Phrygian low before the gate."
11.733: Now Turnus arms for fight. His back and breast
11.734: Well-temper'd steel and scaly brass invest:
11.735: The cuishes which his brawny thighs infold
11.736: Are mingled metal damask'd o'er with gold.
11.737: His faithful fauchion sits upon his side;
11.738: Nor casque, nor crest, his manly features hide:
11.739: But, bare to view, amid surrounding friends,
11.740: With godlike grace, he from the tow'r descends.
11.741: Exulting in his strength, he seems to dare
11.742: His absent rival, and to promise war.
11.743: Freed from his keepers, thus, with broken reins,
11.744: The wanton courser prances o'er the plains,
11.745: Or in the pride of youth o'erleaps the mounds,
11.746: And snuffs the females in forbidden grounds.
11.747: Or seeks his wat'ring in the well-known flood,
11.748: To quench his thirst, and cool his fiery blood:
11.749: He swims luxuriant in the liquid plain,
11.750: And o'er his shoulder flows his waving mane:
11.751: He neighs, he snorts, he bears his head on high;
11.752: Before his ample chest the frothy waters fly.
11.753: Soon as the prince appears without the gate,
11.754: The Volscians, with their virgin leader, wait
11.755: His last commands. Then, with a graceful mien,
11.756: Lights from her lofty steed the warrior queen:
11.757: Her squadron imitates, and each descends;
11.758: Whose common suit Camilla thus commends:
11.759: "If sense of honor, if a soul secure
11.760: Of inborn worth, that can all tests endure,
11.761: Can promise aught, or on itself rely
11.762: Greatly to dare, to conquer or to die;
11.763: Then, I alone, sustain'd by these, will meet
11.764: The Tyrrhene troops, and promise their defeat.
11.765: Ours be the danger, ours the sole renown:
11.766: You, gen'ral, stay behind, and guard the town:"
11.767: Turnus a while stood mute, with glad surprise,
11.768: And on the fierce virago fix'd his eyes;
11.769: Then thus return'd: "O grace of Italy,
11.770: With what becoming thanks can I reply?
11.771: Not only words lie lab'ring in my breast,
11.772: But thought itself is by thy praise oppress'd.
11.773: Yet rob me not of all; but let me join
11.774: My toils, my hazard, and my fame, with thine.
11.775: The Trojan, not in stratagem unskill'd,
11.776: Sends his light horse before to scour the field:
11.777: Himself, thro' steep ascents and thorny brakes,
11.778: A larger compass to the city takes.
11.779: This news my scouts confirm, and I prepare
11.780: To foil his cunning, and his force to dare;
11.781: With chosen foot his passage to forelay,
11.782: And place an ambush in the winding way.
11.783: Thou, with thy Volscians, face the Tuscan horse;
11.784: The brave Messapus shall thy troops inforce
11.785: With those of Tibur, and the Latian band,
11.786: Subjected all to thy supreme command."
11.787: This said, he warns Messapus to the war,
11.788: Then ev'ry chief exhorts with equal care.
11.789: All thus encourag'd, his own troops he joins,
11.790: And hastes to prosecute his deep designs.
11.791: Inclos'd with hills, a winding valley lies,
11.792: By nature form'd for fraud, and fitted for surprise.
11.793: A narrow track, by human steps untrode,
11.794: Leads, thro' perplexing thorns, to this obscure
11.795: High o'er the vale a steepy mountain stands,

11.1246: The winged shaft, predestin'd for the deed;

11.1249: The bowstring touch'd her breast, so strong she
11.1250: Whizzing in air the fatal arrow flew.

11.1254: His flying friends to foreign fields bequeath.
11.1255: The conqu'ring damsel, with expanded wings,
11.1256: The welcome message to her mistress brings.
11.1257: Their leader lost, the Volscians quit the field,
11.1258: And, unsustain'd, the chiefs of Turnus yield.
11.1259: The frighted soldiers, when their captains fly,
11.1260: More on their speed than on their strength rely.
11.1261: Confus'd in flight, they bear each other down,

11.1263: Driv'n by their foes, and to their fears resign'd,
11.1264: Not once they turn, but take their wounds behind.
11.1265: These drop the shield, and those the lance forego,
11.1266: Or on their shoulders bear the slacken'd bow.
11.1267: The hoofs of horses, with a rattling sound,
11.1268: Beat short and thick, and shake the rotten ground.
11.1269: Black clouds of dust come rolling in the sky,
11.1270: And o'er the darken'd walls and rampires fly.

11.1272: Rend heav'n with female shrieks, and wring their
11.1273: All pressing on, pursuers and pursued,
11.1274: Are crush'd in crowds, a mingled multitude.
11.1275: Some happy few escape: the throng too late

11.1277: Ev'n in the sight of home, the wretched sire
11.1278: Looks on, and sees his helpless son expire.
11.1279: Then, in a fright, the folding gates they close,
11.1280: But leave their friends excluded with their foes.
11.1281: The vanquish'd cry; the victors loudly shout;
11.1282: 'T is terror all within, and slaughter all without.
11.1283: Blind in their fear, they bounce against the wall,
11.1284: Or, to the moats pursued, precipitate their fall.
11.1285: The Latian virgins, valiant with despair,
11.1286: Arm'd on the tow'rs, the common danger share:
11.1287: So much of zeal their country's cause inspir'd;
11.1288: So much Camilla's great example fir'd.
11.1289: Poles, sharpen'd in the flames, from high they throw,
11.1290: With imitated darts, to gall the foe.
11.1291: Their lives for godlike freedom they bequeath,
11.1292: And crowd each other to be first in death.
11.1293: Meantime to Turnus, ambush'd in the shade,
11.1294: With heavy tidings came th' unhappy maid:
11.1296: The foes, entirely masters of the field,
11.1297: Like a resistless flood, come rolling on:
11.1298: The cry goes off the plain, and thickens to the
11.1299: Inflam'd with rage, (for so the Furies fire
11.1300: The Daunian's breast, and so the Fates require,)
11.1301: He leaves the hilly pass, the woods in vain
11.1302: Possess'd, and downward issues on the plain.
11.1303: Scarce was he gone, when to the straits, now freed
11.1304: From secret foes, the Trojan troops succeed.
11.1305: Thro' the black forest and the ferny brake,
11.1306: Unknowingly secure, their way they take;
11.1307: From the rough mountains to the plain descend,
11.1308: And there, in order drawn, their line extend.
11.1309: Both armies now in open fields are seen;
11.1310: Nor far the distance of the space between.
11.1311: Both to the city bend. Aeneas sees,
11.1312: Thro' smoking fields, his hast'ning enemies;
11.1313: And Turnus views the Trojans in array,
11.1314: And hears th' approaching horses proudly neigh.
11.1315: Soon had their hosts in bloody battle join'd;
11.1316: But westward to the sea the sun declin'd.
11.1317: Intrench'd before the town both armies lie,
11.1318: While Night with sable wings involves the sky.

12.1: When Turnus saw the Latins leave the field,
12.2: Their armies broken, and their courage quell'd,
12.3: Himself become the mark of public spite,
12.4: His honor question'd for the promis'd fight;
12.5: The more he was with vulgar hate oppress'd,
12.6: The more his fury boil'd within his breast:
12.7: He rous'd his vigor for the last debate,
12.8: And rais'd his haughty soul to meet his fate.
12.9: As, when the swains the Libyan lion chase,
12.10: He makes a sour retreat, nor mends his pace;
12.11: But, if the pointed jav'lin pierce his side,
12.12: The lordly beast returns with double pride:
12.13: He wrenches out the steel, he roars for pain;
12.14: His sides he lashes, and erects his mane:
12.15: So Turnus fares; his eyeballs flash with fire,
12.16: Thro' his wide nostrils clouds of smoke expire.
12.17: Trembling with rage, around the court he ran,
12.18: At length approach'd the king, and thus began:
12.19: "No more excuses or delays: I stand
12.20: In arms prepar'd to combat, hand to hand,
12.21: This base deserter of his native land.
12.22: The Trojan, by his word, is bound to take
12.23: The same conditions which himself did make.
12.24: Renew the truce; the solemn rites prepare,
12.25: And to my single virtue trust the war.
12.26: The Latians unconcern'd shall see the fight;
12.27: This arm unaided shall assert your right:
12.28: Then, if my prostrate body press the plain,
12.29: To him the crown and beauteous bride remain."
12.30: To whom the king sedately thus replied:
12.31: "Brave youth, the more your valor has been tried,
12.32: The more becomes it us, with due respect,
12.33: To weigh the chance of war, which you neglect.
12.34: You want not wealth, or a successive throne,
12.35: Or cities which your arms have made your own:
12.36: My towns and treasures are at your command,
12.37: And stor'd with blooming beauties is my land;
12.38: Laurentum more than one Lavinia sees,
12.40: Now let me speak, and you with patience hear,
12.41: Things which perhaps may grate a lover's ear,
12.42: But sound advice, proceeding from a heart
12.43: Sincerely yours, and free from fraudful art.
12.44: The gods, by signs, have manifestly shown,
12.45: No prince Italian born should heir my throne:
12.46: Oft have our augurs, in prediction skill'd,
12.47: And oft our priests, foreign son reveal'd.
12.48: Yet, won by worth that cannot be withstood,
12.49: Brib'd by my kindness to my kindred blood,
12.50: Urg'd by my wife, who would not be denied,
12.51: I promis'd my Lavinia for your bride:
12.52: Her from her plighted lord by force I took;
12.53: All ties of treaties, and of honor, broke:
12.54: On your account I wag'd an impious war-
12.55: With what success, 't is needless to declare;
12.56: I and my subjects feel, and you have had your share.
12.57: Twice vanquish'd while in bloody fields we strive,
12.58: Scarce in our walls we keep our hopes alive:
12.59: The rolling flood runs warm with human gore;
12.60: The bones of Latians blanch the neighb'ring shore.
12.61: Why put I not an end to this debate,
12.62: Still unresolv'd, and still a slave to fate?
12.63: If Turnus' death a lasting peace can give,
12.64: Why should I not procure it whilst you live?
12.65: Should I to doubtful arms your youth betray,
12.66: What would my kinsmen the Rutulians say?
12.67: And, should you fall in fight, (which Heav'n defend!)
12.68: How curse the cause which hasten'd to his end
12.69: The daughter's lover and the father's friend?
12.70: Weigh in your mind the various chance of war;
12.71: Pity your parent's age, and ease his care."
12.72: Such balmy words he pour'd, but all in vain:
12.73: The proffer'd med'cine but provok'd the pain.
12.74: The wrathful youth, disdaining the relief,
12.75: With intermitting sobs thus vents his grief:
12.76: "The care, O best of fathers, which you take
12.77: For my concerns, at my desire forsake.
12.78: Permit me not to languish out my days,
12.79: But make the best exchange of life for praise.
12.80: This arm, this lance, can well dispute the prize;
12.81: And the blood follows, where the weapon flies.
12.82: His goddess mother is not near, to shroud
12.83: The flying coward with an empty cloud."
12.84: But now the queen, who fear'd for Turnus' life,
12.85: And loath'd the hard conditions of the strife,
12.86: Held him by force; and, dying in his death,
12.87: In these sad accents gave her sorrow breath:
12.88: "O Turnus, I adjure thee by these tears,
12.89: And whate'er price Amata's honor bears
12.90: Within thy breast, since thou art all my hope,
12.91: My sickly mind's repose, my sinking age's prop;
12.92: Since on the safety of thy life alone
12.93: Depends Latinus, and the Latian throne:
12.94: Refuse me not this one, this only pray'r,
12.95: To waive the combat, and pursue the war.
12.96: Whatever chance attends this fatal strife,
12.97: Think it includes, in thine, Amata's life.
12.98: I cannot live a slave, or see my throne
12.99: Usurp'd by strangers or a Trojan son."
12.100: At this, a flood of tears Lavinia shed;
12.101: A crimson blush her beauteous face o'erspread,
12.102: Varying her cheeks by turns with white and red.
12.103: The driving colors, never at a stay,
12.104: Run here and there, and flush, and fade away.
12.105: Delightful change! Thus Indian iv'ry shows,
12.106: Which with the bord'ring paint of purple glows;
12.107: Or lilies damask'd by the neighb'ring rose.
12.108: The lover gaz'd, and, burning with desire,
12.109: The more he look'd, the more he fed the fire:
12.110: Revenge, and jealous rage, and secret spite,
12.111: Roll in his breast, and rouse him to the fight.
12.112: Then fixing on the queen his ardent eyes,
12.113: Firm to his first intent, he thus replies:
12.114: "O mother, do not by your tears prepare
12.115: Such boding omens, and prejudge the war.
12.116: Resolv'd on fight, I am no longer free
12.117: To shun my death, if Heav'n my death decree."
12.118: Then turning to the herald, thus pursues:
12.119: "Go, greet the Trojan with ungrateful news;
12.120: Denounce from me, that, when to-morrow's light
12.121: Shall gild the heav'ns, he need not urge the fight;
12.122: The Trojan and Rutulian troops no more
12.123: Shall dye, with mutual blood, the Latian shore:
12.124: Our single swords the quarrel shall decide,
12.125: And to the victor be the beauteous bride."
12.126: He said, and striding on, with speedy pace,
12.127: He sought his coursers of the Thracian race.
12.128: At his approach they toss their heads on high,
12.130: The sires of these Orythia sent from far,
12.131: To grace Pilumnus, when he went to war.
12.132: The drifts of Thracian snows were scarce so white,
12.133: Nor northern winds in fleetness match'd their flight.
12.134: Officious grooms stand ready by his side;
12.135: And some with combs their flowing manes divide,
12.136: And others stroke their chests and gently soothe their
12.137: He sheath'd his limbs in arms; a temper'd mass
12.138: Of golden metal those, and mountain brass.
12.139: Then to his head his glitt'ring helm he tied,
12.140: And girt his faithful fauchion to his side.
12.141: In his Aetnaean forge, the God of Fire
12.142: That fauchion labor'd for the hero's sire;
12.143: Immortal keenness on the blade bestow'd,
12.144: And plung'd it hissing in the Stygian flood.
12.145: Propp'd on a pillar, which the ceiling bore,
12.146: Was plac'd the lance Auruncan Actor wore;
12.147: Which with such force he brandish'd in his hand,
12.148: The tough ash trembled like an osier wand:
12.149: Then cried: "O pond'rous spoil of Actor slain,
12.150: And never yet by Turnus toss'd in vain,
12.151: Fail not this day thy wonted force; but go,
12.152: Sent by this hand, to pierce the Trojan foe!
12.153: Give me to tear his corslet from his breast,
12.154: And from that eunuch head to rend the crest;
12.155: Dragg'd in the dust, his frizzled hair to soil,
12.156: Hot from the vexing ir'n, and smear'd with fragrant
12.157: Thus while he raves, from his wide nostrils flies
12.158: A fiery steam, and sparkles from his eyes.
12.159: So fares the bull in his lov'd female's sight:
12.160: Proudly he bellows, and preludes the fight;
12.161: He tries his goring horns against a tree,
12.163: He pushes at the winds; he digs the strand
12.164: With his black hoofs, and spurns the yellow sand.
12.165: Nor less the Trojan, in his Lemnian arms,
12.166: To future fight his manly courage warms:
12.167: He whets his fury, and with joy prepares
12.168: To terminate at once the ling'ring wars;
12.169: To cheer his chiefs and tender son, relates
12.170: What Heav'n had promis'd, and expounds the fates.
12.171: Then to the Latian king he sends, to cease
12.172: The rage of arms, and ratify the peace.
12.173: The morn ensuing, from the mountain's height,
12.174: Had scarcely spread the skies with rosy light;
12.175: Th' ethereal coursers, bounding from the sea,
12.176: From out their flaming nostrils breath'd the day;
12.177: When now the Trojan and Rutulian guard,
12.178: In friendly labor join'd, the list prepar'd.
12.179: Beneath the walls they measure out the space;
12.180: Then sacred altars rear, on sods of grass,
12.181: Where, with religious their common gods they place.
12.182: In purest white the priests their heads attire;
12.183: And living waters bear, and holy fire;
12.184: And, o'er their linen hoods and shaded hair,
12.185: Long twisted wreaths of sacred veryain wear,
12.186: In order issuing from the town appears
12.187: The Latin legion, arm'd with pointed spears;
12.188: And from the fields, advancing on a line,
12.189: The Trojan and the Tuscan forces join:
12.190: Their various arms afford a pleasing sight;
12.191: A peaceful train they seem, in peace prepar'd for
12.192: Betwixt the ranks the proud commanders ride,
12.193: Glitt'ring with gold, and vests in purple dyed;
12.194: Here Mnestheus, author of the Memmian line,
12.195: And there Messapus, born of seed divine.
12.196: The sign is giv'n; and, round the listed space,
12.197: Each man in order fills his proper place.
12.198: Reclining on their ample shields, they stand,
12.199: And fix their pointed lances in the sand.
12.200: Now, studious of the sight, a num'rous throng
12.201: Of either sex promiscuous, old and young,
12.202: Swarm the town: by those who rest behind,
12.203: The gates and walls and houses' tops are lin'd.
12.204: Meantime the Queen of Heav'n beheld the sight,
12.205: With eyes unpleas'd, from Mount Albano's height
12.207: But then an empty hill, without a name).
12.208: She thence survey'd the field, the Trojan pow'rs,
12.209: The Latian squadrons, and Laurentine tow'rs.
12.210: Then thus the goddess of the skies bespoke,
12.211: With sighs and tears, the goddess of the lake,
12.212: King Turnus' sister, once a lovely maid,
12.213: Ere to the lust of lawless Jove betray'd:
12.214: Compress'd by force, but, by the grateful god,
12.215: Now made the Nais of the neighb'ring flood.
12.216: "O nymph, the pride of living lakes," said she,
12.217: "O most renown'd, and most belov'd by me,
12.218: Long hast thou known, nor need I to record,
12.219: The wanton sallies of my wand'ring lord.
12.220: Of ev'ry Latian fair whom Jove misled
12.221: To mount by stealth my violated bed,
12.222: To thee alone I grudg'd not his embrace,
12.223: But gave a part of heav'n, and an unenvied place.
12.224: Now learn from me thy near approaching grief,
12.225: Nor think my wishes want to thy relief.
12.226: While fortune favor'd, nor Heav'n's King denied
12.227: To lend my succor to the Latian side,
12.228: I sav'd thy brother, and the sinking state:
12.229: But now he struggles with unequal fate,
12.230: And goes, with gods averse, o'ermatch'd in might,
12.231: To meet inevitable death in fight;
12.232: Nor must I break the truce, nor can sustain the
12.233: Thou, if thou dar'st thy present aid supply;
12.234: It well becomes a sister's care to try."
12.235: At this the lovely nymph, with grief oppress'd,
12.236: Thrice tore her hair, and beat her comely breast.
12.237: To whom Saturnia thus: "Thy tears are late:
12.238: Haste, snatch him, if he can be snatch'd from fate:
12.239: New tumults kindle; violate the truce:
12.240: Who knows what changeful fortune may produce?
12.241: 'T is not a crime t' attempt what I decree;
12.242: Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me."
12.243: She said, and, sailing on the winged wind,
12.244: Left the sad nymph suspended in her mind.
12.245: And now pomp the peaceful kings appear:
12.246: Four steeds the chariot of Latinus bear;
12.247: Twelve golden beams around his temples play,
12.248: To mark his lineage from the God of Day.
12.249: Two snowy coursers Turnus' chariot yoke,
12.250: And in his hand two massy spears he shook:
12.251: Then issued from the camp, in arms divine,
12.252: Aeneas, author of the Roman line;
12.253: And by his side Ascanius took his place,
12.254: The second hope of Rome's immortal race.
12.255: Adorn'd in white, a rev'rend priest appears,
12.256: And off'rings to the flaming altars bears;
12.257: A porket, and a lamb that never suffer'd shears.
12.258: Then to the rising sun he turns his eyes,
12.259: And strews the beasts, design'd for sacrifice,
12.260: With salt and meal: with like officious care
12.261: He marks their foreheads, and he clips their hair.
12.262: Betwixt their horns the purple wine he sheds;
12.263: With the same gen'rous juice the flame he feeds.
12.264: Aeneas then unsheath'd his shining sword,
12.265: And thus with pious pray'rs the gods ador'd:
12.267: For which I have sustain'd so long a toil,
12.268: Thou, King of Heav'n, and thou, the Queen of Air,
12.269: Propitious now, and reconcil'd by pray'r;
12.270: Thou, God of War, whose unresisted sway
12.271: The labors and events of arms obey;
12.272: Ye living fountains, and ye running floods,
12.273: All pow'rs of ocean, all ethereal gods,
12.274: Hear, and bear record: if I fall in field,
12.275: Or, recreant in the fight, to Turnus yield,
12.276: My Trojans shall encrease Evander's town;
12.277: Ascanius shall renounce th' Ausonian crown:
12.278: All claims, all questions of debate, shall cease;
12.279: Nor he, nor they, with force infringe the peace.
12.280: But, if my juster arms prevail in fight,
12.281: (As sure they shall, if I divine aright,)
12.282: My Trojans shall not o'er th' Italians reign:
12.283: Both equal, both unconquer'd shall remain,
12.284: Join'd in their laws, their lands, and their abodes;
12.285: I ask but altars for my weary gods.
12.286: The care of those religious rites be mine;
12.287: The crown to King Latinus I resign:
12.288: His be the sov'reign sway. Nor will I share
12.289: His pow'r in peace, or his command in war.
12.290: For me, my friends another town shall frame,
12.291: And bless the rising tow'rs with fair Lavinia's
12.292: Thus he. Then, with erected eyes and hands,
12.293: The Latian king before his altar stands.
12.294: "By the same heav'n," said he, "and earth, and main,
12.295: And all the pow'rs that all the three contain;
12.296: By hell below, and by that upper god
12.297: Whose thunder signs the peace, who seals it with his
12.298: So let Latona's double offspring hear,
12.299: And double-fronted Janus, what I swear:
12.300: I touch the sacred altars, touch the flames,
12.301: And all those pow'rs attest, and all their names;
12.302: Whatever chance befall on either side,
12.303: No term of time this union shall divide:
12.304: No force, no fortune, shall my vows unbind,
12.305: Or shake the steadfast tenor of my mind;
12.306: Not tho' the circling seas should break their bound,
12.307: O'erflow the shores, or sap the solid ground;
12.308: Not tho' the lamps of heav'n their spheres forsake,
12.309: Hurl'd down, and hissing in the nether lake:
12.310: Ev'n as this royal scepter" (for he bore
12.311: A scepter in his hand) "shall never more
12.312: Shoot out in branches, or renew the birth:
12.313: An orphan now, cut from the mother earth
12.314: By the keen ax, dishonor'd of its hair,
12.315: And cas'd in brass, for Latian kings to bear."
12.316: When thus in public view the peace was tied
12.317: With solemn vows, and sworn on either side,
12.318: All dues perform'd which holy rites require;
12.319: The victim beasts are slain before the fire,
12.320: The trembling entrails from their bodies torn,
12.321: And to the fatten'd flames in chargers borne.
12.322: Already the Rutulians deem their man
12.323: O'ermatch'd in arms, before the fight began.
12.324: First rising fears are whisper'd thro' the crowd;
12.325: Then, gath'ring sound, they murmur more aloud.
12.326: Now, side to side, they measure with their eyes
12.327: The champions' bulk, their sinews, and their size:
12.328: The nearer they approach, the more is known
12.329: Th' apparent disadvantage of their own.
12.330: Turnus himself appears in public sight
12.331: Conscious of fate, desponding of the fight.
12.332: Slowly he moves, and at his altar stands
12.333: With eyes dejected, and with trembling hands;
12.334: And, while he mutters undistinguish'd pray'rs,
12.335: A livid deadness in his cheeks appears.
12.336: With anxious pleasure when Juturna view'd
12.337: Th' increasing fright of the mad multitude,
12.338: When their short sighs and thick'ning sobs she heard,
12.339: And found their ready minds for change prepar'd;
12.340: Dissembling her immortal form, she took
12.341: Camertus' mien, his habit, and his look;
12.342: A chief of ancient blood; in arms well known
12.343: Was his great sire, and he his greater son.
12.344: His shape assum'd, amid the ranks she ran,
12.345: And humoring their first motions, thus began:
12.346: "For shame, Rutulians, can you bear the sight
12.347: Of one expos'd for all, in single fight?
12.348: Can we, before the face of heav'n, confess
12.349: Our courage colder, or our numbers less?
12.350: View all the Trojan host, th' Arcadian band,
12.351: And Tuscan army; count 'em as they stand:
12.352: Undaunted to the battle if we go,
12.353: Scarce ev'ry second man will share a foe.
12.354: Turnus, 't is true, in this unequal strife,
12.355: Shall lose, with honor, his devoted life,
12.356: Or change it rather for immortal fame,
12.357: Succeeding to the gods, from whence he came:
12.358: But you, a servile and inglorious band,
12.359: For foreign lords shall sow your native land,
12.360: Those fruitful fields your fighting fathers gain'd,
12.361: Which have so long their lazy sons sustain'd."
12.362: With words like these, she carried her design:
12.363: A rising murmur runs along the line.
12.364: Then ev'n the city troops, and Latians, tir'd
12.365: With tedious war, seem with new souls inspir'd:
12.366: Their champion's fate with pity they lament,
12.367: And of the league, so lately sworn, repent.
12.368: Nor fails the goddess to foment the rage
12.369: With lying wonders, and a false presage;
12.370: But adds a sign, which, present to their eyes,
12.371: Inspires new courage, and a glad surprise.
12.372: For, sudden, in the fiery tracts above,
12.373: Appears in pomp th' imperial bird of Jove:
12.374: A plump of fowl he spies, that swim the lakes,
12.375: And o'er their heads his sounding pinions shakes;
12.376: Then, stooping on the fairest of the train,
12.377: In his strong talons truss'd a silver swan.
12.378: Th' Italians wonder at th' unusual sight;
12.379: But, while he lags, and labors in his flight,
12.380: Behold, the dastard fowl return anew,
12.381: And with united force the foe pursue:
12.382: Clam'rous around the royal hawk they fly,
12.383: And, thick'ning in a cloud, o'ershade the sky.
12.384: They cuff, they scratch, they cross his airy course;
12.385: Nor can th' incumber'd bird sustain their force;
12.386: But vex'd, not vanquish'd, drops the pond'rous prey,
12.387: And, lighten'd of his burthen, wings his way.
12.388: Th' Ausonian bands with shouts salute the sight,
12.389: Eager of action, and demand the fight.
12.390: Then King Tolumnius, vers'd in augurs' arts,
12.391: Cries out, and thus his boasted skill imparts:
12.392: "At length 't is granted, what I long desir'd!
12.393: This, this is what my frequent vows requir'd.

12.1320: All force of arms and points of art employ'd,
12.1321: The Fury flew athwart, and made th' endeavor void.
12.1322: A thousand various thoughts his soul confound;
12.1323: He star'd about, nor aid nor issue found;
12.1324: His own men stop the pass, and his own walls surround.
12.1325: Once more he pauses, and looks out again,
12.1326: And seeks the goddess charioteer in vain.
12.1327: Trembling he views the thund'ring chief advance,
12.1328: And brandishing aloft the deadly lance:
12.1329: Amaz'd he cow'rs beneath his conqu'ring foe,
12.1330: Forgets to ward, and waits the coming blow.
12.1331: Astonish'd while he stands, and fix'd with fear,
12.1332: Aim'd at his shield he sees th' impending spear.
12.1333: The hero measur'd first, with narrow view,
12.1334: The destin'd mark; and, rising as he threw,
12.1335: With its full swing the fatal weapon flew.
12.1336: Not with less rage the rattling thunder falls,
12.1337: Or stones from batt'ring-engines break the walls:
12.1338: Swift as a whirlwind, from an arm so strong,
12.1339: The lance drove on, and bore the death along.
12.1340: Naught could his sev'nfold shield the prince avail,
12.1341: Nor aught, beneath his arms, the coat of mail:
12.1342: It pierc'd thro' all, and with a grisly wound
12.1343: Transfix'd his thigh, and doubled him to ground.
12.1344: With groans the Latins rend the vaulted sky:
12.1345: Woods, hills, and valleys, to the voice reply.
12.1346: Now low on earth the lofty chief is laid,
12.1347: With eyes cast upward, and with arms display'd,
12.1348: And, recreant, thus to the proud victor pray'd:
12.1349: "I know my death deserv'd, nor hope to live:
12.1350: Use what the gods and thy good fortune give.
12.1351: Yet think, O think, if mercy may be shown-
12.1352: Thou hadst a father once, and hast a son-
12.1353: Pity my sire, now sinking to the grave;
12.1354: And for Anchises' sake old Daunus save!
12.1355: Or, if thy vow'd revenge pursue my death,
12.1356: Give to my friends my body void of breath!
12.1357: The Latian chiefs have seen me beg my life;
12.1358: Thine is the conquest, thine the royal wife:
12.1359: Against a yielded man, 't is mean ignoble strife."
12.1360: In deep suspense the Trojan seem'd to stand,
12.1361: And, just prepar'd to strike, repress'd his hand.
12.1362: He roll'd his eyes, and ev'ry moment felt
12.1363: His manly soul with more compassion melt;
12.1364: When, casting down a casual glance, he spied
12.1365: The golden belt that glitter'd on his side,
12.1366: The fatal spoils which haughty Turnus tore
12.1367: From dying Pallas, and in triumph wore.
12.1368: Then, rous'd anew to wrath, he loudly cries
12.1369: (Flames, while he spoke, came flashing from his
12.1370: "Traitor, dost thou, dost thou to grace pretend,
12.1371: Clad, as thou art, in trophies of my friend?
12.1372: To his sad soul a grateful off'ring go!
12.1373: 'T is Pallas, Pallas gives this deadly blow."
12.1374: He rais'd his arm aloft, and, at the word,
12.1375: Deep in his bosom drove the shining sword.
12.1376: The streaming blood distain'd his arms around,
12.1377: And the disdainful soul came rushing thro' the wound.
